papers.title: Concurrent Pericardial Effusion Leading to Cardiac Tamponade as the Initial Manifestation of Multicentric Lymphoma in a Dog.
papers.authors: Pereira DS, Bezerra GAP, Viana DC, Santos DLD
papers.abstract: Multicentric lymphoma is one of the most common haematopoietic neoplasms in dogs and may present with variable systemic and cardiothoracic manifestations. This report describes a case of multicentric lymphoma in an 8-year-old mixed-breed dog presenting with severe respiratory distress associated with concurrent pleural and pericardial effusions leading to cardiac tamponade. Clinical investigation included thoracic radiography, abdominal ultrasonography, echocardiography, electrocardiography and cytological evaluation of pericardial fluid. Imaging examinations revealed marked cardiomegaly, hepatomegaly, splenic mass and significant thoracic effusions associated with cardiopulmonary compromise. Pericardiocentesis was performed as both therapeutic and diagnostic procedure, allowing temporary haemodynamic stabilization and cytological identification of malignant lymphoid proliferation compatible with multicentric lymphoma. Despite supportive treatment and transient clinical improvement, rapid recurrence of respiratory signs resulted in death. This report highlights the clinical importance of recognizing concurrent thoracic effusions as potential indicators of advanced systemic neoplasia in dogs. The case emphasizes the value of rapid multimodal diagnostic investigation, particularly the integration of imaging techniques and cavitary fluid cytology, in the management of critically ill patients with suspected neoplastic thoracic disease.

papers.title: Effect of pimobendan on right-heart remodeling in dogs with tricuspid valve dysplasia: an exploratory study.
papers.authors: Abbott-Johnson K, Potter B, Visser L, Scansen BA, Arai S
papers.abstract: Tricuspid valve dysplasia (TVD) is a rare congenital heart defect in dogs often resulting in severe tricuspid valve regurgitation (TR). No guidelines for medical therapy have been established for dogs with severe TR. Tricuspid valve repair surgery is available for dogs but carries a moderate risk and high cost. This exploratory study evaluated the effect of oral pimobendan on chamber sizes and remodeling of the right side of the heart in dogs with TVD. Retrospective echocardiographic data from ten dogs with TVD and severe TR were retrieved. All dogs received oral pimobendan (range 0.21-0.31 mg/kg Q12h) for an average of 18 months (range 3-41). The right atrial (RA) diameter, RA area, right ventricular (RV) diameter, RV area and fractional area change, tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), and dimension of the tricuspid valve annulus (TVA) were quantified, and compared before and at a median of 3 months after starting pimobendan therapy. All dogs had severe TR. The normalized RV diameter and TVA decreased after pimobendan administration [1.40 → 1.27 (SD 0.23), p  = 0.027; 11.77 → 10.58 (SD 1.95), p  = 0.01]. No significant changes in RA area, RA diameter, RV area, TAPSE, peak TR velocity, or RV fractional area change were present after pimobendan therapy (all p  > 0.08). No dogs in this study population progressed to right-sided congestive heart failure during the follow-up period. Pimobendan reduced the size of the right ventricle and diameter of the tricuspid annulus compared to baseline, which may limit progression of disease in dogs with TVD with severe TR.

papers.title: Association between lipid profile alterations and azotemia severity in dogs: a cross-sectional study.
papers.authors: Bhardwaj H, Behera A, Kumar A, Singh VK, Bhatt S, Mandal RS, Tiwary R, Kumar R, Singh GD, Kumar D, Kumar K, Kaushik P, Siddique RA, Kumar P, Shekhar P
papers.abstract: Renal dysfunction in dogs is accompanied by metabolic and biochemical disturbances, including dyslipidemia. However, information on the relationship between lipid abnormalities and azotemia severity remains limited. This study evaluated lipid profile alterations and their association with biochemical and hematological parameters in azotemic dogs. Clinical and laboratory records of 100 dogs presented to the Teaching Veterinary Clinical Complex, Bihar Veterinary College, Patna, India, between April 2024 and March 2025 were retrospectively evaluated. The study included 50 healthy and 50 azotemic dogs with serum creatinine >1.7 mg/dl. Azotemic dogs were categorized as Group 1 (1.7- <5.0 mg/dl; n = 17), Group 2 (5.0-15.0 mg/dl; n = 23), and Group 3 (>15.0 mg/dl; n = 10). Hematological, renal, electrolyte, hepatic-associated biochemical, and lipid parameters were evaluated. Data were expressed as median (interquartile range). Group differences were assessed using the Kruskal-Wallis H test followed by Dunn's post-hoc test with Bonferroni correction. Associations were evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (ρ), with p < 0.05 considered significant. Compared with healthy dogs, azotemic dogs had lower hemoglobin and hematocrit and higher blood urea nitrogen, potassium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, and total bilirubin concentrations. Albumin was significantly lower in Groups 2 and 3. Cholesterol, triglycerides, and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) were significantly higher in all azotemia groups than in healthy controls, whereas high-density lipoprotein did not differ significantly. However, cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL did not differ significantly among azotemia groups, indicating no stepwise increase with creatinine-defined severity. In the overall azotemic population, creatinine correlated positively with cholesterol (ρ = 0.393, p < 0.001), triglycerides (ρ = 0.265, p = 0.008), and LDL (ρ = 0.457, p < 0.001). Blood urea nitrogen correlated positively with cholesterol (ρ = 0.455, p < 0.001) and LDL (ρ = 0.571, p < 0.001). Azotemia in dogs is associated with dyslipidemia and broader systemic biochemical alterations. Although cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL were increased in azotemic dogs, they did not progressively increase across creatinine-defined categories. Lipid profiling may therefore serve as an adjunct to metabolic evaluation, while longitudinal studies incorporating additional renal biomarkers are warranted.

papers.title: Efficacy and safety of atinvicitinib and oclacitinib in the control of pruritus in canine allergic dermatitis: a randomized, examiner-masked, positive-controlled multicenter clinical trial.
papers.authors: Heinau LK, Zschiesche E, Hakala M, Kavrik D, Hala P, de Oliveira AD, Suckstorff O, Horspool L, Kuhlmann I
papers.abstract: Atinvicitinib is a Janus kinase 1-selective-inhibitor approved for the treatment of pruritus associated with allergic dermatitis, including canine atopic dermatitis (cAD). An examiner-masked, randomized study assessed safety and clinical improvement in pruritus and dermatitis severity in dogs with allergic dermatitis following treatment with atinvicitinib (Numelvi ® tablets, MSD Animal Health) or oclacitinib (Apoquel ® chewable tablets, Zoetis). Client-owned dogs (n = 69) with allergic dermatitis and a pruritus visual analog scale (PVAS) score ≥ 6 were enrolled at nine veterinary clinics in Portugal and Spain and treated with either atinvicitinib (0.8-1.2 mg/kg once daily with food, n = 34) or oclacitinib (0.4-0.6 mg/kg, with or without food, twice daily for 14 days then once daily, n = 35) for 28 (± 1) days. Safety was assessed based on adverse event (AE) reporting. Owners assessed PVAS on day (D) 0, 7, 14, 21 and 28, including overall response to treatment (ORTT-VAS) on D28. Veterinarians performed physical examinations and dermatitis VAS score (DVAS) on D0 and 28. Efficacy was evaluated as the percentage reduction in PVAS and DVAS from baseline. A dynamic longitudinal model was used to compare effectiveness between groups. On D28, 70% atinvicitinib- and 65% oclacitinib-treated dogs had PVAS < 2 (normal). Dynamic longitudinal modelling showed that pruritus reduction after 28 days of atinvicitinib was non-inferior to that with oclacitinib at label doses. There was a 74% reduction in DVAS in both treatments by D28. All of the few AEs observed were consistent with approved product information. Atinvicitinib once daily with food is safe and effective in reducing pruritus and dermatitis severity in dogs with allergic dermatitis.

papers.title: Immediate behavioural outcomes of owner-delivered support during novel object exposure in dogs.
papers.authors: Miller J, Cavalli C, Azadian A, Protopopova A
papers.abstract: Fearfulness is one of the most common behavioural concerns in domestic dogs, which can be observed in response to a wide range of stimuli, including sudden noises and novel objects. Because fear responses can adversely affect welfare, identifying effective ways to reduce fear is important. Given that dogs are highly responsive to human social cues, owner behaviour in the presence of a stressor may influence dogs' responses. This study investigated the effects of typical owner-delivered support strategies on dogs' behaviour and stress levels during exposure to a novel object. A survey was first conducted to identify the strategies that owners perceived as most useful and reported using most frequently. Subsequently, 48 dog-owner dyads were quasi-randomly allocated to one of four conditions: calming (petting the dog and speaking in a soothing voice), approach (approaching the object and verbally encouraging the dog), treats (offering food), or control (remaining passive). First, owners applied the assigned strategy during a 1 min presentation of a remote-controlled car (Phase 1). To assess maintenance effects, the car was presented again, but all owners remained passive (Phase 2). Measures included stress-related body language, holistic stress scores, affiliative behaviours, and object-directed behaviours. Exploring the object and encouraging the dog to do the same was rated as useful by the highest proportion of owners, while the lowest proportion of owners considered ignoring the dog as a useful strategy. During the in-person experiment dogs in all experimental conditions gazed at the owner more than controls. Dogs in the approach group spent more time in proximity to the object and showed higher holistic stress scores in the first phase than in the second phase. None of the owner-delivered strategies reliably reduced stress-related behaviour versus passive control in this setting. Owner actions mainly influenced the dogs' social behaviours and proximity to the object. Given the mild stressor and brief exposure, future experiments using repeated pairings may be needed to clarify the effectiveness of these techniques.

papers.title: Cystic clear cell thymoma in a cat: clinical, imaging, anatomopathological and immunohistochemical findings.
papers.authors: Maia LVP, Serakides R, Pastor FM, de Oliveira LED, Ferrante B, de Souza AM, Nepomuceno AC
papers.abstract: Thymomas are uncommon thymic epithelial neoplasms in cats and may present uncommon histological variants, such as cystic clear cell thymoma. The aim of this case report was to describe the clinical, imaging, anatomopathological, and immunohistochemical findings of a cystic clear cell thymoma in a four-year-old mixed-breed female cat presented with anorexia and progressive dyspnea. Imaging examinations revealed a large heterogeneous mediastinal mass with cystic components, accompanied by pleural effusion and pulmonary compression. Ultrasound-guided cytology was inconclusive. Despite intensive supportive care, the patient died due to respiratory failure. Necropsy revealed a large mediastinal mass occupying approximately 70-80% of the thoracic cavity, accompanied by compressive pulmonary atelectasis and hydrothorax. Histologically, the neoplasm was predominantly composed of carbohydrate-rich clear epithelial cells accompanied by cystic structures, scattered mature lymphocytes and rare Hassall's corpuscles. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong nuclear expression of p40, p63 and CKAE1/AE3 in the neoplastic cells, whereas CD3 labeling was restricted to non-neoplastic lymphocytes, supporting the diagnosis of cystic clear cell thymoma. This report expands the current knowledge of this rare tumor variant in cats and highlights the importance of imaging examinations, histopathology, and immunohistochemistry for establishing a definitive diagnosis.

papers.title: Investigation of the Bacterial Flora of External Reproductive System in Female and Male Stray Cats.
papers.authors: Garoussi MT, Sheibani N, Zahraei TS, Malmasi AA
papers.abstract: Various infectious agents can infect the reproductive system. This study aimed to analyse the status of bacterial flora at external parts of reproductive system of female and male stray cats which may affect recognizing of healthcare risks and transfer of pathogens from animals to the human and public health. Totally, 116 samples of male (no. 54, 46.55%) and female (no. 62, 53.44%) cats without owners were taken from external organs of reproductive system (included penis and prepuce, vagina and vulva, respectively) using sterilized swab. The extracted swabs were cultured in appropriate media. Morphological and biochemical tests were conducted on isolates to determine the microorganism (no. 335 out of 696 cultures, 48.13%). In total, 21 isolates were determined. Escherichia coli (40.59%) was the most prevalent. A significant relationship was observed among the age of animals (1-2 years) and rate of infection (p < 0.05). However, there was no significant relationship between weight and infected animals (p > 0.05). It was concluded that female and male stray cats with different ages and various weights can be infected by bacterial agents, which could have endogenous or environmental origin. Most of the bacterial infections of reproductive system are created by endogenous microflora with the presence of susceptive factors. It may be a risk factor for human sanitation.

papers.title: Suspected Anaphylactoid Reaction Induced by Intravenous Propofol Administration in a Dog.
papers.authors: Marangoni M, Marques ALR, Cordeiro HV, Dalmolin F, Benvegnú DM, Braz PH, Santos PS, Freitas GC, Champion T
papers.abstract: This report describes a case of suspected peri-induction hypersensitivity reaction associated with propofol administration in a dog. A 14-month-old female Shih-Tzu underwent anaesthetic induction with propofol and lidocaine for elective ovariohysterectomy. Shortly after induction, the patient developed severe hypotension refractory to fluid therapy and dobutamine, followed by cardiopulmonary arrest. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was successfully performed. Post-resuscitation findings included marked gallbladder wall thickening and transient free peritoneal fluid on ultrasonography, as well as a marked increase in alanine aminotransferase activity. Supportive care, including vasopressor therapy and corticosteroid administration, resulted in progressive hemodynamic and biochemical recovery. A suspected hypersensitivity reaction temporally associated with anaesthetic induction was considered the most likely differential diagnosis. However, alternative mechanisms such as post-arrest hypoperfusion and venous congestion could not be excluded. This report highlights the diagnostic challenges in distinguishing hypersensitivity reactions from other causes of acute hemodynamic instability.

papers.title: Innate and adaptive immunity in diseases of dogs and cats associated with Candida spp., Malassezia spp. and Cryptococcus spp.: a critical review.
papers.authors: Łagowski D, Wykrętowicz K, Krawczak A, Dors A, Pomorska-Mól M
papers.abstract: The interactions between hosts and Malassezia spp., Candida spp., and Cryptococcus spp. can cause infections in dogs and cats and are associated with colonisation, overgrowth, hypersensitivity reactions, and localised or invasive disease. This review examines the roles and importance of innate and adaptive immunity in infections caused by these fungi. Focusing mostly on canine and feline literature, experimental literature was considered when lacking. In Malassezia-associated disease, serum antibody concentrations have not consistently reflected clinical activity, while experimental studies indicate that fungal control and inflammatory damage are not necessarily coupled. In candidiasis, the importance of epithelial immunity, neutrophils, and other phagocytes varies by site of infection, and most mechanistic data are derived from C. albicans. In cryptococcosis, experiments show that phagocytes suppress fungal proliferation and provide an intracellular niche for them. The role of each mechanism depends on infection site and clinical form of the disease. There is limited literature on veterinary immunotherapy, including allergen-specific immunotherapy for hypersensitivity to Malassezia spp. Vaccine-, cytokine-, and immune-checkpoint-based therapies have mostly been tested experimentally. In animal infections, especially in dogs and cats, correlations have been reported for the mechanisms discussed. One of the biggest gaps in the literature is the lack of studies linking these mechanisms to disease course, recurrence, fungal clearance, and treatment efficacy.

papers.title: Presumed vitamin K-dependent coagulopathy secondary to low-grade alimentary lymphoma in a cat.
papers.authors: Harlow HY, Frederick SW, Chapman PS
papers.abstract: A 10-year-old, male castrated domestic shorthair cat was evaluated for a 1-year history of progressive small bowel diarrhea, vomiting, and significant weight loss despite a good appetite. Diagnostic evaluation included an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, after which the cat developed severe anemia due to gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Coagulation testing revealed prolonged prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time with decreased factor VII activity. The cat had no access to the outdoors and no rodenticide was kept in the home. Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy and liver dysfunction were ruled out. Endoscopic biopsies were consistent with low-grade alimentary lymphoma. This, in combination with clinical support for malabsorptive disease, suggested vitamin K malabsorption as the underlying cause for the cat's coagulopathy. Despite aggressive critical care with vitamin K supplementation and packed red cell and plasma transfusions, the cat developed complications and ultimately humane euthanasia was elected. This case highlights suspected malabsorptive vitamin K-deficient coagulopathy secondary to chronic gastrointestinal disease in a cat. Coagulopathy screening or pre-treatment with vitamin K may be warranted before endoscopic gastrointestinal biopsies in these cases.

papers.title: Surgical management of proximal tibial caudal angulation deformity in a cat with cranial cruciate ligament rupture.
papers.authors: Arai K, Yogo S, Ueda K, Miyazaki M, Sakai O, Yoshitake R, Matsuda A
papers.abstract: A 5-year-old, neutered male Bengal cat presented with right hindlimb lameness after being accidentally stepped on by the owner. Orthopaedic and radiographic examination revealed right cranial cruciate ligament rupture. Furthermore, bilateral proximal tibial caudal angulation deformity resulted in a right and left tibial plateau angle (TPA) of 59.4° and 59.3°, respectively, and a right and left anatomical-mechanical axis (AMA) angle of 10.9° and 10.6°, which exceeded normal values (mean TPA: 23.4°; mean AMA angle: 6.5°). The abnormal right angles and tibial caudal angulation deformity were subsequently corrected via modified cranial closing wedge osteotomy. Because the planned postoperative TPA was high (29.7°), a lateral fabellotibial suture was concurrently performed to further stabilise the stifle joint. Lameness improved immediately within the postoperative period, and limb function normalised at 3 months. This case report describes a novel surgical strategy, guided by TPA and AMA assessment, for the management of a rare case of proximal tibial caudal angulation deformity concurrent with cranial cruciate ligament rupture in a cat.

papers.title: Extrahepatic biliary obstruction secondary to right-sided diaphragmatic hernia in a juvenile cat.
papers.authors: Chevalier L, Mouroz E, Dunham O, Giberto L, François C, Noël S
papers.abstract: A 10-month-old, spayed female European Shorthair cat was presented for a 3-week history of progressive vomiting, lethargy and hyporexia. Complete blood count was unremarkable, while serum biochemistry revealed increased alanine aminotransferase, gamma-glutamyl transferase and total bilirubin at the upper limit of the reference interval. Physical examination identified mild dehydration and marked cranial abdominal distension. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated gastric atony, severe intra- and extrahepatic biliary duct dilatation, a distended gallbladder and focal duodenal dilatation at the expected location of the major duodenal papilla, with a hyperechoic interface producing distal acoustic shadowing, raising suspicion of a duodenal foreign body causing papillary obstruction. Emergency exploratory laparotomy revealed a right-sided dorsolateral circumferential diaphragmatic hernia containing the proximal descending duodenum, pancreas and omentum. Reduction of the herniated viscera and herniorrhaphy were performed, and biliary decompression was achieved by gentle gallbladder expression alone. A history of blunt trauma was reported only after surgery, supporting a chronic, presumptively traumatic hernia. The postoperative course was complicated by the development of cervicothoracic subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum and a small pneumothorax, which were managed conservatively. The cat's appetite returned, and she was discharged 3 days postoperatively with residual subcutaneous emphysema. At 1 and 5 months postoperatively, the owner reported no gastrointestinal or respiratory signs. This report describes an unusual cause of feline extrahepatic biliary obstruction secondary to a chronic, presumptively traumatic diaphragmatic herniation, resulting in mechanical obstruction at the level of the major duodenal papilla. Recognition of this rare mechanism may help prevent misdiagnosis as primary hepatobiliary disease.

papers.title: Deep Fibromucinous Disease With Features of Scleromyxedema in a Dog Managed With Leflunomide.
papers.authors: Sanchez MD, Bensignor E, Degorce-Rubiales F, Husson JC, Abadie J, Fusselier-Tesson M, Brement T
papers.abstract: A 5-month-old female English bulldog was presented with firm, linear subcutaneous plaques associated with muscular involvement. Histopathological evaluation revealed mucin deposition, fibroblast proliferation and dermal fibrosis, consistent with fibromucinous disease with features consistent with scleromyxedema-like disease. Treatment with leflunomide resulted in clinical improvement and lesion stability during a 4-year follow-up period.

papers.title: Preliminary Investigation of Ilunocitinib Versus Prednisolone for the Management of Atopic Dermatitis in Client-Owned Dogs: A Double-Blind, Randomised Comparative Study.
papers.authors: Menegon FG, Risse SD, Lima ACC, Gmyterco VC, Ludwig LA, Weber SH, de Farias MR
papers.abstract: Canine atopic dermatitis (cAD) is a chronic, inflammatory and pruritic skin disease characterised by skin barrier dysfunction and T-cell dysregulation. Ilunocitinib, a nonselective Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor, is a promising therapeutic option for the control of cAD. To perform a preliminary comparison of the clinical efficacy and safety of ilunocitinib and prednisolone in cAD. Twenty dogs with cAD were randomly allocated into two experimental groups (n = 10 each). Group 1 received oral prednisolone at 0.5-1 mg/kg every 24 h for 7 days, followed by every 48 h for 7 days, and subsequently every 72 h for 45 days. Group 2 received oral ilunocitinib at 0.6-0.8 mg/kg every 24 h for 60 days. Clinical evaluations were performed on Day D0, D7, D15, D30 and D60, including physical examination and scoring for pruritus (via pruritus Visual Analog Scale [pVAS]), lesions (via Canine Atopic Dermatitis Extent and Severity Index, 4th iteration [CADESI-4]) and otitis (via 0-3 Otitis Index Score [OTIS-3]). Median pVAS decreased from 9 to 4.5 in Group 1 and from 9.5 to 2.5 in Group 2. Median CADESI-4 scores decreased from 40 to 17 in Group 1 and from 35.5 to 5.5 in Group 2. Differences between groups were observed for pVAS on D7 and D60 and for CADESI-4 on D15 and D60. Prednisolone was associated with increased fibrinogen and triglyceride concentrations, while dogs treated with ilunocitinib showed eosinopenia. In this preliminary study, daily use of ilunocitinib was associated with improvements in pruritus and skin lesions, supporting its potential role in the management of cAD.

papers.title: Prevalence, risk factors of intestinal parasitic infections in companion animals and associated owner knowledge, attitudes and practices in Jiangsu province, China.
papers.authors: Ni B, Zhang Q, Tang F, Zhang J, Gong X, Mao F, Liu Y
papers.abstract: Intestinal parasitic infection in companion animals threaten both animal health and public health due to their zoonotic potential. This study investigated the prevalence and risk factors of intestinal parasites in companion animals across Jiangsu province of China, and evaluated the pet owners' knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding intestinal parasites in companion animals. A cross-sectional study was conducted in Jiangsu between June 2024 and November 2025. A total of 1,348 fecal samples from companion dogs and cats were examined by microscope while a structured questionnaire was used to collect KAP data from pet owners. The overall prevalence of intestinal parasites in companion animals was 7.05% (95/1,348), with Toxocara spp. being the most prevalent parasite (2.23%). The prevalence was significantly higher in cats (8.76%) than in dogs (5.45%), and higher in rural areas (10.85%) than urban areas (3.26%). Independent risk factors for intestinal parasitic infection in companion animals included companion cat, rural residence, residence in northern Jiangsu, raw food consumption, and failure to deworm (all P < 0.05). Area, region, education level and occupation significantly influenced pet owners' total KAP scores (all P < 0.001). Rural and northern Jiangsu pet owners scored lower, while pet owners with higher education and non-farming occupations scored higher. This study reveals a notable intestinal parasites burden in companion animals of Jiangsu, with disparities by host species and residence. The findings underscore the need for integrated and multi-level interventions, including enhanced veterinary services, targeted health education for pet owners, promotion of regular deworming, and proper pet feeding to interrupt zoonotic transmission within the One Health framework.

papers.title: Creation of the Portuguese version of the Dog Impulsivity Assessment Scale and initial psychometric evaluation.
papers.authors: Alves JC, Santos A, Jorge P, Mendonça T
papers.abstract: Impulsivity, a reduced ability to tolerate delay of reinforcement that is related to inhibitory control, is relevant for behavioural problems, training success and welfare in dogs, particularly in working dogs. The Dog Impulsivity Assessment Scale (DIAS) is a handler-completed questionnaire developed in the United Kingdom. As there is no validated Portuguese version available, this study aimed to translate the DIAS into Portuguese and to perform its initial psychometric evaluation. The scale was translated and back-translated, and the Portuguese version was completed online by the handlers of 182 police working dogs of the Portuguese Gendarmerie (GNR). Principal component analysis with varimax rotation, parallel analysis, Cronbach's α and Spearman's correlations between scores were used. Sampling adequacy was moderate (Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin = 0.70). Six components had eigenvalues > 1 (62.62% of the variance), but the scree plot and parallel analysis supported three components (43.76%), which only partly matched the original structure and showed modest internal consistency (α = 0.61-0.73); α for all 18 items was 0.50. The overall score correlated positively with the three component scores (rs = 0.32-0.62), whereas the component scores were weakly or not correlated with each other. The sample was homogeneous, with a narrow dispersion of scores, and test-retest reliability was not assessed. The Portuguese DIAS is a promising tool, but its validation in more heterogeneous dog populations, including test-retest reliability, is required before it can be recommended for clinical or research use.

papers.title: Serum cytokine concentrations in dogs with idiopathic and structural epilepsy: an exploratory cross-sectional study.
papers.authors: Trevisan YPA, Torres BBJ, Fagundes-Triches DLG, Cardoso SP, Dalegrave S, Ribeiro LS, Bortolini J, Sousa VRF
papers.abstract: Neuroimmune mechanisms may contribute to epilepsy but circulating cytokine patterns in dogs with distinct clinical classifications of epilepsy remain incompletely characterized. This exploratory cross-sectional study compared serum concentrations of seven cytokines associated with Th1, Th2, Th17, inflammatory, and regulatory immune responses among healthy dogs and dogs clinically classified as having idiopathic epilepsy (IE) or structural epilepsy (SE). Twenty-eight dogs were included: health controls (n = 11), IE (n = 10), and SE (n = 7). Serum concentrations of IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-10, IL-17, TNF-α, and IFN-γ were measured using a human Cytometric Bead Array previously applied to canine samples. Dogs clinically classified as having SE showed lower measured serum IFN-γ concentrations than healthy controls [median (IQR): [6.95 (5.68) vs. [7.66 (14.8) pg/mL; p = 0.010]. No statistically significant differences were detected for the other cytokines or between dogs with IE and healthy controls. These findings indicate that the evaluated epilepsy groups did not exhibit a generalized serum cytokine signature, but the lower measured IFN-γ concentration may represent a specific peripheral immune alteration associated with the clinical classification of structural epilepsy. Although the specific underlying etiologies of the SE cases were not established, these results provide a basis for further investigation of cytokine dynamics and immune phenotypes in canine epilepsy longitudinal designs.

papers.title: Correction to: Analytical and clinical agreement between the Siemens Immulite 2000 veterinary cortisol and standard cortisol assays in canine serum.
Correction to: ACVIM consensus statement on the treatment of immune thrombocytopenia in dogs and cats.
Intra-arterial vinblastine is well tolerated for the treatment of urothelial cell carcinomas and prostatic carcinomas in dogs.
papers.authors: Vigouroux O, Horton A, O'Keeffe J, Letwin L, McLauchlan G
papers.abstract: To describe the treatment and outcome for dogs with lower urinary tract carcinoma or prostatic carcinoma treated with intra-arterial vinblastine. 14 client-owned dogs from a single private referral center identified through a search of the medical records as having either urothelial cell carcinoma (n = 8) or prostatic carcinoma (6) treated with intra-arterial vinblastine from September 1, 2016, through September 30, 2023. The most commonly reported clinical signs were pollakiuria, stranguria, and hematuria alone or in combination. Median duration of clinical signs prior to vinblastine treatment was 5 weeks (range, 1 to 18 weeks). Median body weight and age at intra-arterial vinblastine treatment were 14.85 kg (range, 5.7 to 33.5 kg) and 8 years (range, 6 to 11 years). There were 9 castrated males and 5 spayed females. Vinblastine was successfully administered via the internal iliac arteries in all cases. Clinical outcome was reported in 10 dogs: 9 improved, and 1 had stable clinical signs. Restaging was available for 8 dogs, of which 2 of 8 were classified as having partial response, 4 of 8 stable disease, and 2 of 8 progressive disease. Intra-arterial vinblastine was well tolerated in dogs in this study and may contribute to rapid clinical improvement. Intra-arterial vinblastine shows promise in treating urothelial cell carcinoma and prostatic carcinoma in dogs; however, additional research is needed.

papers.title: Spatial accuracy and clinical feasibility of CT/US fusion imaging for hepatic interventions in dogs.
papers.authors: Lee HW, Lee K, Lee SK
papers.abstract: Computed tomography (CT)-ultrasound (US) fusion imaging is widely used for hepatic interventions in human medicine, but its technical performance has not been evaluated in dogs. This study assessed the spatial accuracy, fusion time, and image quality of CT/US fusion imaging in the canine liver. In this prospective experimental study, ten healthy Beagle dogs underwent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT followed immediately by CT/US fusion imaging under the same general anesthesia without repositioning. Fusion was performed at three scan sites (midline subcostal, right intercostal, and left intercostal) using plane registration and three-point manual landmark registration with the gallbladder (GB) as the target structure. Spatial accuracy was quantified as the positional discrepancy between the CT and US GB margins in transverse (left-right, ventral-dorsal) and sagittal (cranial-caudal) planes. Fusion quality was scored on a 5-point scale for the GB center, GB border, vessel alignment, and liver surface alignment. Statistical analyses were performed using nonparametric tests with a significance threshold. Fusion was successful in 58/60 planned image sets; two subcostal studies failed due to intragastric gas. The mean fusion time was 72.7 ± 30.2 s and did not differ significantly among scan sites. Across all sites and planes, the mean CT/US discrepancies were ≤ 2 mm. Qualitative scores were uniformly high (median 5 for all criteria) without relevant site- and plane-dependent degradation. CT/US fusion imaging provided rapid, accurate, and visually reliable co-registration of canine liver anatomy, supporting its potential clinical use for image-guided hepatic interventions in dogs.

papers.title: Feasibility and clinical safety of cytokine-activated anti-tumor lymphocytes infusion in dogs with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: a pilot study.
papers.authors: Capellero S, Maga I, Donini C, Galiazzo E, Sapino A, De Maria R, Leuci V, Massa A, Sangiolo D, Marconato L, Aresu L
papers.abstract: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common histologic subtype of lymphoma in dogs. Although using cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone (CHOP) chemotherapy is the standard treatment, outcomes remain suboptimal, emphasizing the need for novel therapeutic strategies. Evaluate the feasibility and potential therapeutic benefit of adoptive immunotherapy using ex vivo-expanded cytokine-activated anti-tumor lymphocytes (CATLs) in dogs with DLBCL treated using CHOP chemotherapy and an autologous tumor vaccine. Seven client-owned dogs with naturally occurring DLBCL. Dogs received CHOP-based chemotherapy and the APAVAC® autologous vaccine. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were expanded ex vivo for 14 days using interleukin-2 and anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation. The CATLs were characterized by flow cytometry and reinfused. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were successfully expanded. After 14 days, the median cell yield was 728 × 106 cells (range, 162.4 × 106-1 500 × 106), corresponding to a median 8.6-fold expansion. Median fold increases of positive cells were 7.23 (interquartile range [IQR], 6.46-9.64) for CD3+, 8.56 (IQR, 7.11-14.56) for CD4+, 8.41 (IQR, 6.24-9.29) for CD5+, 10.35 (IQR, 7.63-14.67) for CD8+, and 16.16 (IQR, 12.22-30.40) for CD4+CD8+ cells. Reinfused CATLs ranged from 162.4 × 106 to 1 500 × 106 cells. Ex vivo expansion and reinfusion of autologous CATLs in dogs with DLBCL receiving CHOP chemotherapy and APAVAC® vaccination are feasible and induce robust T-cell expansion, suggesting this combined chemo-immunotherapeutic approach may enhance anti-tumor immunity and warrants further investigation in larger clinical studies.

papers.title: Intracameral lidocaine-epinephrine has minimal effect on heart rate and blood pressure and is an effective sole mydriatic during phacoemulsification in dogs.
papers.authors: Pumphrey SA, Gibson LK, Maggio F, Lindsey J, Wetmore LA
papers.abstract: To investigate heart rate (HR) and rhythm, blood pressure (BP), and pupil diameter in dogs that received intracameral (IC) preservative-free lidocaine-epinephrine (ILE) as a sole mydriatic agent during phacoemulsification. Records were retrospectively reviewed for HR and BP data and anesthesia concerns following administration of ILE during cataract surgery (IC group, 130 eyes from 83 dogs). Similar data were obtained for a control group undergoing phacoemulsification that received topical mydriatics (topical treatment [TT] group, 40 eyes from 21 dogs). Pupil diameter was measured prospectively following administration of ILE in an additional 20 eyes from 11 dogs. Average baseline HR was 13 beats/min higher in the TT group than in the IC group for both eyes operated (P ≤ .04). Heart rate increased more from baseline in the IC group than in the TT group at 15 and 20 minutes after administration, but the difference was not clinically significant (average of 4 beats/min). Changes in BP were minimal and did not differ between groups. No significant arrhythmias or other anesthetic complications were noted in either group. Mean pupil diameter was 11.3 mm (95% CI, 11, 11.6) immediately following ILE administration and 11.8 mm (95% CI, 11.5, 12.1) at the conclusion of surgery. ILE produced adequate, durable mydriasis when used as a sole mydriatic in canine eyes undergoing phacoemulsification. Intracameral lidocaine-epinephrine does not appear to affect cardiovascular parameters when administered during phacoemulsification in dogs. ILE is a reasonable mydriatic choice for canine phacoemulsification.

papers.title: Evaluation of the efficacy of extended-release buprenorphine (Ethiqa XR) using objective gait analysis in dogs.
papers.authors: Tiffinger K, Benito de la Vibora J, Hall A, Hall N, Taylor R, Enomoto H, Love KR, Mishra SK, Lascelles BDX, Enomoto M
papers.abstract: To evaluate the efficacy of an extended-release formulation of buprenorphine HCl (XR-Bup) using objective gait analysis in a canine stifle arthrotomy model. We hypothesized that a single SC injection of XR-Bup would reduce postoperative pain and improve limb function. In a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled crossover study design, 8 purpose-bred Beagles underwent 2 unilateral stifle arthrotomies, randomized to XR-Bup for 1 procedure and placebo for the other, separated by a washout period. Kinetic and static ground reaction force data were collected at baseline (pretreatment) and multiple time points up to 72 hours after arthrotomy. Symmetry indices were calculated for ground reaction force variables and compared between groups using a repeated-measures analysis. Overall, symmetry indices of static body weight distribution (%BWdistrib) showed significantly greater limb use symmetry following XR-Bup compared to placebo. There was significant time and treatment interaction (P = .025) for %BWdistrib to the operated limb, with %BWdistrib approaching baseline levels more quickly when treated with XR-Bup. Similarly, kinetic variables demonstrated higher limb use in the XR-Bup group, although the treatment effects were not significant. All dogs experienced nausea and hyporexia/anorexia after XR-Bup over 72 hours. Vomiting occurred in 6 of 9 and regurgitation was observed in 8 of 9 arthrotomy cases. XR-Bup treatment was associated with greater limb usage (static and dynamic) at all time points, with data indicating effective pain alleviation in a small cohort of dogs. Although Ethiqa XR may be an alternative option for postoperative pain control, its clinical utility at the dose evaluated in this study may be limited by the occurrence of adverse events.

papers.title: Clinical outcomes were evaluated in 82 dogs with B-cell lymphoma treated with adoptive T-cell therapy following cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone chemotherapy.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Westfall TE, Impellizeri JA
papers.abstract: To describe clinical outcomes and adverse events in dogs with B-cell lymphoma treated with adoptive T-cell therapy (ACT) following cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (CHOP) chemotherapy. Medical records of 82 dogs with B-cell lymphoma that received ACT following CHOP chemotherapy between 2017 and 2025 were retrospectively reviewed. Overall survival was defined as the time from lymphoma diagnosis to death from any cause or last follow-up. Post-ACT survival was defined as the time from first ACT infusion to death from any cause or last follow-up. Time to next anti-lymphoma treatment was defined as the time from first ACT infusion to initiation of subsequent lymphoma-directed therapy. Survival outcomes were estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis. 82 dogs met inclusion criteria. Median overall survival from diagnosis was 660 days (95% CI, 539 to 781 days). Median post-ACT survival was 368 days (95% CI, 261 to 474 days), and median time to next anti-lymphoma treatment was 317 days (95% CI, 284 to 350 days). Adoptive T-cell therapy was generally well tolerated following CHOP chemotherapy. Adverse events occurred in 5% (4 of 82) of dogs; most were grade 1 or 2, with 1 grade 3 event reported. Clinical outcomes varied among dogs with B-cell lymphoma treated with ACT following CHOP chemotherapy. Adoptive T-cell therapy was generally well tolerated, with adverse events reported in 4 of 82 dogs. This study describes clinical outcomes and adverse events in 82 dogs with B-cell lymphoma that received ACT following CHOP chemotherapy. These findings provide clinical data on the use of ACT in this patient population and may inform the design of prospective controlled studies evaluating ACT in canine B-cell lymphoma.

papers.title: Electrochemotherapy achieves high local control of lingual and tonsillar tumors in dogs and cats.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Vizcay J, Portillo F, Sabella T, Diaz M, Impellizeri J, Maglietti F, Tellado M
papers.abstract: To describe local response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS) in dogs and cats with lingual or tonsillar tumors treated with electrochemotherapy (ECT) alone or combined with surgery. Medical records were retrospectively reviewed for dogs and cats with a histologically or cytologically confirmed tumor of the tongue or tonsil treated with ECT alone or combined with surgery, with ≥ 1 posttreatment follow-up. Twenty-nine client-owned animals, 7 dogs and 7 cats with lingual tumors and 15 dogs with tonsillar tumors, were included. Response was assessed by modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors; PFS and OS were estimated by Kaplan-Meier analysis. In dogs with lingual tumors, the objective response rate (ORR) was 85.7% (complete response [CR], 71.4%); the median OS was 270 days, with 2 dogs alive at 980 and 1,090 days, and the median PFS was 263 days. In cats with lingual tumors, the ORR was 71.4% (CR, 57.1%), the median OS was 240 days, and all cats died, most of local progression; the median PFS was 215 days. In dogs with tonsillar tumors, the ORR was 80.0% (CR, 66.7%), the median OS was 240 days, and all dogs died, predominantly of pulmonary metastasis; the median PFS was 210 days. ECT can provide high local response rates in dogs and cats with lingual tumors. In dogs with tonsilar tumors, even when high local response rates are achieved, patients die predominantly from distant metastasis, warranting a multimodal treatment approach. ECT achieved high local response rates in all groups. It appears most useful for function-preserving treatment for lingual tumors. The combination with surgery allows treatment of larger tumors than ECT alone. The survival of dogs with tonsillar tumors was limited by metastatic dissemination, supporting a multimodal approach.

papers.title: Gene electrotransfer for DNA immunotherapy in veterinary oncology: Technical Tutorial Video.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Impellizeri JA, Vigodny A, Sanchez E, Aurisicchio L, Conforti A
papers.abstract: To demonstrate the technique of gene electrotransfer (GET) for administration of plasmid DNA immunotherapy in veterinary oncology. The method demonstrated in the video is relevant to both canine and feline cancer patients undergoing administration of DNA immunotherapies. This Technical Tutorial Video demonstrates patient preparation, IM plasmid administration, electrode positioning, electroporation pulse delivery, and postprocedural assessment for a GET procedure. Required equipment, procedure workflow, and practical technical considerations are reviewed. The video illustrates the general workflow for delivery of plasmid DNA immunotherapy using IM GET under general anesthesia, including patient preparation, plasmid administration, pulse delivery, and patient monitoring. GET is increasingly used in veterinary oncology to facilitate delivery of DNA immunotherapies targeting tumor-associated antigens and immunomodulatory molecules. This tutorial provides a practical overview of the technique.

papers.title: Surgical debulking and electrochemotherapy, including a tetrapolar single-needle electrode, are associated with clinical benefit in dogs with intranasal tumors.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Rangel MMM, Holanda AGA, Linhares LCM, Suzuki DOH, Bispo GA, de Nardi AB
papers.abstract: To evaluate the feasibility and preliminary clinical outcomes of surgical debulking combined with electrochemotherapy (ECT) using a multielectrode approach, including a tetrapolar single-needle electrode, in dogs with intranasal tumors. This retrospective observational study included client-owned dogs with intranasal tumors treated from 2017 through 2024 at a veterinary oncology referral center. Dogs were included if they underwent at least 1 surgical procedure combined with intraoperative bleomycin-based ECT using a multielectrode approach and had a minimum follow-up period of 2 months. 12 dogs were included, and most had advanced local disease (83% stages T3 to T4). Epithelial tumors predominated (91%), mainly adenocarcinoma (42%). Clinical response was observed in all dogs, including complete clinical response in 75% and partial clinical response in 25%. Local progression was documented by CT in 5 dogs (42%). Repeat procedures were performed in 67% of dogs because of persistent clinical signs or tumor progression. The median progression-free interval was 492 days, and the median survival time was 694 days. Treatment-related adverse events were frequent but predominantly mild to moderate, including partial wound dehiscence (50%), crust formation (42%), infection (25%), and oronasal fistula (25%). No procedure-related deaths occurred. Surgical debulking combined with ECT using a multielectrode approach, including a tetrapolar single-needle electrode, was feasible and associated with clinical benefit in dogs with intranasal tumors. These findings support further prospective investigation of this approach for intranasal tumors in dogs. This approach may represent a treatment option for dogs with locally advanced intranasal tumors, particularly when radiotherapy is unavailable.

papers.title: BRAFV595E mutation detected across the disease spectrum from non-neoplastic urothelium to invasive urothelial carcinoma in dogs.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Dhawan D, Sola MF, Nelson JB, Lanman NA, Enstrom AW, Fourez LM, Tersey SA, Knapp DW
papers.abstract: The goal was to determine the presence of a driver mutation in dogs with and without detectable cancer to set the stage for future cancer prevention research exploiting processes that inhibit cancer development in the presence of such mutations. The objective was to detect the v-raf murine sarcoma viral oncogene homolog B (BRAF) mutation BRAFV595E across the disease spectrum from non-neoplastic urothelium to invasive urothelial carcinoma (UC) in dogs. Scottish Terriers ≥ 6 years old with no outward evidence of urinary disease (n = 120) were screened for UC by urinalysis, urinary tract ultrasonography, follow-up cystoscopic biopsy, and necropsy when possible. Initial results were published in 2022. Extended follow-up is presented here. The BRAFV595E mutation was detected in urine sediment by droplet digital PCR and in bladder tissues by immunohistochemistry. For 120 dogs screened, biopsy-confirmed UC was found in 41 dogs including 31 high-grade UC, 6 low-grade UC, 1 carcinoma in situ, and 3 dysplasias that progressed to high-grade UC. The BRAFV595E mutation was found in the urine of 23 of 26 dogs with high-grade UC, 4 of 5 dogs with low-grade UC, 2 of 3 dogs with dysplasia, and 12 of 66 dogs with no UC detected over a median of 14 months of follow-up (range, 4 to 71 months). The BRAFV595E mutation was detected in UC and non-neoplastic urothelium by immunohistochemistry. The BRAFV595E mutation is present in various stages of canine UC and non-neoplastic urothelium. This knowledge will contribute to future cancer prevention research. Urothelial carcinoma screening should be implemented for Scottish Terriers and potentially dogs in other high-risk breeds. Biopsy and standardized imaging remain essential in UC management.

papers.title: Gilvetmab advances immune checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy for canine cancer.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Chon E, Greene LM, Stock ML
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized human oncology and are emerging as a promising strategy in veterinary cancer care. These agents unleash antitumor immunity by targeting inhibitory pathways that suppress T-cell function, enabling durable responses in select patients. In dogs, the immune checkpoint programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) axis is a primary focus due to conserved structural and functional homology with the PD-1 axis in humans, documented PD-1/programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) signaling in the canine tumor microenvironment, and its role in reversing tumor-induced immune exhaustion. Several caninized anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 antibodies have demonstrated favorable safety profiles and notable antitumor activity in spontaneously occurring canine cancers, particularly melanoma and mast cell tumors. Gilvetmab, currently the only veterinary ICI available commercially, has conditional licensure in the United States for these indications. This caninized anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody has demonstrated target engagement, acceptable tolerability, and clinical efficacy in a subset of treated dogs. Although reported adverse events are generally manageable, further work is needed to better characterize immune-mediated toxicities. Furthermore, response patterns may differ from those of cytotoxic therapies, including potential pseudoprogression, necessitating careful selection of response assessment methods. Key challenges remain in optimizing patient selection, refining biomarker development, establishing effective combination strategies, and defining the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade across diverse tumor histologic subtypes (histotypes). Continued study of gilvetmab and related agents should advance the clinical application of immunotherapy in veterinary oncology and inform the next generation of comparative cancer care.

papers.title: Electrochemotherapy with interleukin-12 gene electrotransfer can turn local tumor ablation into a systemic antitumor response in veterinary patients.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Čemažar M, Lampreht Tratar U, Milevoj N, Serša G, Tozon N
papers.abstract: Veterinary medicine serves as an important translational bridge between preclinical studies and human medicine, offering a valuable model for investigating naturally occurring diseases and generating data unattainable from purely experimental animal models. This is particularly relevant for evaluating novel cancer treatment approaches. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) and gene electrotransfer represent 2 such approaches in both human and veterinary clinical oncology. Current evidence indicates that ECT achieves excellent local ablative control of treated tumors; however, its principal limitation is that ECT does not reliably control untreated or metastatic disease. One strategy to overcome this limitation is combining ECT with the systemic immunomodulatory action of IL-12 gene electrotransfer as both modalities rely on the same platform technology, electroporation. In veterinary medicine, this combined approach has been successfully applied across various tumor types in dogs, demonstrating excellent local antitumor control alongside indications of systemic effects. These have been clinically associated with prolonged survival, regression of distant untreated tumors and lymph node metastases, and reduced invasive tumor growth. Immunological studies are also consistent with systemic immune activation, with flow cytometry analysis of peripheral blood demonstrating transient increases in circulating CD8+ cells following each therapeutic session. Further studies are needed to find the suitable biomarkers for selecting the appropriate patients for the selected treatments.

papers.title: Feasibility of bone-targeted electrochemotherapy for palliation of bone tumors in dogs and cats.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Zanasi A, Vigodny A, Finotello R, Tornago R, Cadossi M, Impellizeri JS, Impellizeri JA
papers.abstract: Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a minimally invasive locoregional treatment that combines reversible electroporation with cytotoxic agents to enhance intracellular drug delivery. Although its efficacy is well established in cutaneous malignancies, its role in bone tumors has only recently been explored in veterinary medicine. This narrative review integrates preclinical evidence, human clinical data, and early veterinary experience with an original 4-case series to evaluate the translational potential of ECT in bone oncology. Preclinical studies demonstrate effective tumor ablation within bone while preserving extracellular matrix integrity and enabling bone tissue regeneration. Clinical studies in humans report consistent pain relief, meaningful local tumor control, and acceptable safety profiles, including in complex scenarios, such as radiotherapy-resistant metastatic epidural spinal cord compression. In contrast, veterinary evidence remains limited to isolated case reports, in part due to limited dedicated technologies. Taken together, available data suggest that ECT may represent a function-preserving alternative for selected bone tumors. Prospective studies are warranted to define its clinical role in veterinary medicine.

papers.title: Occurrence of Toxocara spp. in companion animals and serological evidence of human exposure at the human-companion animal interface in Giza, Egypt.
papers.authors: Gouda MA, Shalaan FH, Seleem AA, Anwer AZ, Bakry NM
papers.abstract: Toxocariasis, caused by Toxocara spp., is one of the most neglected zoonotic parasitic diseases worldwide. In Egypt, integrated One Health studies investigating human, animal, and occupational risk factors remain limited. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of zoonotic Toxocara spp. in companion animals and to identify associated risk factors within a One Health framework. A cross-sectional study was conducted in Giza, Egypt, including dogs (n = 70) and cats (n = 35) from animal shelters and veterinary clinics, eosinophilic children (n = 227), and shelter workers (n = 22). Animal fecal samples were examined microscopically for intestinal parasites, while human serum samples were tested for anti-Toxocara IgG antibodies using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Demographic characteristics and potential risk factors were collected through standardized questionnaires. Associations were evaluated using Pearson's Chi-square or Fisher's exact tests, followed by binary logistic regression to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Toxocara canis-like eggs were detected in a percentage of 17.1% in canine cases, with no significant difference in positivity rates regarding sex. In contrast, T. canis positivity rate was significantly correlated with younger age, lack of anthelmintic medication, and concurrent detection of Cystoisospora species. Among the studied eosinophilic children, anti-Toxocara IgG antibodies were detected in 41/227 (18.1%). In the univariable analysis, rural residence was significantly associated with anti-T. canis IgG seropositivity (COR = 2.08, 95% CI: 1.00-4.32; P = 0.047). Similarly, contact with soil (COR = 2.51, 95% CI: 1.17-5.42; P = 0.02), consumption of unpurified water (COR = 2.80, 95% CI: 1.15-6.82; P = 0.02), and interaction with pets (COR = 3.19, 95% CI: 1.48-6.87; P = 0.002) were significantly associated with anti IgG seropositivity. In the multivariable binary logistic regression model, contact with soil remained significantly associated with anti-T. canis IgG seropositivity (AOR = 3.10, 95% CI: 1.17-8.66; P = 0.02). Consumption of unpurified water (AOR = 2.64, 95% CI: 1.03-6.78; P = 0.04) and interaction with pets (AOR = 3.60, 95% CI: 1.60-8.10; P = 0.002) were also independently associated with seropositivity. In contrast, the association with rural residence was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for the other variables included in the model (AOR = 0.55, 95% CI: 0.25-1.17; P = 0.12). This study demonstrates substantial exposure to T. canis-like eggs among companion animals and children in Giza, Egypt, highlighting the need for integrated One Health interventions. Regular deworming of pets, public health education, and coordinated veterinary-medical surveillance are recommended to reduce toxocariasis at the human-companion animal interface.

papers.title: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Enterobacter hormaechei and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from mammary and postoperative wounds in canine oncology patients.
papers.authors: Ferraz CM, Teixeira MM, Dos Santos VB, Lutzke D, da Silva EC, Gutierrez KP, Senhorello ILS, Possebon FS, Sellera FP, Furlan JPR, Rossi GAM
papers.abstract: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales represent an increasing challenge in small animal medicine due to their limited treatment options and potential for dissemination in clinical settings. Although ESBL-positive Enterobacterales are increasingly recognized in dogs, their detection and clinical significance among dogs with cancer remain poorly investigated. Herein, we report the detection and genomic characterization of three ESBL-producing isolates recovered from wound samples of two dogs with neoplastic diseases. One Enterobacter hormaechei isolate was recovered from an ulcerated mammary tumor, whereas another E. hormaechei isolate and a Klebsiella pneumoniae isolate were recovered from a postoperative wound following thoracic nodulectomy. All three isolates were classified as multidrug-resistant and belonged to clinically relevant sequence types: E. hormaechei sequence type (ST) 114 and ST133, and K. pneumoniae ST11. All isolates carried bla CTX-M-15 , while K. pneumoniae ST11 additionally harbored bla CTX-M-8 . Genomic analyses also identified multiple virulence-associated determinants, including siderophore-associated genes in E. hormaechei ST133. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first published report of E. hormaechei ST133 in a dog. These findings highlight the detection of clinically relevant ESBL-producing lineages in canine oncology patients and reinforce the importance of microbiological surveillance and antimicrobial susceptibility testing in veterinary practice.

papers.title: Surgical management of type I atresia ani using Heineke-Mikulicz-like anoplasty: A case series of 11 kittens (2022-2025).
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Berlemont L, Bondonny L, Massinon J, Chanoit G, Taroni M, Ferrand FX
papers.abstract: Type I atresia ani is rare in cats, and there is limited published data on the surgical management and prognosis of this condition in feline patients. Appropriate surgical planning requires thorough examination of the rectum, anus, and perineum to accurately diagnose atresia ani and rule out the presence of a rectovaginal or rectourethral fistula. Type I atresia may be treated with balloon dilatation or bougienage but there may be recurrence, and several procedures may be required before complete resolution of the stenosis. The objective of this retrospective case series was to describe, for the first time, the clinical application and postoperative outcomes of a Heineke-Mikulicz-like anoplasty technique in kittens with type I atresia ani. The surgical technique was adapted from the Heineke-Mikulicz anoplasty technique described in humans. In total, 11 cats with a mean age of 12.3 weeks (range 8-20) were included in this study. Heineke-Mikulicz-like anoplasty was performed in all cases without intraoperative complications. Major postoperative complications occurred in 1/11 (9%) case, with wound dehiscence 2 days after surgery. However, complete healing was achieved after revision surgery. At long-term follow-up over 13.6 months (range 6-24), no recurrence was reported in 11/11 (100%) cases. Although permanent fecal incontinence was reported in 1/11 (9%) cat, long-term outcomes were excellent in 9/11 (81%) cats. These data suggest that Heineke-Mikulicz-like anoplasty is appropriate for the management of type I atresia ani in cats.

papers.title: Evaluation of urine clusterin and cystatin B concentrations in relation to histopathologic findings of renal disease in dogs.
papers.authors: Rivera C, Hines ES, Schultz D, Cianciolo RE, Jeffery N, Hokamp JA, Linn-Peirano SC, Grossi DA, Ouyang Z, Peterson S, Nabity MB
papers.abstract: Conventional markers of kidney disease detect altered kidney function but do not consistently identify active kidney injury. Urine clusterin (uClust) and cystatin B (uCysB) are renal injury biomarkers, but their evaluation is limited in dogs with biopsy-confirmed diagnoses. Determine the association of uClust and uCysB with conventional biomarkers, category of renal disease, severity of renal injury, and survival in dogs with biopsy-confirmed kidney disease. Urine from client-owned dogs (n = 199) submitted to the International Veterinary Renal Pathology Service between 2008 and 2018 with corresponding kidney biopsy samples. Retrospective study. Urine clusterin and uCysB were measured using an ELISA, and correlations with serum creatinine (sCr), symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA), urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPC), and histopathology severity scores were determined. Significant differences in uClust and uCysB among conventional biomarker groups were determined using analysis of variance. Multivariate survival analysis was performed. Concentrations of uClust and uCysB were highest in dogs with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) and mixed MPGN, and they were positively correlated with sCr, SDMA, UPC, and histopathology scores (r = 0.25-0.50). Risk of death was higher in dogs with uCysB > 238 ng/mL (hazard ratio, 2.40; P < .05), whereas uClust > 7329 ng/mL was associated with lower risk of death (hazard ratio, 0.32; P < .01). Higher uCysB was associated with more severe disease and decreased survival; therefore, uCysB might identify dogs with active renal injury and worse prognosis. Although uClust was associated with more severe disease, its association with survival needs further investigation.

papers.title: Reassessing outcome and adverse events associated with ventral slot decompression for cervical intervertebral disc disease in dogs: 241 cases (2021-2024).
papers.authors: Marocco P, Taylor AR
papers.abstract: Cervical intervertebral disc herniations (IVDH) are a common cause of cervical myelopathy in dogs, with ventral slot decompression (VSD) often being the surgical treatment of choice. The contemporary United States breed population has changed since the large retrospective review on VSD outcomes in 2013, with French bulldogs increasing in popularity.4,8 A 2025 retrospective study evaluated outcomes in patients receiving VSD but it was a single institution United Kingdom based cohort that focused on concomitant fenestration.7. Evaluate adverse events (AEs) and outcomes in dogs that underwent VSD for cervical IVDH since the increase in French bulldog prevalence in US populations. We hypothesized that there would be an increase in the number of reported AEs with no difference in outcome. A total of 241 dogs from 4 private neurology practices treated between 2021 and 2024. Retrospective case series. Most cases had excellent or good outcomes (n = 182/241 and 34/241, respectively), with poor outcomes in 9 cases. Overall AE rate was 25% (n = 60/241). A negative outcome was significantly associated with increased body weight (P < .001), higher AE grades (P < .001), higher AE severity (P < .001), caudal disc spaces (P = .04), and lateralized extruded material (P = .01). Outcome was not significantly associated with sex, surgical or anesthetic duration, surgeon experience, prior ventral slot surgery, perioperative hypotension, or hemorrhage. Despite the increased prevalence of French bulldogs undergoing VSD in US populations, this surgery continues to have favorable outcomes.

papers.title: Anesthesia for electrochemotherapy in dogs and cats: a mini-review of current practices and future considerations.
papers.authors: Seliškar A, Klasić M, Tomsič K
papers.abstract: Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a short, minimally invasive procedure that causes mild to moderate pain. In humans, ECT can often be performed under sedation and local anesthesia, whereas general anesthesia is generally preferred in veterinary medicine. Anesthesia of dogs and cats undergoing ECT can be challenging because of altered clinical status, paraneoplastic syndromes, and concurrent chronic comorbidities. Recent evidence suggests that anesthetic and analgesic agents, particularly opioids, may modulate antitumor immune responses and potentially influence oncological outcomes, although the clinical relevance of these effects requires further investigation. Effective peri-procedural pain management is essential for patient recovery and welfare, and opioid-free or opioid-sparing strategies incorporating locoregional anesthesia may reduce opioid requirements while providing effective analgesia. The growing clinical evidence supporting the efficacy of ECT in veterinary oncology highlights the need for updated patient-tailored anesthetic and analgesic protocols. Moreover, it supports the potential of ECT as a useful research model for investigating tumor-anesthesia interactions, with translational relevance to human oncology. This mini-review summarizes current practices and practical considerations in veterinary onco-anesthesia and identifies priorities for future research.

papers.title: Dynamics of salivary cortisol and oxytocin during standardized field training in search-and-rescue (SAR) dogs.
papers.authors: Bolechová P, Chmelíková E, Polónyiová A, Vostrá-Vydrová H, Dokoupilová A, Svobodová I
papers.abstract: Search and rescue (SAR) dogs perform physically and cognitively demanding tasks under complex field conditions. The aim of this study was to characterize temporal changes in salivary cortisol and oxytocin concentrations during standardized simulated SAR field training and to explore their associations with selected dog- and training-related factors. Twenty-one working dogs participated in three standardized simulated field-training exercises. Saliva samples were collected at six sampling points covering the pre-workload, workload, and early recovery phases. Temporal changes were evaluated using generalized linear mixed-effects models accounting for repeated measurements within dogs, while associations with dog- and training-related factors were examined as secondary or exploratory analyses. Salivary cortisol showed a significant overall effect of sampling phase, with a statistically significant difference from the pre-workload sampling point observed only at the later workload sampling point, whereas the other pairwise comparisons, including the final recovery sampling point, were not statistically significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons. Salivary oxytocin also showed a significant overall sampling-phase effect, but no individual pairwise comparison remained statistically significant after adjustment. Oxytocin concentrations showed a non-monotonic descriptive pattern and were numerically lower than the pre-workload concentration at the final sampling point. These findings should be interpreted as preliminary information on endocrine responses associated with standardized simulated SAR field training rather than as direct evidence of positive or adverse welfare states or incomplete physiological recovery. Further studies integrating endocrine, behavioral, autonomic, performance-related, physical, and other welfare-related measures are needed to clarify the functional significance of these responses.

papers.title: Adapting human multidisciplinary tumor boards to veterinary oncology: a closed-loop framework for integrated decision-making and organizational learning.
papers.authors: Sebastián-López C
papers.abstract: Multidisciplinary tumor boards are established in human oncology to integrate information and reasoning from several specialties around patient-level management decisions. Veterinary oncology already relies on multimodal care and specialist collaboration, but there is still limited standardization of how relevant clinical and contextual information should be prospectively integrated, how the reasoning supporting decisions should be documented, how decisions should be revisited as new information emerges, and how completed cases should inform future practice. This Conceptual Analysis proposes an adaptable veterinary multidisciplinary tumor board (VMTB) for dogs and cats with complex oncologic conditions, including solid tumors and selected hematologic malignancies when multidisciplinary input may change, clarify, or contextualize management. The framework distinguishes essential clinical functions from local implementation configuration and uses a modular seven-step pathway beginning with a time-stamped pre-board management intention. Depending on the clinical question, the VMTB may produce a preferred integrated recommendation or a structured set of clinically defensible alternatives. This approach is consistent with the veterinary Spectrum of Care concept, which recognizes that more than one evidence-informed and clinically acceptable management pathway may exist, and provides a structured basis for subsequent owner-centred shared decision-making. Relevant specialist input may be provided on site, remotely, or through structured external consultation. Cases may re-enter clinical review when definitive pathology, treatment response, progression, or other new information could alter current management. This patient-level re-entry is distinct from the post-case return process: review results in organizational learning only when a clinically relevant observation generates a practice change that is subsequently applied and reassessed. The framework does not assume that VMTB review or management change improves clinical outcomes. Initial evaluation should determine whether the VMTB is feasible and timely, whether its influence on decision-making is traceable, whether the owner's subsequent decision and implementation of the selected plan can be documented, whether essential functions are delivered with fidelity, and whether the post-case return process is completed. Only after reliable implementation has been established should potential clinical benefit be investigated.

papers.title: Octreotide treatment improves multiple domains of cognitive performance in aged beagle dogs.
papers.authors: LaCroix-Fralish ML, Juarez-Salinas D, Marietti E, Silva E, Tovar A, Chen F, Greenwood K, Peloquin M, Halioua-Haubold CL
papers.abstract: Aging in dogs is accompanied by progressive cognitive decline and neuropathological changes that parallel key features of human brain aging and dementia, making canines a highly valuable naturally occurring model for studying aging and neurodegenerative disease. Across species, reduced growth hormone/insulin-like growth factor-1 (GH/IGF-1) signaling is associated with extended lifespan and preserved late-life cognition, whereas chronically elevated somatotropic activity is linked to deficits in memory, attention, and executive function. The effects of pharmacologic GH/IGF-1 suppression on cognition in naturally aging animal models remain unclear. We investigated whether attenuation of IGF-1 signaling with the long-acting somatostatin analog octreotide improves cognitive performance in aged dogs. Twenty-eight aged beagle dogs (7-15 years) experienced in neuropsychological testing were enrolled in a randomized, placebo-controlled study. After a 28-day baseline, dogs received either long-acting octreotide (Sandostatin LAR, 10 mg, i.m.) or placebo, followed by a wash-in interval and 28 days of post-treatment testing. A validated cognitive battery assessed executive function and cognitive flexibility (discrimination reversal), selective attention (variable oddity), and visuospatial working memory (variable delayed non-matching to position). Treated dogs demonstrated significantly improved performance relative to placebo across the three behavioral paradigms with the primary effect being reductions in response latency and task engagement. Pharmacologic IGF-1 suppression with octreotide improves cognitive response efficiency and engagement in aged dogs, particularly in executive and attentional domains. These results support a functional role for somatotropic signaling in late-life cognition and highlight the aged canine as a valuable translational model for geroscience-based interventions targeting age-related cognitive decline.

papers.title: Daily supplementation with canine-isolated Limosilactobacillus reuteri ATCC PTA 6127 is well tolerated, improves stool consistency, and modulates gut microbiome in dogs.
papers.authors: Rendina DN, Commichaux S, Roos S, Axelsson J, Lundqvist C, Hibberd AA
papers.abstract: Probiotics are increasingly incorporated into companion animal diets to support gastrointestinal function, yet strain-specific evidence in dogs remains limited. This study evaluated the safety, tolerability, and gastrointestinal effects of daily supplementation with Limosilactobacillus reuteri PureStrong™ (ATCC PTA 6127) in healthy adult dogs. Sixteen purpose-bred Beagle dogs (8/group; balanced by sex) were enrolled in a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled trial and received either 1 × 10 8  CFU/d of L. reuteri ATCC PTA 6127 or placebo for 28 days. At study initiation, dogs underwent a standardized transition from a dry diet to a canned wet diet, representing a dietary challenge associated with transient gastrointestinal and microbiome changes. Safety was assessed through clinical observations, body weight, food intake, hematology, and serum biochemistry; gastrointestinal outcomes included daily fecal scoring and periodic measurement of fecal pH, moisture, and microbiome composition (16S rRNA gene sequencing). All dogs completed the study without adverse events, and clinical pathology values remained within reference intervals with no treatment-related differences. Dogs receiving L. reuteri exhibited a lower incidence of poorly formed stools compared with placebo (0.58% vs. 6.33%) and were significantly less likely to be assigned to poorer fecal consistency categories ( β = -1.31, p  = 0.033), indicating improved stool quality during supplementation. By Day 28, fecal pH was significantly lower in the probiotic group compared with placebo after baseline adjustment (Δ = -0.22; 95% CI: -0.403 to -0.045; p  = 0.018). Microbiome analyses indicated that the transition from dry to wet food was the dominant driver of microbial community restructuring. Against this background, probiotic supplementation was associated with an early increase in fecal L. reuteri abundance and more positive longitudinal changes in several lactic acid bacteria and commensal taxa during the first 2 weeks. Most treatment-associated differences were no longer evident by Day 28. In summary, daily supplementation with L. reuteri ATCC PTA 6127 was safe and well tolerated and was associated with improved fecal consistency, lower fecal pH at Day 28, and transient differences in microbiome adaptation during a dietary challenge. These findings provide strain-specific evidence supporting the potential of ATCC PTA 6127 as a dietary probiotic supplement for gastrointestinal stability in dogs.

papers.title: Retrospective analysis of feline heartworm disease ( Dirofilaria immitis ): diagnostic patterns in cats presenting with respiratory or vomiting signs (2013-2023, USA).
papers.authors: Whittle A, Ferguson B, Taylor-Rakocevic M, Poulsen Nautrup B, Topdijan K, Sheehy J, Mwacalimba K
papers.abstract: Feline heartworm infection, caused by the mosquito-borne nematode Dirofilaria immitis , is a serious and potentially fatal disease in cats. The true prevalence of this infection is likely underestimated due to the nonspecific nature of clinical signs, such as coughing, vomiting, or respiratory distress, and the diagnostic limitations of current feline heartworm antigen (Ag) and antibody (Ab) assays. This study aimed to enhance understanding of its recognition and detection by linking diverse clinical presentations with diagnostic test results. Anonymized feline medical records spanning 10 years from more than 1,000 Banfield U.S. veterinary clinics were analyzed using machine learning methods. Cats were included if records contained respiratory, vomiting, or heartworm-specific diagnostic codes and at least one heartworm Ag or Ab test. Test positivity rates were linked to clinical signs. For cats tested with both assays, concordance between results was assessed. Of 146,111 eligible cats, 91,438 (62.58%) underwent heartworm testing, and 1,555 (1.70%) were positive on at least one assay. Cats with heartworm-specific diagnostic codes had the highest positivity, but those with respiratory or vomiting codes accounted for 7.01 and 10.10% of all positives. Among 127 cats tested with both assays, 24.41% were discordant, mainly Ag-positive/Ab-negative. Heartworm infection should be considered in any cat with respiratory signs (including asthma-like presentations) or vomiting. To improve its detection, both heat-treated Ag and Ab assays should be used to screen cats annually, and in cats presenting with respiratory signs or vomiting.

papers.title: Molecular evidence of vector/blood borne and hemotropic bacteria in dogs and cats from El Salvador, Central America.
