papers.authors: Alabí Córdova AS, Rivera MHR, Calchi AC, Micolta LFB, das Neves LF, de Moura FMB, da Silva JVDSA, Lee DAB, Machado RZ, André MR
papers.abstract: Latin America's high biodiversity, together with socioeconomic and ecological conditions, favors the persistence of vectors and vector-borne bacterial pathogens in domestic animals. Data on vector-borne pathogens in domestic dogs and cats in Central America remain limited, and reports from El Salvador are scarce. This study aimed to investigate the occurrence of Bartonella spp., Anaplasma spp., Ehrlichia spp., and hemotropic Mycoplasma spp. in domestic dogs and cats from the metropolitan area of San Salvador, El Salvador. For this purpose, blood samples were collected from 269 dogs and 59 cats in veterinary clinics. Four feline (6.78%; 95% CI: 2.67-16.18%) and one canine (0.37%; 95% CI: 0.07-2.08%) samples were positive for Bartonella spp. by a quantitative real-time TaqMan based PCR (qPCR) based on the NADH dehydrogenase gamma subunit (nuoG) gene. In a TaqMan-based multiplex qPCR targeting the gene encoding the 60-kDa heat shock protein (groEL gene), whereas 19 canine (7.06%; 95% CI: 4.57-10.77%) and our feline (6.78%; 95% CI: 2.67-16.18%) samples were positive for Ehrlichia spp., eight canine (2.97%; 95% CI: 1.51-5.76%) and one feline (1.69%; 95% CI: 0.30-9.00%) samples were positive for Anaplasma spp. Five feline (8.47%; 95% CI: 3.67-18.35%) and three canine (1.12%; 95% CI: 0.38-3.23%) samples were positive in a SYBRGreen-based qPCR targeting the 16 S rRNA gene of hemotropic Mycoplasma spp. Sequencing and phylogenetic analyses allowed the identification of Bartonella henselae in four (one dog and three cat samples) of the five Bartonella-positive animals, and 'Candidatus Mycoplasma haemominutum' in three out of five hemoplasma-positive cats analyzed. In dogs, hemoplasma species could not be determined due to the lack of sequencing data. The Anaplasma spp. and Ehrlichia spp. positive samples did not yield amplicons in the conventional PCR assays for sequencing, precluding molecular identification at the species level. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first molecular detection of Bartonella spp. and hemoplasmas in domestic dogs and cats from El Salvador and the first molecular evidence of Anaplasma spp. and Ehrlichia spp. in domestic cats in the country.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Hyperammonemia in cats with acute (on chronic) kidney disease: associations with urea cycle amino acids, azotemia and acid-base status.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: McFadden K, Labato MA, Linder DE, Webster CR
papers.abstract: ObjectivesHyperammonemia occurs in cats with kidney disease although the pathophysiology is poorly understood. The objective of this study was to determine if hyperammonemia in cats with kidney disease is associated with decreased concentrations of plasma amino acids involved in the urea cycle and more severe acid-base derangements.MethodsTwenty cats presenting with acute kidney injury (AKI) and acute on chronic kidney disease (AoCKD) were prospectively enrolled. Fasting blood samples were analyzed for ammonia, pH, anion gap, electrolytes, lactate, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine and phosphorus. Plasma was frozen at -80 o C and shipped for amino acid analysis.ResultsFive of 20 cats had an AKI and 15/20 had AoCKD. Median age and weight were 12 years (range 3-14) and 4.5 kg (range 3-5.6), respectively. Seven cats were hyperammonemic (median 252 µmol/l, range 113-886) and 13 were not (median 23 µmol/l, range 11-49). Creatinine, BUN and phosphorus were significantly higher in hyperammonemic cats. BUN and phosphorus correlated with ammonia. Fifteen of 20 cats (75%) were acidotic but there was no difference in lactate or blood and urine pH between the cats with and without hyperammonemia. The anion gap was higher (29.6, range 27-40 vs 25.1, range 11-34) and serum bicarbonate lower (9 mEq/L, range 4.8-13.5 vs 11.9, range 8-24.2) in hyperammonemic cats. Median plasma citrulline (47 nMol/mL, range 31-128 vs 22, range 12-37) and ornithine (20 nMol/mL, range 12-33 vs 10, range 7-35) but not arginine concentrations were significantly higher in hyperammonemic cats (p<0.05). Plasma citrulline concentrations were positively correlated with serum creatinine (r = 0.621, p = 0.003).Conclusions and relevanceHyperammonemic cats with AKI/AoCKD do not have deficiencies in urea cycle amino acid concentrations but do have more severe azotemia with accompanying high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Increases in citrulline may reflect decreased kidney function.

papers.title: Echocardiographic prevalence and attachment-site patterns of left ventricular bands in cats.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Van den Noortgate G, Zablotski Y, Wess G
papers.abstract: The aim of the present study was to determine the echocardiographic prevalence and attachment-site patterns of left ventricular bands (LVBs) in cats and assess whether LVB counts differed by sex, sedation status, or echocardiographic group. In this prospective observational study, 200 cats undergoing complete transthoracic echocardiographic examination were evaluated for the presence, number, and attachment-site patterns of LVBs. LVBs were defined as discrete intracavitary linear structures connecting two myocardial structures within the left ventricle without insertion into the mitral valve leaflets. Each visible connection was classified according to predefined attachment-site categories. For the phenotype comparison, cats with normal left ventricular wall thickness or focal insertion-site thickening (n = 89) were compared with cats with a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) phenotype (n = 86). A total of 884 LVBs were identified. At least one LVB was detected in 199/200 cats, yielding an echocardiographic prevalence of 99.5%. The median number was four LVBs per cat (range 0-10). The most frequently observed attachment patterns involved the interventricular septum and papillary muscle or accessory papillary muscle-like structures. Overall, 51.9% of LVBs had at least one septal attachment, and 94.3% involved a papillary muscle or accessory papillary muscle-like structure. LVB counts did not differ by sex ( P  = 0.47), sedation status ( P  = 0.26), or between the combined normal/focal insertion-site thickening group and HCM phenotype group ( P  = 0.98). LVBs were identified in nearly all cats examined and represent a common echocardiographic finding. Most involved septal and papillary muscle-related attachment sites. Sex and sedation status were not significantly associated with LVB number, and no significant difference was identified between the normal/focal insertion-site thickening and HCM phenotype groups. These findings provide a reference framework for the echocardiographic recognition and classification of LVBs in cats under clinical imaging conditions. Thin tissue bands in the left side of the heart are visible on ultrasound in almost all cats Thin bands of tissue can cross the main pumping chamber on the left side of the heart. These structures are called left ventricular bands. Although they have been described in cats, it was unclear how often they can be seen on heart ultrasound and where they usually attach. We examined 200 cats who underwent a complete heart ultrasound examination. We recorded whether these bands were visible, how many were present, and which parts of the heart they connected with. Each clearly visible connection was counted separately, including branches within network-like structures. At least one band was visible in 199 of the 200 cats. In total, 884 connections were identified, with a typical count of four per cat and a range from none to 10. Most bands were attached to the wall separating the two pumping chambers and to muscles that help support the valve on the left side of the heart, or to smaller muscle-like structures. The number of bands did not differ between male and female cats, between sedated and non-sedated cats, or between cats with an ultrasound pattern of heart muscle thickening called hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and the study’s comparison group. These findings show that left ventricular bands are a very common ultrasound finding in cats. The study did not determine whether unusually thick bands or dense networks affect heart function or whether the visible connections correspond exactly to complete anatomical bands.

papers.title: Pull-out strength of cannulated compression headless screws and cortical screws in the feline sacrum.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Kornmayer M, Klement J, Zablotski Y, Thorwächter C, Wieser J
papers.abstract: The aim of this study was to compare the pull-out strength of cannulated compression headless screws (CCHSs) of two different lengths with that of cortical screws in the feline sacrum. In this experimental study, 30 cadavers of adult domestic shorthair cats were randomly assigned to three groups: single 2.4 mm cortical screws engaging 60% of the sacral width (CS 60, n = 10), 2.5 mm CCHSs engaging 60% of the sacral width (CCHSs 60, n = 10), and 2.5 mm CCHSs engaging 40% of the sacral width (CCHS 40, n = 10). Screws were inserted into feline sacra and tested for pull-out strength using a universal testing machine at a constant displacement rate of 0.2 mm/s up to 20 mm. Peak pull-out force (PPF), displacement at PPF, and stiffness were calculated from the load-displacement curves and compared among groups using Fisher's ANOVA and the Welch test. Post-hoc pairwise comparisons were performed using Student's t -tests and the Games-Howell test. Statistical significance was set at P ⩽0.05. Pairwise comparison of PPF showed significant differences between the CS 60 and CCHS 60 groups ( P  = 0.05) and between the CS 60 and CCHS 40 groups ( P  = 0.05). No significant difference was detected between the CCHS 60 and CCHS 40 groups ( P  = 0.98). For displacement at PPF and stiffness, no significant differences were identified in the pairwise comparison. Fully threaded cortical screws provide greater holding strength than partially threaded CCHSs in cadaveric feline sacra. In addition, a single short CCHS offers holding strength comparable to that of a CCHS of the conventionally recommended length.

papers.title: Renal health in cats with feline infectious peritonitis treated with GS-441524: Baseline findings and longitudinal effects.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: de Witt Curtius CC, Meli ML, Crespo Bouzon A, Wenk J, Stachowski JM, Cerchiaro I, Pineroli B, Unterer S, Felten S, Major A, Meunier SM, Howard J, Zwicklbauer K, Dorsch R, Hartmann K, Hofmann-Lehmann R, Spiri AM
papers.abstract: The aim of the present study was to assess renal health in cats with feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) undergoing antiviral treatment. GS-441524 is effective against FIP but its potential renal toxicity remains debated. Cats with confirmed FIP (n = 80) receiving oral GS-441524 for 42 days were assessed before (day 1; D1), during (D7, D42) and after treatment (D84, D183). Assessments included urine specific gravity (USG), urine protein:creatinine (UPC) ratio, urinary cystatin B (uCysB), urine protein electrophoresis, serum creatinine, urea and symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA). The term potential renal dysfunction was used for cats fulfilling the following criteria: creatinine ⩾140 µmol/l or SDMA ⩾18 µg/dl and USG <1.035. Serum amyloid A (SAA) and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein (AGP) were assessed in serum, feline coronavirus (FCoV) RNA in blood and urine (D1-D42). At baseline, 97.5% of cats had creatinine concentrations <140 µmol/l; by D183, 23.8% exceeded this threshold (D1-D183: P D <0.0001). Potential renal dysfunction criteria were met in 2.5% of cats at baseline and 8.8% at D183. In contrast, uCysB was increased in 83.8% of cats at D1 and declined during treatment (D1-D183: P D <0.0001). Cats with uCysB >100 ng/ml had higher UPC values ( P MWU <0.0001). Most cats had elevated AGP and SAA at baseline, which normalised during treatment (D1-D42: P D <0.0001). Proteinuria (UPC >0.2) was present in 91.3% on D1 and 3.8% on D183; urine protein electrophoresis at D1 revealed predominantly tubular and mixed patterns. Urine was more frequently FCoV RNA-positive than blood on D1 (68.8% vs 61.3%), but not on D7 (16.3% vs 45.0%). Treatment reversed FIP-associated renal abnormalities and inflammation observed at baseline. A small subset of cats met criteria compatible with potential renal dysfunction during the study. Even though it remains unknown whether these findings reflect delayed FIP-related renal insults or adverse antiviral effects, treatment duration should, in accordance with antimicrobial stewardship principles, be kept to the shortest effective period.

papers.title: Cutaneous Effects of Oral Polystyrene Microplastic Exposure in Mice: Oxidative Stress, Inflammation, and FGF5 Gene Dysregulation.
papers.authors: Islam MS, Koedrith P
papers.abstract: Microplastic (MP) pollution represents an escalating threat to mammalian health, yet the potential effects of oral MP exposure on mammalian skin remain poorly understood. This study investigated the effects of oral polystyrene microplastic (PS-MP) exposure on skin integrity, oxidative balance, and the expression of the Fibroblast Growth Factor 5 (FGF5) gene a key regulator controlling the transition between hair growth and regression phases in the hair cycle. Male Swiss albino mice were orally exposed to PS-MPs (4.8-5 µm) at low (0.1 mg) and high (0.2 mg) doses for 28 consecutive days. Biochemical analyses evaluated oxidative stress markers (CAT, SOD, POD, ROS, and MDA), serum enzyme activity (ALT, AST, ALP, and amylase), and mineral concentrations (Ca, Mg, and phosphate). Histopathological examination of H&E-stained skin sections assessed epidermal thickness, keratinocyte density, and dermal inflammation. Quantitative real-time PCR was used to measure FGF5 gene expression in dorsal skin, with Hprt1 as the internal control. Oral PS-MP exposure was associated with dose-dependent oxidative stress in skin tissue, reflected by elevated ROS (0.545 → 1.99 U/mg) and MDA (1.49 → 7.37 nmol/L) levels and significant depletion of antioxidant enzymes such as CAT (10.2 → 4.33 U/mg protein). Serum biochemical disturbances confirmed systemic metabolic stress. Histopathology revealed epidermal hyperplasia (16.46 → 34.18 µm), reduced keratinocyte density (22.1 → 7.0), and marked inflammatory infiltration. Importantly, FGF5 expression increased 1.35-fold, suggesting altered regulation of pathways associated with hair-follicle cycling. Oral PS-MP exposure was associated with oxidative stress, structural alterations, inflammation, and FGF5 upregulation in mouse skin. These findings suggest a potential association between oral PS-MP exposure and disruption of skin and hair-follicle homeostasis in mammals.

papers.title: Early Changes in Serum Protein Electrophoresis and Gamma Globulin during Initial 4 Weeks of Remdesivir Therapy in FIP Cats.
papers.authors: Khalili K, Cheraghi H, Saljooghian Isfahani MH
papers.abstract: Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) is a fatal multisystem inflammatory disorder of cats that was historically considered untreatable before the emergence of direct-acting antivirals. The objective of the study was to evaluate early serial changes in serum protein electrophoresis (SPE) patterns in cats treated with remdesivir for FIP, emphasizing gamma-globulin concentrations and percentages. Animals included eighteen client-owned cats diagnosed with FIP based on clinical presentation, standard clinicopathological profiles, and confirmatory RT-PCR. Cats received remdesivir for 4 weeks and were monitored weekly through clinical examinations and laboratory evaluations. Blood samples were collected at baseline (prior to treatment initiation) and weekly for 4 weeks. The SPE analyzed the blood taken every week for the serum protein fractions, such as albumin and the different globulins, namely α1-, α2-, β1-, β2-, and γ-globulins. The albumin to globulin ratio (A/G ratio) was also determined. Gamma globulins were found to be significantly reduced from a median of 3.1 g/dL at week 2 to a median of 2.2 g/dL at the end of week 4 (p < .05) in cats that showed clinical response. Notably, ROC curve analysis identified that a gamma-globulin percentage <23% at week 4 and 18.96% by week 6 (AUC = 0.9105) was strongly associated with complete clinical recovery and sustained relapse-free remission. Serial monitoring of serum protein electrophoresis, particularly longitudinal trends in gamma-globulin percentages and the A/G ratio, provides an objective, practical biomarker strategy to evaluate treatment response and guide the safe timing of antiviral therapy cessation in cats with FIP.

papers.title: Intratumoral STING agonist therapy as a potential bridge to surgery in canine sarcoma.
papers.authors: Hildebrand KM, Qiu RY, Salazar Arcila C, Park YJ, Hildebrand KN, Harris B, Kendal JK, Monument MJ
papers.abstract: Sarcomas are rare and aggressive malignancies in humans. Management of sarcoma primarily involves surgical intervention with neoadjuvant radiotherapy. Many sarcomas are refractory to existing immunotherapies. Recent studies in murine sarcoma have shown that activation of the stimulator of interferon genes pathway (STING) can induce tumor eradication. Although sarcomas are rare in humans, they occur frequently in dogs. Studying STING therapy in canine sarcoma patients provides a unique opportunity to explore a clinically translational animal model that recapitulates tumor size and clinical progression of human disease. Four sarcoma-bearing dogs were recruited for this study. All subjects underwent weekly intratumoral STING therapy until a surgical or humane-endpoints were reached. Tumor volume, vital signs, and weight were measured at each visit. Two STING agonists were studied (ADU-S100 - CDN and E7766). Sera were collected prior to and 6h following STING immunotherapy to measure systemic cytokine levels. Histologic assessment of tumors was completed at time of biopsy or necropsy. All dogs experienced a reduction in tumor volume. Two dogs became surgical candidates following STING treatment. Overall survival varied between 14-736 days among treated dogs. Systemic cytokine elevation was observed following STING therapy. At time of necropsy, none of the dogs showed macroscopic evidence of metastatic disease. Intralesional STING immunotherapy is a feasible treatment for dogs with sarcoma, demonstrating biological activity enabling surgical intervention in 2/4 dogs. At time of necropsy, no metastatic disease was observed. Future prospective cohort studies should be completed to further investigate this translational immunotherapy.

papers.title: Molecular and epidemiological characterization of Sporothrix brasiliensis isolates from canine sporotrichosis cases in Southeastern Brazil.
papers.authors: de Almeida LHM, Colombo SA, Tavares GC, Robe LJ, Bastos CV, de Azevedo MI
papers.abstract: Sporothrix brasiliensisis the main etiological agent of zoonotic sporotrichosis in Brazil and has been increasingly identified in animal hosts, including dogs. This study aimed to perform the characterization epidemiological and molecular of Sporothrix spp. isolates from canine hosts in an endemic urban region of southeastern Brazil. Fifteen isolates obtained from dogs diagnosed with sporotrichosis were confirmed as S. brasiliensis by PCR. Most affected dogs were domiciled and had no free access to the streets (86.7%), while 53.3% had a history of contact with cats presenting lesions and suspected of sporotrichosis, suggesting that exposure to potentially infected cats may represent an important risk factor for canine sporotrichosis. Lesions predominantly affected the nasal region, and the fixed cutaneous form was the most common clinical presentation. Network analyses based on partial sequences of the CAL and EF1α genes revealed eight haplotypes for CAL and four for EF1α, with haplotypes shared among isolates from humans, cats, and dogs across different Brazilian states. No clear host-associated pattern was evident in the analyzed dataset. These findings reinforce the relevance of dogs in the epidemiological context of sporotrichosis and contribute to our understanding of the genetic diversity of S. brasiliensis in non-feline hosts.

papers.title: Multimodal diagnostic imaging facilitates diagnosis and surgical approach in a cat with complete and partial left divisional liver lobe torsion.
papers.authors: Lee CCH, Fuchter LM, Crowley JD, Klever J
papers.abstract: A 1-year-old, male neutered domestic shorthair cat was presented to a referral hospital with a 24-h history of vomiting and anorexia and marked biochemical hepatopathy. Multiple imaging modalities, including radiography, ultrasonography and multiphase multidetector CT, were utilised and the diagnosis of liver lobe torsion (complete and partial torsion) was reached. The patient underwent exploratory celiotomy for liver lobectomy and made a full recovery. The cause of the liver lobe torsion was not evident on histological examination. This is a case report describing multiphase multidetector CT, along with radiographic and ultrasonographic findings of liver lobe torsion in a cat. Multiphase CT is valuable in identifying complete and partial liver torsion, with the portal venous phases key to assessing vascular integrity and the extent of ischaemia.

papers.title: Use of subconjunctival cyclosporine implants for treatment of feline eosinophilic keratoconjunctivitis: A case report.
papers.authors: Willems L, Roberts JK
papers.abstract: A 5-year-old, neutered male domestic shorthair cat was presented for evaluation of chronic bilateral eosinophilic keratoconjunctivitis (EK). The patient had a history of recurrent corneal plaques and conjunctivitis that were initially managed with systemic and topical immunosuppressive therapy. Long-term disease control was limited by poor tolerance of topical ophthalmic medications, resulting in inconsistent treatment and repeated disease recurrence affecting both eyes. Over several years, the cat was treated with subconjunctival triamcinolone acetonide, antiviral therapy, and topical megestrol acetate, with only partial and temporary improvement. As a result of persistent disease and inability to administer long-term topical therapy reliably, bilateral subconjunctival cyclosporine implants were surgically placed. Postoperative management included short-term topical antibiotic therapy. At 10-week and 7-month postoperative examinations, marked clinical improvement was observed, with resolution of most corneal plaques and substantial reduction in conjunctival inflammation. Feline EK is a chronic immune-mediated ocular surface disease that typically requires long-term topical immunosuppressive therapy. Successful management may be limited in patients who are resistant to medication administration. This case demonstrates that subconjunctival cyclosporine implants may represent a viable long-acting treatment option for feline EK when topical therapy cannot be consistently administered. To the authors' knowledge, the use of cyclosporine implants for the management of feline EK has not previously been reported. Use of long-acting cyclosporine implants for treatment of chronic inflammatory eye disease in a cat Feline eosinophilic keratoconjunctivitis is a chronic inflammatory eye disease that usually requires long-term treatment with immunosuppressive eye drops. However, some cats do not tolerate frequent eye medications, making consistent treatment difficult and allowing the disease to recur. This case report describes a cat with chronic eosinophilic keratoconjunctivitis who continued to have recurrent disease despite multiple medical treatments because long-term topical therapy could not be administered reliably. To provide sustained delivery of medication, cyclosporine implants were surgically placed beneath the conjunctiva of both eyes. After surgery, the cat showed marked improvement, with resolution of most corneal plaques and substantial reduction in conjunctival inflammation that persisted for at least 7 months. Although this report describes only a single patient, the results suggest that subconjunctival cyclosporine implants may provide a long-acting treatment option for cats with when topical medications cannot be administered consistently. Additional studies are needed to evaluate the safety, effectiveness, and long-term outcomes of this treatment in a larger number of cats.

papers.title: Common bile duct adenocarcinoma in a cat treated with surgical excision, choledochoduodenostomy and adjuvant toceranib phosphate.
papers.authors: Chan QYP, Lai A
papers.abstract: A 2-year-old male neutered domestic shorthair cat was referred 1 month after medical management of extrahepatic biliary tract obstruction for progressive lethargy and hyperbilirubinaemia. Abdominal ultrasonography identified a 10 mm obstructive common bile duct mass. The cat underwent common bile duct mass resection, choledochoduodenostomy and oesophagostomy tube placement, complicated by transient cardiac arrest. Histopathology confirmed biliary adenocarcinoma. Ongoing toceranib phosphate (toceranib) (2.44 mg/kg PO Monday, Wednesday, Friday; Palladia; Zoetis) was initiated 11 days postoperatively. Monitoring consisted of haematology, serum biochemistry, thoracic radiography and abdominal ultrasonography. Follow-up abdominal ultrasonography at 6 weeks, 14 weeks and 10.5 months documented a pyloric mass, absence of ultrasonographic evidence of the pyloric lesion and diffuse hepatic progression, respectively. Cytology of the pyloric mass and hepatic lesions confirmed carcinoma. Despite progression, the cat remained clinically well with normal serum total bilirubin and continued toceranib postoperatively for 18 months. This report presents the first documented management of feline common bile duct adenocarcinoma combining surgical resection and oral toceranib, with objective assessment of treatment response. Toceranib therapy was ongoing 7.5 months after ultrasonographic disease progression, and the cat remained alive at that time, achieving a survival duration far exceeding previously reported median survival times for treated feline biliary carcinoma. Toceranib was well tolerated, with adverse effects limited to antiemetic-responsive nausea.

papers.title: Surgical management of bilateral atypical tibial fractures associated with long-term bisphosphonate therapy in a cat.
papers.authors: Wong JKW, Colthurst SMM
papers.abstract: An 8-year-old, indoor, male neutered Oriental mixed-breed cat was presented with acute bilateral pelvic limb lameness without preceding trauma. The cat had received oral alendronate for 4.5 years for the management of feline idiopathic hypercalcaemia. Radiographs revealed bilateral, closed, comminuted proximal tibial and fibular fractures with cortical sclerosis. Staged bilateral open reduction and internal fixation were performed using orthogonal locking compression plates. Alendronate therapy was discontinued, and the cat remained normocalcaemic during 8 months of follow-up. Despite robust stabilisation, traumatic re-fracture of the right tibia occurred after inadequate confinement, necessitating revision fixation with longer implants and the addition of allogeneic demineralised bone matrix (DBM). Delayed union and marked callus formation were observed in the left tibia, consistent with suppressed bone remodelling secondary to chronic alendronate therapy. In contrast, the revised right tibial fracture, treated with adjunctive DBM, demonstrated faster progression of healing. Radiographic monitoring demonstrated osseous union without further complications or evidence of additional fractures, illustrating that favourable outcomes are achievable in cats with bilateral bisphosphonate (BP)-associated insufficiency fractures when appropriately managed. This report represents the second documented case of BP-associated fractures in a cat managed surgically with extensive follow-up. It is the first to describe bilateral tibial fracture repair and the use of adjunctive DBM for BP-associated fractures. It highlights that favourable outcomes are achievable in these cases through orthogonal plating combined with adjunctive DBM, and discontinued BP therapy to reduce future fracture risk. This report also supports serial radiographic monitoring, particularly within 5 years of treatment initiation.

papers.title: A case of portal vein thrombosis in a cat with partial splenic rotation and intermittent colonic displacement.
papers.authors: Kim H, Jo Y, Song J
papers.abstract: A 4-year-old, neutered male Turkish Angora cat presented with lethargy, mental dullness, and lower urinary tract signs. Hematological and biochemical analyses confirmed hepatic dysfunction. Diagnostic imaging identified portal vein thrombosis (PVT), an extrahepatic portosystemic shunt, and collateral vessels surrounding the PVT. In addition, partial splenic rotation and intermittent colonic displacement were identified. Primary hepatic disease, a common cause of PVT, could not be excluded in this patient, and visceral positional abnormalities were considered to have played a significant role in the development of PVT. Initial treatment consisted of anticoagulant therapy with rivaroxaban and symptomatic management of hepatic dysfunction and secondary complications. After initiation of therapy, the patient remained clinically stable, with resolution of clinical signs despite persistent imaging evidence of PVT. This is the first report in veterinary medicine to identify partial splenic rotation and intermittent colonic displacement as possible causes of PVT. Furthermore, this case demonstrates that a favorable clinical outcome may be achieved through conservative medical management of PVT secondary to abdominal visceral positional abnormalities.

papers.title: Lymphocytic ganglionitis associated with intestinal obstruction in two cats with chronic enteropathy.
papers.authors: Tirelli I, Crisonà M, Muscatello LV, Fumeo M, Fidanzio F, Mattioli G, Del Magno S, Diana A, Del Baldo F, Corsini A
papers.abstract: Neuromuscular gastrointestinal disorders are rarely reported in cats and may cause severe dysmotility. We describe two cats with chronic gastrointestinal signs in which histopathology revealed lymphocytic enteric ganglionitis involving both the myenteric and submucosal plexuses, associated with lymphoplasmacytic enteritis. In case 1, chronic gastric stasis and anorexia progressed to vomiting and proximal gastrointestinal dilation, and surgery identified duodenal adhesions and stenosis; the cat deteriorated postoperatively and was euthanased. In case 2, abdominal distension and suspected obstruction were associated with severe intestinal gas distension, faecal impaction and ileocolic stenosis requiring surgical resection. Pyridostigmine was started but discontinued because of suspected adverse effects, and the cat later died of congestive heart failure. This case series highlights lymphocytic enteric ganglionitis as a possible cause or contributor to chronic intestinal dysmotility in cats, even in the presence of concurrent obstructive lesions. It also expands the limited veterinary literature on this condition and supports its inclusion among differential diagnoses in cats with chronic pseudo-obstructive gastrointestinal signs. Intestinal nerve inflammation as a possible cause of chronic digestive disease in cats Chronic digestive disorders caused by abnormal movement of the intestine are uncommon in cats and can be difficult to diagnose. In some cases, these problems are linked to inflammation affecting the network of nerves that controls the normal movement of food through the gastrointestinal tract. In this report, we describe two cats with long-term digestive signs in which microscopic examination of intestinal tissue identified inflammation affecting these intestinal nerves, together with chronic intestinal inflammation. Both cats also had narrowing of part of the intestine that may have contributed to their clinical signs. However, their clinical history suggested that impaired intestinal movement was already present and played an important role in the disease. These cases suggest that inflammation of the intestinal nerves may contribute to chronic digestive disorders in cats, even when a physical narrowing of the intestine is also present. Veterinarians should therefore consider this condition as a possible cause of chronic gastrointestinal disease associated with poor intestinal motility.

papers.title: Azotemia does not clinically affect the interpretation of increased serum pancreatic lipase activity or pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity in dogs.
papers.authors: Niemann L, Vigani A, Torgerson PR, Kook PH
papers.abstract: The objective was to compare paired pancreatic lipase immunoreactivity (PLI) concentrations and pancreatic lipase activity in serum samples in a population of azotemic dogs. This observational study included client-owned dogs with azotemia and serum lipase activity above the reference interval (17 to 156 U/L). Lipase activity (Roche LIPC lipase colorimetric assay, substrate 1,2-o-dilauryl-rac-glycero-3-glutaric acid-[60-methylresorufin] ester) and serum creatinine concentration were measured as part of routine clinical diagnostics. Monthly screening identified leftover serum samples from azotemic dogs with hyperlipasemia. The PLI concentration was measured from banked serum aliquots of those samples. Associations between serum creatinine concentration, lipase activity, and PLI concentration were evaluated using correlation analysis and generalized linear mixed-effects models. 49 serum samples from 32 dogs were included. Serum creatinine concentration weakly correlated with lipase activity (Spearman rank correlation coefficient = 0.36) and PLI concentration (Spearman rank correlation coefficient = 0.30). Generalized linear mixed-effects modeling identified a significant association between azotemia and lipase activity, whereas no significant association was identified for PLI concentration. Per 0.3-mg/dL increase in serum creatinine concentration, lipase activity increased by 1.11 U/L. Although azotemia was statistically associated with a significant increase in lipase activity in azotemic dogs, the magnitude of this effect was negligible. Azotemia has no clinically relevant effect on the diagnostic interpretation of increased lipase activity in dogs.

papers.title: Cavitary effusion patterns are associated with different survival times in dogs with pulmonary hypertension and right-sided congestive heart failure.
papers.authors: Cho J, Kim M, Choi M, Lee J, Park C
papers.abstract: To describe and compare clinical characteristics and survival among dogs with pulmonary hypertension-associated right-sided congestive heart failure (RCHF) according to cavitary effusion pattern. This retrospective multicenter observational study included client-owned dogs with pulmonary hypertension-associated RCHF presented to 3 referral hospitals from February 2021 through April 2025. Pulmonary hypertension was assessed echocardiographically, and RCHF was defined by ascites with caudal vena cava dilation. Dogs were categorized as having ascites alone, ascites with pleural effusion, or ascites with pericardial effusion. Clinical and imaging characteristics were compared among groups, and survival was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier and exploratory Cox regression analyses. 61 dogs were included: 40 with ascites alone, 16 with pleural effusion, and 5 with pericardial effusion. Median survival was 157, 42.5, and 7 days, respectively. In an exploratory multivariable Cox model adjusted for age and grouped etiology, pericardial effusion was associated with a higher mortality hazard compared with ascites alone. Pleural effusion was not significantly associated with mortality. Survival differed according to cavitary effusion pattern in this retrospective cohort of dogs with RCHF. Dogs with concurrent pericardial effusion had the shortest observed survival and a higher adjusted mortality hazard, although this finding should be interpreted cautiously because only 5 dogs had pericardial effusion. Cavitary effusion pattern may provide additional descriptive information when assessing dogs with RCHF. Concurrent pericardial effusion may identify a subgroup with shorter observed survival, but its prognostic value requires confirmation in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Distribution and clinical features of raccoon roundworm (Baylisascaris procyonis) infection in dogs and cats as detected by fecal quantitative polymerase chain reaction.
papers.authors: Teng E, Kimmerlein AK, Jimenez Castro PD, Kerl ME, Evason M, Willcox JL, Tereski J, Loo S, Leutenegger CM
papers.abstract: To describe the geographic distribution and clinical features of dogs and cats with Baylisascaris procyonis detected by fecal quantitative PCR (qPCR). Dogs and cats in the US and Canada that were diagnosed with B procyonis via fecal qPCR performed by a veterinary diagnostic laboratory from March 3, 2022, through November 1, 2023, were identified. Details about patient demographics, clinical signs, treatment, and outcome were retrospectively captured via questionnaires sent to each pet's primary care veterinarian. Descriptive statistics were calculated. B procyonis was detected in 74 dogs and 3 cats through fecal qPCR screening. Dogs were from Canada (n = 22) and the US (52), and cats were from the US (3). The US-detected samples were from the Midwest (35%) and Northeast (22%). Most US-detected cases (69%) resided in a suburban environment, and most Canadian cases (80%) resided in an urban environment. Clinical signs were not reported in most (62%) cases with fecal qPCR-detected B procyonis. Gastrointestinal signs were reported in 36% of cases, and resolution of gastrointestinal signs following anthelmintic treatment was reported in most (72.9%) of those. The geographic distribution of detected B procyonis in dogs and cats is similar to that reported in raccoons. Reported clinical disease appears mild and responsive to anthelmintic treatment in most dogs and cats. Veterinarian awareness of risk regions for raccoon roundworm detection is critical for One Health. Detection of B procyonis through routine fecal screening of dogs and cats informs risk of environmental exposure and zoonoses and allows for targeted antiparasitic prevention.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-based dental screening using a cellular phone in dogs: a practical tool for detecting visible calculus and gingivitis.
papers.authors: Kim P, Kim SE, Lee E, Huh EA, Kim H, Park S, Jeon J, Seo K
papers.abstract: To train, validate, and evaluate a cellular phone-based AI system for image-level classification of visible dental calculus and gingivitis in conscious dogs. This multicenter retrospective study used dental photographs collected from 12 veterinary hospitals (2022 through 2024). Dental photographs were obtained from conscious dogs using cellular phone cameras. A single veterinarian assigned reference labels using standardized criteria. Separate binary datasets for dental calculus and gingivitis were split by dog into training, validation, and independent test datasets. A convolutional neural network was trained using transfer learning, and final models were selected by validation loss. A total of 3,170 dogs were included in this study. For dental calculus, 2,771 images were analyzed: 2,451 for training and validation and 320 in the independent test dataset. For gingivitis, 1,684 images were analyzed: 1,434 for training and validation and 250 in the independent test dataset. On the independent test datasets, the dental calculus model achieved precision of 0.977 (95% CI, 0.941 to 0.991), sensitivity of 0.965 (95% CI, 0.926 to 0.984), specificity of 0.973 (95% CI, 0.932 to 0.989), accuracy of 0.969 (95% CI, 0.943 to 0.983), and F1 score of 0.971. The gingivitis model achieved precision of 0.912 (95% CI, 0.855 to 0.948), sensitivity of 0.950 (95% CI, 0.901 to 0.976), specificity of 0.881 (95% CI, 0.807 to 0.929), accuracy of 0.920 (95% CI, 0.880 to 0.948), and F1 score of 0.931. The AI system demonstrated high classification performance for visible dental calculus and gingivitis in conscious dogs. This system may serve as an adjunctive screening and triage tool but is not intended to replace comprehensive oral examination or dental radiography.

papers.title: Characteristics of veterinary surgical patient safety events: a multicenter retrospective analysis.
papers.authors: Tobias JS, Frederick SW, Shaw SP, Kerl ME, Smith KC, Low RM
papers.abstract: To characterize voluntarily reported surgical patient safety events (SPSEs) occurring in primary care, specialty, and emergency veterinary facilities in North America and Europe. This retrospective study evaluated SPSE reports submitted to a single proprietary veterinary patient safety event recording platform in North America and Europe between March 1, 2023, and June 8, 2026. Facility type, patient species, event subtype, injury, severity, and reporter-perceived risk of recurrence were collected. Associations between species, veterinary facility type, event subcategory, SPSE severity score, and future risk of a similar SPSE occurring were evaluated using a χ2-test of independence. A total of 3,822 SPSEs were reported at 2,046 facilities during the study window, with most (n = 2,336 [61.1%]) reports made from primary care facilities. There were 2,487 (65.1%) dog SPSEs and 734 (19.2%) cat SPSEs. Serious harm or death was reported in 1,340 (35.1%) SPSEs, while the remaining 2,482 (64.9%) reported minor harm, no harm, or a near miss. Unexpected complication (n = 1,398 [36.6%]) and recognized complication (n = 927 [24.3%]) were the most common injury types. Only 7.1% (n = 270) SPSEs were rated very likely to recur. Cat SPSEs were overrepresented in primary care compared to specialty facilities, and cat SPSEs were more likely to describe mortality. Prolonged procedure time was more common in specialty (23.6%) than primary care (2.6%) facilities. Surgical patient safety events occurred across a broad range of veterinary practice settings and were associated with potentially devastating outcomes. Robust patient safety event reporting platforms facilitate identification of common SPSEs, which may guide quality improvement initiatives.

papers.title: Approaching canine inflammatory myopathy by cluster analysis: an immunohistopathological observational study.
papers.authors: Alf V, Kolb N, Zablotski Y, Mandigers PJJ, Matiasek K, Rosati M
papers.abstract: Immune-mediated inflammatory myopathies (IMs) in dogs represent a heterogeneous group of disorders with incompletely characterized histopathological and immunophenotypic characteristics. This study aimed to identify multiparametric histological and immunophenotypic patterns in canine IMs to support accurate diagnosis from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) muscle biopsies. A cohort of 162 dogs was retrospectively analyzed using a standardized 91-variable histopathological grading scheme, immunohistochemistry for CD3, CD8, CD20, IBA-1, and MHC II, and hierarchical k-means cluster analysis. Multimodel inference was applied to identify associations between immune markers and infiltrating cells with the presence of myonecrosis, fibrosis, myoregeneration, and muscle atrophy within the study population. Four distinct histopathological subgroups were identified. Cluster 1 (56%) was characterized by fiber-invasive, endomysial infiltration with CD3 + T-cell predominance over CD20 + B-cells and extensive myonecrosis, encompassing cases of polymyositis, infectious myositis, and breed-specific myositides. Cluster 2 (28%) demonstrated broad, compartment-spanning infiltration with CD20 + B-cell predominance over T-cells, lower rates of myonecrosis, and included masticatory muscle myositis cases alongside limb muscle polymyositis of similar immunophenotype. Cluster 3 (10%) exhibited diffuse, severe inflammatory infiltration with a balanced B/T-cell composition and marked fibrosis, representing end-stage disease. Cluster 4 (6%) was defined by vasculocentric inflammatory infiltration, B-cell predominance over T-cells, and minimal myonecrosis, consistent with immune-mediated vasculitis. Multimodel inference further revealed that B-cell infiltration was negatively associated with myonecrosis across the total cohort, while macrophages and mast cells were positively associated with fiber destruction. B-cells and plasma cells were independently associated with fibrosis across multiple clusters. These findings establish a histopathology- and immunophenotype-based classification framework for canine IMs, highlighting the need for subtype-specific diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Short-term clinical outcomes of feline maxillofacial trauma management.
papers.authors: Palmquist J, Rawlinson JE, Hoyer NK
papers.abstract: Maxillary and mandibular fractures frequently occur in cats presenting with maxillofacial trauma, and prompt evaluation and management are essential for soft and hard tissue healing. The aim of this retrospective descriptive study was to evaluate the immediate outcomes and complications associated with emergent maxillofacial trauma management in cats. The study included 42 cats that presented to a tertiary animal hospital for maxillofacial trauma. All medical records and imaging were reviewed for etiology, concurrent trauma, fracture location, treatment, treatment revisions, complications, and management of complications. The most common location for trauma was the mandibular ramus (23%) and the mandibular symphysis (22%), followed by the temporomandibular joint (Fracture: 11%, Luxation: 7%). Trauma associated with the maxilla (26%) and mandible (67%) were disproportionate. The most utilized management techniques were symphyseal fixation (29%), tape muzzle (15%), rigid maxillomandibular fixation (RMMF) (15%), and modified maxillomandibular fixation (BMMF) (15%). Thirty-nine of 42 (93%) cases had satisfactory outcomes with a complication rate of 54% (21/39), the most common complication being malocclusion (20/21; 95%). Three of 42 patients had unsatisfactory recoveries with 2 dying of unrelated causes prior to bony healing and 1 lost to follow-up following temporomandibular joint (TMJ) ankylosis. Acute diagnosis and management of feline maxillofacial trauma can have satisfactory healing and good outcomes if complications can be managed effectively. Trauma management and technique selection depends heavily on fracture location, available dentition, patient factors, and owner ability to manage postoperative care.

papers.title: Exclusive feeding of a highly hydrolyzed herring-protein diet is associated with reduced CIBDAI scores and body-weight gain in dogs with severe chronic enteropathy: a prospective open-label pilot study.
papers.authors: Malewska K, Jank M, Otto S, Kurosad A
papers.abstract: Chronic enteropathy (CE) is common in dogs, and hydrolyzed protein diets are a mainstay of management, particularly in food-responsive enteropathy. Evidence for exclusive feeding of highly hydrolyzed fish-protein diets in client-owned dogs with high clinical activity scores remains limited. This pilot study does not claim that enrolled dogs had failed a previous hydrolyzed-protein trial. Ten client-owned dogs with severe CE (Canine Inflammatory Bowel Disease Activity Index [CIBDAI] ≥ 7) were enrolled in an open-label, uncontrolled, prospective pilot study. All dogs were fed exclusively a commercial diet containing highly hydrolyzed herring protein (manufacturer specification: 70% of peptides <2 kDa; remainder ≤5 kDa) for 8 weeks. CIBDAI, an ordinal composite score, was the principal clinical outcome and was analyzed only with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and reported as median (IQR). Body weight and a clinicopathological panel were recorded at baseline and day 56. CIBDAI was assigned at both time points by the same attending clinician at the enrolment site. Owners completed a non-validated, exploratory questionnaire on palatability, acceptance and perceived well-being. CIBDAI decreased from a median of 9 (IQR 8-11) at day 0 to 0 (IQR 0-1) at day 56 (Hodges-Lehmann median change = -8.5 points, approximate 95% CI -10 to -7.5; Wilcoxon exact p  = 0.002). Body weight increased in all 10 dogs, from 7.89 ± 4.04 kg to 9.38 ± 4.55 kg (mean change +1.49 kg, 95% CI 1.04-1.94). Serum total protein and albumin increased within adult reference intervals (mean changes +2.6 g/L and +2.5 g/L). Exploratory increases in ALT, creatinine and fructosamine were also observed; these analytes are not markers of protein status and are not interpreted as beneficial nutritional endpoints. Owners reported perceived clinical improvement within 1-3 days in 6/10 dogs and within 3-6 days in 4/10 dogs. The diet was described as palatable in 9/10 dogs. No dog had a documented unsuccessful prior hydrolyzed-protein trial: 5/10 owners had been offered such a diet and declined it, 4/10 had never been offered one, and 1/10 could not recall. Available detail on prior diets is given in supplementary table. In this small, uncontrolled, open-label pilot cohort, exclusive feeding of the test diet was associated with a large reduction in CIBDAI and with weight gain. The design cannot establish the efficacy of herring hydrolysate, the relevance of peptide molecular size or superiority over other hydrolyzed or elimination diets, and it does not support a recommendation to use this formulation before immunosuppressive therapy. Randomized, blinded, comparator-controlled studies with predefined primary endpoints are required.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Dysbiosis correlates with more severe changes in intestinal function in cats with chronic enteropathy.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Chen CC, Moraiti KT, Giordano MV, Blake AB, Pilla R, Giaretta PR, Tolbert MK, Xenoulis PG, Crisi PE, Boari A, Suchodolski JS
papers.abstract: BackgroundMultiple pathophysiological mechanisms have been reported in animals with chronic enteropathy, as reflected by altered serum and fecal metabolites indicative of mucosal damage (e.g., fecal cholesterol, nervonic acid, arachidonic acid), malabsorption (e.g., serum cobalamin, fecal glucose), and loss of microbial function (e.g., fecal bile acid conversion). Furthermore, in dogs, marked intestinal dysbiosis has been linked to more severe underlying intestinal dysfunction, but this relationship is less characterized in cats.ObjectivesCharacterizing fecal microbiome and metabolome in healthy cats (HC), and cats with chronic enteropathy (FCE), either with increased dysbiosis index (DI > 0) or normal DI (< 0).MethodsRetrospective cross-sectional study including 49 HC and 71 cats with FCE. Fecal microbiome was assessed by DNA shotgun sequencing and qPCR-based DI. Targeted fecal metabolites (long-chain fatty acids, sterols, bile acids, and carbohydrates) were measured by mass spectrometry-based platforms.ResultsMultivariate analysis accounted for age, showed significant differences in metabolomic (median R 2 [95% CI]: 0.19 [0.15-0.24]), microbial (0.17 [0.11-0.24]), and functional gene (0.16 [0.10-0.25]) profiles in cats with FCE (adjusted-P < 0.01), with more pronounced shifts in those with increased DI. Fecal cholesterol, nervonic acid, and arachidonic acid were higher in FCE (adjusted-P < 0.01) and correlated positively with DI (r = 0.33, 0.41, and 0.44, respectively; adjusted-P < 0.01). Increased fecal glucose and primary bile acid percentage were observed only in FCE-increased DI. A significantly lower cobalamin concentration was observed in cats with increased DI compared to those with a normal DI.Conclusions and relevanceFCE is associated with multiple functional marker alterations, including intestinal cell structural damage, malabsorption, and disrupted microbial function. These changes are not present in all cats, confirming that FCE is heterogeneous with varying degrees of underlying pathology. Cats with FCE with increased dysbiosis index exhibited more severe functional changes compared to those with normal dysbiosis index.

papers.title: Antibiograms generated in the United States support use of potentiated sulfonamides and intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanic acid when antimicrobials are needed in Escherichia coli canine pyometra.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Marino KN, Buote N, Glass J, Guarino C, Sobkowich K, Szlosek D, Cazer CL
papers.abstract: Evaluate antimicrobial susceptibility patterns among bacterial pathogens isolated from canine pyometra cases and generate a cumulative antibiogram to inform evidence-based treatment recommendations. This observational retrospective study included canine uterine samples submitted for antimicrobial susceptibility testing to Idexx Laboratories and the Cornell University Animal Health Diagnostic Center between 2007 and 2023 in the US. Susceptibility results were interpreted according to current Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute criteria. Cumulative antibiograms were generated with an interactive app for analysis of diagnostic antimicrobial susceptibility test data (AMR Visualizer; RShiny). Across the 2 laboratories, 6,462 bacterial isolates were included. Escherichia coli was the predominant pathogen (71.7%). Among E coli isolates, poor susceptibility was observed to penicillins, β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations, tetracyclines, and chloramphenicol. Excellent susceptibility was maintained to aminoglycosides, third-generation cephalosporins, potentiated sulfonamides, and imipenem. Most E coli isolates were susceptible-dose-dependent to fluoroquinolones and susceptible with increased exposure to intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. Most canine pyometras are caused by E coli. The in vitro antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of these isolates contribute to understanding resistance trends and support antimicrobial stewardship efforts. Susceptibility should be interpreted in the context of regimens used for breakpoint development. When perioperative antimicrobial therapy of pyometras is appropriate, veterinarians can use antibiograms to assist in selecting an effective and appropriate antimicrobial before susceptibility test results are available. These antibiograms suggest that folate-pathway inhibitors could be effective empiric choices that align with antimicrobial stewardship principles. High-exposure intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanic acid could be an effective choice in regions where the product is available.

papers.title: Escherichia coli isolated from canine pyometra show decreased susceptibility to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid in dogs.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Fautz Z, Amato N, Windsor R
papers.abstract: To describe bacterial culture results and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns for dogs undergoing surgical treatment for pyometra. This retrospective study included dogs that underwent ovariohysterectomy at referral hospitals and had a positive bacterial culture of uterine fluid or histopathologic changes consistent with pyometra between January 2020 and December 2024. Data collected from medical records included clinical signs on presentation, hematological and biochemical abnormalities, aerobic and anaerobic bacterial isolates, antimicrobial susceptibility results, and peri- and postoperative antimicrobial administration. Prevalence of antimicrobial susceptibility was compared across select geographic regions and between Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) susceptibility interpretation guideline editions. 278 dogs were included. Neutrophilia was identified in 74.2% of dogs. Only 1 bacterium was isolated in 88.8% of dogs, while 10.4% of cases were polymicrobial. Escherichia coli was the most common isolate (73.1%). Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and enrofloxacin were prescribed postoperatively to 77.6% and 51.1% of dogs, respectively. Using CLSI VET01S edition 4, E coli susceptibility to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and enrofloxacin was present in 30.3% and 96.9% of isolates, respectively. Reclassification using CLSI VET01S edition 7 resulted in lower susceptibility classifications in 9 of 10 antimicrobials evaluated, including reductions of 46.9% for amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and 3.1% for enrofloxacin. Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid was frequently prescribed despite limited susceptibility among E coli isolates. Updated CLSI breakpoints reclassified susceptibility for most antimicrobials despite unchanged MICs. Regional antibiograms may show decreased susceptibility compared to historical recommendations. Judicious empiric antimicrobial selection should be guided by antimicrobial stewardship principles rather than routine reliance on any single antimicrobial.

papers.title: Sepsis and elevated creatinine predict poor outcomes in uncomplicated canine pyometra, and empirically prescribed antibiotics do not match bacterial susceptibility or improve survival.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Jones AE, Rishniw M, Raux IL, Rosselli D, Thomas D, Westmoreland C, Thieman K, Coleman KA, Gollnick H, Hildebrandt I, Gibson EA, Brison BA, Gao Q, Tillson M, Lux CN, Buote NJ
papers.abstract: To identify variables associated with prolonged hospitalization or nonsurvival in the surgical management of pyometra in dogs and to report uterine bacterial susceptibility in comparison with empirically prescribed antibiotics. Retrospective study of dogs that underwent ovariohysterectomy for management of pyometra at 8 tertiary referral centers between December 1, 2008, and December 31, 2023. Data collected included signalment, preoperative/operative data, antibiotic utilization, and clinical follow-up. 625 dogs met inclusion criteria. Forty dogs (6.4%) experienced major short-term complications, and 604 dogs (96.6%) survived to discharge. Elevated preoperative creatinine concentration and sepsis increased the risk of nonsurvival. Survival to discharge did not differ between nonseptic dogs that received pre- or intraoperative antibiotics and those that did not. Sepsis, elevated creatinine, and interaction between elevated creatinine and altered mentation increased hospitalization duration. At least 1 inappropriate outpatient antibiotic was prescribed in 34.4% (116 of 337) of cases; most dogs that received inappropriate antibiotics were empirically prescribed amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (102 of 116 [87.9%]). Surgical management of pyometra in the tertiary referral setting had a good prognosis regardless of prescribed antibiotic bacterial susceptibility. Elevated creatinine and/or sepsis increased risk of mortality and prolonged hospitalization. The use of pre- and intraoperative antibiotics in nonseptic dogs was not associated with outcome. There was no clear clinical benefit of antibiotic use in the surgical management of pyometra in nonseptic dogs. If empiric antibiotics are indicated, the bacterial susceptibility profile of this patient population suggests a high likelihood of resistance to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid.

papers.title: Skin fragility in a 12-year-old domestic shorthair cat.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Athayde CO, Hartmann G, Bandinelli MB, Pöppl ÁG, Pavarini SP

papers.title: Comparing compressed 2-dose and 3-dose melarsomine protocols in the era of adjunctive therapy: a randomized clinical trial of 168 dogs with heartworm disease.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Jacobson LS, Dyer JL, Van Vlake A, DiGangi BA, Horowitz MA, Levy JK
papers.abstract: To test the hypothesis that, when used with doxycycline, moxidectin, and prednisone, 2-dose melarsomine would be as safe and effective as 3-dose melarsomine. A randomized clinical trial was conducted from April 2024 to December 2025, comparing compressed 2-dose and 3-dose melarsomine protocols. Dogs with Class 1 or 2 heartworm disease received sustained-release moxidectin, doxycycline, prednisone, and 2 or 3 injections of melarsomine. Melarsomine was administered on days 14 and 15 (2-dose group) or days 14, 44, and 45 (3-dose group). Dogs were exercise restricted for 4 weeks following melarsomine. Daily clinical observations were made until the last day of exercise restriction. Antigen tests were performed 6 or 9 months after melarsomine. 168 dogs completed treatment (2-dose group, n = 85; 3-dose group, 83), and 165 were retested (2-dose group, 85; 3-dose group, 80). There was no significant difference in efficacy between the 2-dose group (95.3%; 95% CI, 88.4% to 98.7%) and the 3-dose group (98.8%; exact 95% CI, 93.2% to 100.0%). The sample size was insufficient for conclusive noninferiority analysis at the predefined noninferiority margin of 4%. Survival was 100%. Complications were rare, with 7 dogs requiring thoracic radiographs with or without additional treatment, but none requiring intensive management. Incidence of post-melarsomine cough, increased respiratory effort, and weakness was not significantly different between groups. A compressed 2-dose melarsomine protocol, with doxycycline, moxidectin, and prednisone, was safe and effective. Compared with 3-dose protocols, the 2-dose melarsomine protocol reduces the cost, resources, and time required to treat heartworm disease.

papers.title: Canine parvovirus cases (2010-2023): a retrospective study of 78,977 cases demonstrates declining incidence, but mortality risk remains.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Morrison J, George CM, Kollasch TM, Pattee JC, Ryan WG, Moore GE
papers.abstract: To investigate changes in characteristics of dogs diagnosed with canine parvovirus (CPV) disease presenting to a national network of primary care veterinary hospitals. Records were searched from January 1, 2010, through June 30, 2023. Data were collected on signalment, clinical signs, laboratory results, and mortality for CPV-affected dogs. Variables were assessed via stepwise logistic regression models for association with mortality. Across > 1,000 hospitals, CPV was diagnosed in 78,977 dogs, declining from 45.2 cases per 10,000 dogs per year in 2010 to 6.5 cases per 10,000 dogs per year in 2022. Diagnoses were greatest in April to June, while 46.3% of cases were aged between 8 and 16 weeks. From 2010 to 2022, median age at diagnosis declined from 17 to 14 weeks. The most commonly affected breeds were pit bull-type dog, Chihuahua, Labrador Retriever, German Shepherd Dog, and mixed breed (combined, 54.3% of the study population). Of 37,707 patients with 14-day survival information, 43.6% died or were euthanized. Being neutered or spayed (OR, 0.04; 95% CI, 0.02 to 0.08), having increased body weight, or having multiple intestinal parasites significantly reduced odds of mortality. Variables significantly associated with increased odds of mortality were hypoproteinemia (OR, 4.44; 95% CI, 2.01 to 9.81), underweight (OR, 2.99; 95% CI, 1.40 to -6.36), lymphopenia, leukopenia, and increased ALT. The number of CPV cases and mortality declined over the study period. However, CPV infections still occur in thousands of dogs annually, and risks of mortality persist. Dogs remain at risk of fatal CPV infection. Identification of mortality-associated factors may allow more targeted interventions and improve prognostic capabilities.

papers.title: Retrospective analysis of 68 domestic ferrets with urethral obstruction shows high rate of euthanasia at presentation despite good survival to discharge.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: O'Malley B, Sadar MJ, Alexander AB, Bercier M
papers.abstract: To establish a hospital proportional morbidity rate (HPMR) for urethral obstructions (UOs) in domestic ferrets; describe clinical presentation, interventions, and outcomes; and report associations with UO etiologies and survival. In this retrospective, descriptive, epidemiological study, electronic medical records were evaluated from ferrets presenting to 3 academic institutions in the US between 2013 and 2023. Descriptive and bivariate statistical analyses were performed. Parametric and nonparametric results are reported as mean ± SD or median (IQR). A total of 3,242 records were reviewed. The HPMR was 2.09% (68 of 3,242). Urethral obstruction etiologies included urolithiasis (57.4% [39 of 68]), adrenal disease-associated prostatic disease (19.12% [13 of 68]), and undiagnosed etiology (23.53% [16 of 68]). Twenty-seven of 66 ferrets (40.91%) were euthanized on presentation. Of the remaining ferrets, 92.31% (36 of 39) survived to discharge. Average hospitalization time was 2.82 ± 2.21 days. Complications occurred in 23.08% (9 of 39) of ferrets, and recurrence rate after discharge was 31.6% (6 of 19) with a median of 19 days (IQR, 1 to 1,164 days). Ferrets with urolithiasis were significantly younger (median, 2 years old) and had significantly higher blood glucose (median, 127 mg/dL) compared to ferrets with adrenal disease-associated prostatic disease (median age, 5 years old; median blood glucose, 91 mg/dL). Ferrets that survived to discharge had significantly higher body temperature on admission (median, 37.4 °C [99.4 °F]) compared to ferrets that were euthanized (median, 36.7 °C [98 °F]). Ferrets with UO had an HPMR, hospitalization times, and survival and recurrence rates that were similar to those of cats. These findings provide objective prognostic data to better inform treatment recommendations and client decision-making.

papers.title: Diagnostic performance of 1,2-O-dilauryl-rac-glycero glutaric acid-(6'-methylresorufin) ester lipase activity in cats presenting to a veterinary referral hospital.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Rodriguez Godoy J, Willems A, Ibarrola P, Rishniw M
papers.abstract: To determine the prevalence of increased 1,2-O-dilauryl-rac-glycero glutaric acid-(6'-methylresorufin) ester (DGGR) lipase activity in cats with and without pancreatitis, and to evaluate its diagnostic performance relative to a clinical diagnosis of pancreatitis and ultrasonographic assessments. Serum DGGR lipase activity was measured with the Randox lipase assay and considered increased if > 25 U/L. A board-certified internal medicine clinician, blinded to DGGR results, gave each cat a clinician-assigned score from 0 (no pancreatitis) to 4 (definite pancreatitis). Ultrasonographic scores (0 to 4) were assigned on the basis of the number of changes supportive of pancreatitis. DGGR lipase performance was compared with clinical and ultrasonographic scores. A total of 231 cats were included; 59 of 231 (25.5%) had increased DGGR lipase activity. Clinical scores were 0 in 47 of 231 cats (20.3%), 1 in 128 of 231 (55.4%), 2 in 36 of 231 (15.6%), and 3 in 20 of 231 (8.7%); no cats had a score of 4. With the use of a clinical score of 3 as the reference, DGGR lipase activity had a sensitivity of 70% and specificity of 79% (positive predictive value, 24%; negative predictive value, 97%). DGGR lipase activity was significantly lower in cats with an ultrasound score of 0 compared to scores of 1, 2, and 3. DGGR lipase activity was lower in cats with clinician-assigned scores of 0 and 1 compared to scores of 2 and 3. DGGR lipase activity was lower in cats with lower clinical and ultrasonographic scores and demonstrated a high negative predictive value. In this low-prevalence referral population, a normal DGGR lipase result reduced the likelihood of clinician-suspected pancreatitis.

papers.title: Poorly concentrated urine is associated with an increased risk of developing chronic kidney disease in apparently healthy cats.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Rudinsky AJ, Morrison JA, Parker VJ, Spofford N, Topdjian K, Byron JM, Winston JA, Bechtold MA, Langston C, Quimby JM
papers.abstract: To evaluate medical records from mature and senior cats stratified by urine specific gravity (USG; ≥ 1.035 or < 1.035) to examine the development of presumptive chronic kidney disease (CKD). 15,027 apparently healthy cats were evaluated for inclusion in a 2-year longitudinal retrospective study. Outcome during the study period was a presumptive CKD diagnosis or development of creatinine > 1.6 mg/dL and USG < 1.035 with consistent clinical signs. Cats were grouped by age (mature, 11 to 15 years; senior, > 15 years) and USG values for contingency and survival analyses. A CKD assignment was precluded in cases where historical information, physical examination findings, diagnoses for each visit, and available diagnostic results over the study period contradicted a CKD diagnosis. 504 mature cats with a USG < 1.035, 1,872 mature cats with a USG ≥ 1.035, 89 senior cats with a USG < 1.035, and 149 senior cats with a USG ≥ 1.035 were included. In mature cats, contingency analysis using χ2 test found statistically significant differences in proportions of the population diagnosed presumptively with CKD during the study period, with an increased OR of 3.191 (CI, 1.611 to 6.231) as well as a shorter time to CKD diagnosis in the cats with USG < 1.035 at initial assessment. Identification of a USG < 1.035 appears to facilitate earlier renal disease detection and inform more individualized diagnostics in mature feline patients. Identification of inadequate urine concentration in mature cats should raise concern for future renal disease detection and impact clinical assessment and monitoring.

papers.title: Survey of veterinarians' receptivity to a canine vaccine for Rocky Mountain spotted fever reveals a potential vaccine market and opportunities for education.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Moore TS, Pikel L, Horiuchi K, Biggerstaff BJ, Brophy MK, Carpenter A, Szymanski D, Salzer JS
papers.abstract: To understand veterinary practitioner awareness about Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) and their receptivity and clients' perceived receptivity to a vaccine to protect dogs from RMSF. The survey tool was developed in collaboration with the CDC and AVMA. Responses were collected June 9, 2025, through July 1, 2025. Respondents were surveyed on whether they had ever diagnosed a case of RMSF and their confidence in identifying the symptoms of RMSF, receptivity to a canine RMSF or anti-tick vaccine, and clients' perceived receptivity to a vaccine. We calculated survey-weighted estimates for the companion- and mixed-animal practitioner population for proportions (95% CIs) and multinomial logistic regression to compute ORs (95% CIs) for comparisons of interest. Free-text responses to questions on vaccines were also collected for educational purposes. Eligible respondents included 731 (91.3%) companion-animal practitioners and 70 (8.7%) mixed-animal practitioners. The odds of practitioners recommending a vaccine who felt very confident in recognizing symptoms were 3.9 (95% CI, 3.1 to 4.9) times that of those who felt not confident at all. Fifty-four percent (95% CI, 50% to 58%) of practitioners' clients would be interested in a canine RMSF vaccine, and 79% (95% CI, 76% to 82%) of practitioners were interested in a combined anti-tick vaccine. Vaccine interest was not limited to a single geographic or practice environment. A potential market for a canine RMSF vaccine and a more general combined anti-tick vaccine exists across geographic regions and practice environments. Vaccine receptivity and patient care could be improved through education about RMSF and vaccine technology.

papers.title: Are common clinical protocols prioritizing detection over prevention in canine Dirofilaria immitis?
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Horvath M
papers.abstract: Owner noncompliance, not preventive failure, drives most canine Dirofilaria immitis infections in established patients. Only 24.4% of dogs under care achieve full-year purchase compliance with monthly macrocyclic lactones. Informal data suggest far more practices send annual testing reminders than monthly dosing reminders. The primary goal is continuous chemical protection, not annual detection of prior failures. This viewpoint argues for tracking adherence rates, routine adherence counseling, and prospective evaluation of adherence-first protocols in standard prescription-renewal settings.

papers.title: Isorhythmic atrioventricular dissociation detected during anesthesia in a geriatric cat.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
papers.authors: Sugimoto K, Fujiwara K, Tsuji K, Miyazaki M, Kobayashi K, Kanda T

papers.title: Gastric ulcers in cats with feline infectious peritonitis.
papers.authors: Tres GZ, da Silva VGC, Cony FG, Schwertz CI, Piva MM, Rissi DR, Howerth EW, McCullough K, Driemeier D, Pavarini SP
papers.abstract: Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) is one of the leading causes of death in cats worldwide. Although multiple organs can be affected, gastric ulcers have not been previously described as part of the pathological picture. Here we describe the macroscopic, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features of gastric ulcers of four domestic cats with FIP. The mean age of affected cats was 19 months. The affected cats had multisystemic involvement and the disease was classified as three mixed and one non-effusive case of FIP. Gross changes in the stomach were identified in all cases and consisted of single or multiple ulcers of variable diameter that were surrounded by a hyperemic halo. Histologically, ulcerated lesions consisted of areas of mucosal loss with coagulative necrosis surrounded by fibrin and cellular debris and, in some cases, pyogranulomatous inflammation. In the submucosa there was pyogranulomatous vasculitis, thrombosis, and fibrinoid vascular necrosis. All cases had positive immunolabeling for FCoV in the cytoplasm of macrophages within the gastric mucosa and submucosa. Although ulcerative gastritis is not a classic manifestation of FIP, the vasculitis and thrombosis observed in these cases likely contributed to the development of gastric ulcers. FIP should be considered as a differential diagnosis in cats with gastric ulcers associated with pyogranulomatous inflammatory infiltrate.

papers.title: Impacts of dietary alpha-lipoic acid on testicular hemodynamics, semen quality, and hormonal levels with respect to nitric oxide and antioxidant levels in aged dogs.
papers.authors: Abdelnaby EA, Alhaider AK, Emam IA
papers.abstract: This study investigated, for the first time, the impacts of alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) as a dietary supplement on semen quality, testicular artery (TA) hemodynamics, antioxidant status, and reproductive hormones (testosterone [T], estradiol [E2], follicle-stimulating hormone [FSH]), and nitric oxide (NO) in aged dogs. German Shepherd medium-sized dogs (n = 20; aged 8 ± 0.5 years) were categorized into two groups: either supplemented with 600 mg ALA/ kg diet daily for 80 days (A-LA group; n = 10) or not (control; n = 10). Animals were examined for ultrasound scanning, Doppler examination, semen collection, and blood sampling every 10 days. Testicular volume and echotexture were not affected by supplementation (P > 0.05). The total testicular colored areas were increased in the ALA-supplemented group, accompanied by a reduction (P ≤ 0.05) in both Doppler indices (resistance index [RI] and pulsatility index [PI]). T, E2, and NO were increased (P ≤ 0.05) in ALA -supplemented dogs until reaching a peak at day 60. Motility, viability, normal morphology percentages, and concentration increased until reaching a peak at day 60 of supplementation compared to control males, with a significant elevation (P ≤ 0.05) in sperm kinetic parameters, measured by CASA. Total antioxidant capacity (TAC), and catalase (CAT) increased in ALA -supplemented males, reaching a peak at day 60 (P ≤ 0.05), with a decline in malondialdehyde (MDA) levels (P ≤ 0.05). ALA dietary supplementation (600 mg/kg diet) improved aged dogs' reproductive performance by improving semen quality through increased testicular hemodynamics (a decrease in Doppler indices), elevated T, E2, and NO levels, and reflected the upregulation of antioxidant enzymes, leading to increased TAC.

papers.title: Electrochemotherapy for urinary bladder botryoid rhabdomyosarcoma in a dog: case report.
papers.authors: Holliday PB, Nakagaki KYR, Dias RG, Horta RDS, Pimentel PAB
papers.abstract: Urinary bladder rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is a rare malignant neoplasm in dogs, most commonly affecting young animals and frequently arising from the trigone region, where complete surgical removal is challenging. Reported median survival time for dogs with vesical RMS is 45 days, ranging from 20 to 120 days. This report describes the diagnosis and multimodal treatment of a six-month-old intact female Golden Retriever diagnosed with vesical botryoid rhabdomyosarcoma. The patient presented with urinary incontinence, dysuria, and hematuria and was initially treated for suspected cystitis without clinical improvement. Ultrasonography identified a bladder mass located in the trigone region, and exploratory cystotomy with surgical debulking was performed. Intraoperative electrochemotherapy with bleomycin was administered, followed by six sessions of systemic doxorubicin chemotherapy. Complete remission was achieved, but recurrence was noted after 183 days, and the patient presented a survival time of 277 days, exceeding previously reported outcomes for this neoplasm. Although disease progression ultimately occurred, this case suggests that incorporating electrochemotherapy into a multimodal protocol may improve locoregional control in infiltrative vesical rhabdomyosarcoma and potentially prolong survival in dogs affected by this malignancy.

papers.title: Diagnosis and surgical management of a type IVb dermoid sinus between the parietal and occipital bones in a young cat.
papers.authors: Fish SE, Adrian A, Matiasek K, Matiasek L
papers.abstract: A dermoid sinus is a congenital, tubular skin defect caused by incomplete separation of the skin and nervous system during embryonic development. It is more common in dogs and usually located along the spine. Intranasal or superficial cranial forms have been occasionally reported. This case describes a dermoid sinus on the head of a cat with intracranial extension, illustrating diagnostic and surgical challenges. A 1.5-year-old, female British Shorthair cat was evaluated for a recurring, previously superficially resected, cutaneous mass on her head with an abnormal pattern of hair growth. MRI and CT revealed an extra-axial mass extending in a tubular fashion through a midline defect between the parietal and occipital bones, continuing caudally along a malformed tentorium. Mild focal cerebellar compression and suspected secondary meningitis, more evident on the right side, were also identified. Surgery was performed via a combined caudotentorial and limited right-sided rostrotentorial craniectomy. Careful dissection along the lesion margins and durectomy of focally attached thickened meninges allowed complete resection. No postoperative complications or further neurological deficits occurred.
