Histopathology confirmed a dermoid sinus. Follow-up after 28 months revealed no recurrence. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first reported case of a type IVb dermoid sinus in a cat to be successfully managed surgically. This case provides important clinical information regarding the diagnosis, imaging features and surgical management of complex intracranially extending dermoid sinuses in feline patients.

papers.title: Microwave ablation of a primary renal tumor in a cat.
papers.authors: Pope EA, Green EM, Makary MS, Selmic LE
papers.abstract: An 11-year-old, male neutered domestic shorthair cat with pre-existing International Renal Interest Society stage 3 chronic kidney disease and paraneoplastic polycythemia was presented for evaluation of a left renal mass. Cytology was consistent with nephroblastoma, well-differentiated carcinoma, adenoma or papilloma. Owing to the cat's compromised renal function, nephrectomy was considered high risk, and ultrasound-guided microwave ablation (MWA) was performed as a nephron-sparing alternative. The procedure was well tolerated without immediate complications. Renal values remained stable throughout follow-up, and the paraneoplastic polycythemia resolved after ablation. A delayed complication of recurrent abscess and fistula formation at the probe insertion site extending along the body wall occurred, but resolved with surgical debridement, drainage and an extended course of antibiotic therapy. Near-total resolution of the renal mass was confirmed on follow-up ultrasound, and the cat remained clinically well 462 days after ablation without evidence of recurrence or metastasis. Primary renal tumors in cats are uncommon, and nephrectomy is the recommended treatment; however, it may be contraindicated in cats with concurrent renal disease. There is no established role for chemotherapy in feline primary renal tumors, leaving limited options for cats who cannot undergo surgery. Although MWA is widely used in human medicine for small renal tumors and has been reported in other tumor types in dogs, it has not been described in cats. This case demonstrates that MWA may be a feasible and potentially effective nephron-sparing treatment option for feline primary renal tumors, and that MWA may be effective at resolving paraneoplastic polycythemia in cases where nephrectomy may be contraindicated. Microwave ablation in a renal tumor in a cat Kidney tumors in cats are uncommon but serious, and surgical removal of the affected kidney is the standard treatment. However, some cats cannot safely undergo surgery because their kidney function is already compromised. This creates a difficult situation for veterinarians and pet owners, as there are currently no well-established alternative treatments. This report describes a new approach to treating a kidney tumor in a cat utilizing microwave ablation (MWA). MWA is a minimally invasive procedure that uses microwave energy to generate heat within a tumor, effectively destroying the cancerous tissue without the need for major surgery. Although commonly used in human medicine to treat kidney tumors, particularly in patients who are not healthy enough for surgery, it had never previously been reported in cats. The patient was an 11-year-old cat with pre-existing kidney disease who was also experiencing an abnormally high red blood cell count (polycythemia), suspected to be caused by the tumor. Because removing the kidney would have put the cat at serious risk of kidney failure, he was treated using MWA instead. A small probe was inserted through the skin into the tumor under CT scan guidance, and microwave energy was used to destroy the mass. The cat recovered well from the procedure. Kidney function remained stable and the high red blood cell count returned to normal after treatment, an outcome previously only seen after complete kidney removal. The tumor nearly completely disappeared on follow-up imaging and the cat remained healthy, with no signs of recurrence more than 18 months after the procedure. The only complication was a recurrent abscess at the probe site, which resolved with surgical drainage and antibiotics. This case suggests that MWA may be a safe and effective treatment option for cats with kidney tumors who cannot undergo surgery and warrants further investigation.

papers.title: Correction: Lee et al. Hematologic and Renal Trends in Cats Undergoing Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy: A Retrospective Case Series with Molidustat Use. Vet. Sci. 2026, 13 , 973.
papers.authors: Lee G, Lee J, Song KH

papers.title: Technique and short-term outcomes associated with a minimally invasive endoscopically assisted thoracolumbar hemilaminectomy in 40 dogs.
papers.authors: Rocheleau PJ, Robson A, Bird SD, Domney LN, Holz KA
papers.abstract: To describe the technique and short-term outcomes associated with endoscopically assisted hemilaminectomy. Dogs were included if they had a minimally invasive endoscopic hemilaminectomy due to compressive disc disease with minimum 8-week follow-up. A small surgical approach was performed between the affected dorsal spinous processes and the associated articular facet removed. The remainder of the procedure including bone removal and spinal decompression was performed using endoscopic control. Outcome measures included signalment, weight, body-condition score, duration of signs, and pre- and post-operative physical and neurological examination findings, CT imaging, surgical time and complications. Forty client-owned dogs met the inclusion criteria for the study. Mean surgery time was 57 min (range 20-95). There was a significant decrease in neuroscore from pre-intervention (mean 3.14, 95% CI 2.70-3.58) to post-intervention (mean 1.31, 95% CI 0.83-1.79), mean difference = -1.83, 95% CI -1.40 to -2.26. The average length of hospitalization following surgery was on average 1.9 days (IQR 1.75). Five dogs experienced post-operative complications. Post-operative CTs revealed no visible residual disc material in any patient, which was consistent with endoscopic findings. Body condition score had no effect on any outcome measures. The technique described here was safe and effective and allowed for good visualization and access to the spinal canal. Most complications were manageable and within commonly accepted limits. Endoscopically assisted hemilaminectomy can be performed effectively with commonly available instrumentation and may be considered to minimize surgical trauma.

papers.title: Untargeted Plasma Metabolomics Reveals Metabolic Alterations Associated With Idiopathic Epilepsy in Dogs.
papers.authors: Nakorn PN, Chantong B, Chatchaisak D, Phochantachinda S
papers.abstract: Canine idiopathic epilepsy (IE) is one of the most common chronic neurological disorders in dogs, however, its underlying pathophysiology remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to characterise plasma metabolomic alterations associated with canine IE at two clinical points using an untargeted metabolomic approach. Plasma samples were collected from nine client-owned healthy dogs (Normal), and nine dogs with idiopathic epilepsy evaluated at acute seizure state (Epilepsy_D0) and after a 14-day seizure-free interval following antiepileptic treatment (Epilepsy_D14). For metabolomic analysis, plasma from three dogs was pooled to generate three biological pools per condition. Untargeted plasma metabolomic profiling was performed using LC-QTOF-MS in positive ionisation mode. A total of 491 metabolites were retained for downstream analysis. Exploratory heatmap and principal component analyses showed differences in overall metabolic patterns among three groups. Differential abundance analysis identified distinct metabolite changes across the pairwise comparison. Pathway enrichment analysis of the significantly altered metabolites using the study-specific metabolite set as a custom background did not identify any pathway reaching statistical significance. Six metabolites of interest, namely pyridoxal, methylimidazoleacetic acid, 2-methylbutyroylcarnitine, indolelactic acid, homocitrulline and DL-Normetanephrine, showed distinct abundance patterns across the study conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence of plasma metabolic alterations associated with canine IE and differences between the acute seizure state and the 14-day seizure-free interval. Given the pooled biological design and limited effective sample size, these findings should be considered exploratory and require validation in larger cohorts using individual biological samples.

papers.title: Genomic characteristics and preliminary study on in vitro infection properties of canine parvovirus type 2c derived from a canine anal swab sample.
papers.authors: Mou D, Chen Y, Wu S, Huang J, Guo Y, Bai X
papers.abstract: This study aimed to determine the genomic characteristics and genotype of a CPV isolate (MDC-CPV) recovered from a vaccinated dog, and to investigate its in vitro infectivity and replication features in A72 and CRFK cell lines. Clinical samples were subjected to nucleic acid detection for common canine pathogens and CPV antigen testing. Sequencing was performed using the Illumina NovaSeq PE150 platform. Following quality control, assembly, and annotation, the near-complete genome sequence of MDC-CPV was obtained. Homology searches were conducted using BLASTn. Genotyping was determined based on key amino acid residues in VP2, and phylogenetic analyses were performed using both the full-length VP2 coding sequence (CDS) and the whole-genome reference sequences. In vitro infection was subsequently validated in A72 and CRFK cells. Viral infection-associated characteristics were evaluated by observing cytopathic effects (CPE), and through Western blot, immunofluorescence, qPCR, TCID50 assay, and transmission electron microscopy. The genome length of MDC-CPV was 5,358 nucleotides, with no ambiguous bases identified. Genome annotation revealed that MDC-CPV contains typical CPV coding regions, including NS1, NS2, VP1, and VP2. The VP2 CDS was 1755 nucleotides in length, encoding 584 amino acids. Key VP2 residues for MDC-CPV were 297Ala/426Glu, along with a combination of other residues (87Leu, 101Thr, 300Gly, 305Tyr, 324Ile, 375Asp, 555Val, 564Ser, and 568Gly), supporting its classification as CPV-2c. Phylogenetic analysis placed MDC-CPV within the CPV-2c clade, showing close genetic relatedness to several CPV-2c reference strains from China and other regions in East Asia. In in vitro infection assays, CPE was observed in both A72 and CRFK cells inoculated with MDC-CPV. Furthermore, CPV-related protein expression and virus-like particles were detected. Quantitative PCR and TCID50 assays in CRFK cells demonstrated productive replication, with viral DNA levels and infectious virus titers increasing substantially from 48 h post-infection, reaching peak titers of approximately 5.8 log10 TCID50/1 mL at 96 h post-infection. MDC-CPV is a CPV-2c strain isolated from a clinical sample of a vaccinated dog. Its genomic and VP2 genotypic characteristics are consistent with recently circulating CPV-2c strains. These findings provide a reference for molecular epidemiological surveillance of CPV-2c in the Sichuan region and for research on CPV infection in the context of vaccination.

papers.title: Evaluation of intrarenal hypoperfusion and renal congestion assessed by intrarenal Doppler ultrasonography in dogs with myxomatous mitral valve disease.
papers.authors: Iwai Y, Morita T, Terukina H, Yamasaki M
papers.abstract: While the predictive value of venous impedance index (VII) for evaluating renal congestion is reported in dogs with myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD), an ultrasonographic index of renal perfusion has not been reported. Low renal perfusion assessed by interlobar renal artery velocity time integral (VTI) is associated with a worse prognosis in dogs with MMVD. Combining VTI and VII provides additional prognostic information. Sixty-two client-owned dogs without heart disease evaluated for preanesthetic or general health assessment and 80 client-owned dogs with MMVD. Prospective cohort study. The VTI was measured by manually tracing the spectral velocity envelope of interlobar arteries. The primary endpoint was defined as the composite of cardiac-related death and renal-related death. The VTI was corrected for the effect of heart rate (VTIc) because VTI and heart rate were negatively correlated in dogs without heart disease. In dogs with MMVD, the VTIc decreased with higher ACVIM stage. Dogs with lower VTIc (< 8.3) had significantly shorter survival times (median, not reached; 95% CI, 98 days-not reached; P < .001) than those with normal VTIc (median, not reached; 95% CI, not reached). In multivariable Cox analysis, VII remained significantly associated with outcome (HR, 1.24 per 0.1-unit increase; 95% CI, 1.07-1.42). Exploratory classification combining VII (<0.37 or ≥0.37) and VTIc (≥8.3 or < 8.3) identified 4 subsets with different survival outcomes. The VTIc might be associated with outcome in dogs with MMVD and combined assessment might provide additional exploratory prognostic information. Myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) is a common heart disease in dogs and can affect blood flow within the kidneys. We investigated whether Doppler ultrasonography could detect reduced kidney blood flow and kidney congestion in dogs with this disease. Reduced kidney blood flow was observed as heart disease became more severe and was associated with shorter survival. Kidney congestion was also associated with outcome. Assessing both kidney blood flow and congestion might provide additional information about prognosis in dogs with MMVD.

papers.title: Abnormalities in cobalamin status in dogs with congenital portosystemic shunt before and after shunt closure.
papers.authors: Proksch AL, Kunath T, Heilmann RM, Schneider MA, Kaline M, Dreller V, Langenstein J, Bauer N, Moritz A
papers.abstract: Cobalamin dysvitaminosis occurs with congenital portosystemic shunt (cPSS). Limited data exist on the effects of cPSS-type, cPSS-closure, and association with hyperammonemia. Cobalamin and folate status differ between healthy and cPSS-dogs, before and after cPSS-closure, between complete and incomplete cPSS-closure, and cPSS-types. Cobalamin dysvitaminosis is associated with hyperammonemia, which ameliorates after cPSS-closure. Eighty-three dogs. Concentrations of cobalamin, transcobalamin (TCB), metabolites (homocysteine [HCy], serum [sMMA], urinary [uMMA:crea] methylmalonic acid), folate, and blood ammonia were prospectively compared between 44 cPSS-dogs and 39 age and body weight matched controls. Compared were 32 out of 44 intrahepatic (cIPSS) and 12 out of 44 extrahepatic (cEPSS) cPSS-dogs, before (PSS-0) and 12 weeks (PSS-12) after cPSS-closure, and complete versus incomplete cPSS-closure. Hypocobalaminemia occurred in 2 out of 44 PSS-0-dogs (cIPSS) and hypercobalaminemia in 8 out of 44 PSS-0-dogs (5/12 cEPSS, 3/32 cIPSS). Of 34 normocobalaminemic PSS-0-dogs, in 47% available HCy samples concentrations were below the reference interval, whereas sMMA and uMMA:crea were higher in 61% and 27%. PSS-0-dogs had lower HCy, higher sMMA and uMMA:crea, and lower folate concentrations than controls (each P < .0001). Hyperammonemia occurred in 35 out of 43 PSS-0-dogs, but ammonia did not correlate with any variable. Of 32 out of 38 normocobalaminemic PSS-12-dogs, 31% had supraphysiologic sMMA and 10% supraphysiologic uMMA:crea concentrations. PSS-12-dogs had lower cobalamin (P = .0001) and TCB (P = .014), higher HCy (P < .0001), lower uMMA:crea (P = .0002), and higher folate concentrations (P < .0001) than PSS-0-dogs. At PSS12, cIPSS-dogs had significantly higher sMMA concentrations (P = .0001) than cEPSS-dogs. Lower sMMA (P = .0001) and uMMA:crea (P = .003) were more common with complete than incomplete cPSS-closure. Dysvitaminosis is common in cPSS-dogs persisting in some cPSS-dogs after cPSS-closure. Some dogs are born with an abnormal blood vessel that allows blood to bypass the liver causing liver dysfunction and malnutrition such as vitamin deficiency. We compared 44 affected dogs with 39 healthy dogs. We measured blood levels of vitamin B12 and folate and vitamin-dependent substances that increase during B12 and folate deficiency. These vitamin-dependent substances help to identify vitamin deficiency within cells despite normal vitamin blood concentrations. Before treatment, most affected dogs had normal vitamin B12 levels in their blood. However, many had higher amounts of vitamin-dependent substances in their blood or urine, suggesting altered vitamin B12 and folate processing and thus, vitamin deficiency within cells. Twelve weeks after surgical treatment to close the abnormal blood vessel, several blood variables of vitamin concentrations and vitamin-dependent substances improved, although some dogs still had abnormal results. In dogs with complete vessel closure vitamin blood concentrations and vitamin-dependent substances were more often normal than in dogs with incomplete closure, indicating better vitamin availability after vessel closure. Our findings suggest that dogs with this liver blood vessel anomaly often have abnormalities of vitamin B12 and folate concentrations (blood concentrations and within cells) and that abnormalities can persist 12 weeks after treatment.

papers.title: Immunogenicity of half-dose versus full-dose Leptospira quadrivalent vaccine in dogs: a prospective randomized pilot study.
papers.authors: Craig C, Pastey MK
papers.abstract: In clinical veterinary practice, incomplete vaccine administration can occur because of movement or partial injection loss; however, the immunologic consequences of reduced vaccine dosing are unknown. To compare antibody responses after administration of a half-dose versus a full-dose of a quadrivalent leptospirosis vaccine in dogs. Ten client-owned, healthy dogs (body weight range, 9-31 kg) with no history of leptospirosis vaccination. Prospective randomized pilot study. Dogs were assigned to receive either a full-dose (n = 5) or a half-dose (n = 5) of a quadrivalent inactivated leptospirosis vaccine. Serum samples were collected before vaccination and 4 weeks after vaccination. The primary outcome was post-vaccination microscopic agglutination test (MAT) titers against vaccine-associated serovars. Secondary outcomes included cross-reactive titers and associations with body weight. All dogs were seronegative before vaccination. Dogs receiving the full-dose developed relatively uniform MAT responses against vaccine serovars, whereas responses in the half-dose group varied among individual dogs and serovars. Half-dose titers ranged from 1:100 to 1:3200, compared with 1:800 to 1:3200 in the full-dose group. Cross-reactive titers to Leptospira bratislava were detected in both groups, whereas all dogs remained seronegative for Leptospira hardjo. Within the half-dose group, dogs weighing < 50 lb had higher observed titers than dogs weighing ≥50 lb for several vaccine serovars. Reduced vaccine dosing resulted in variable antibody responses, with lower observed titers for some vaccine serovars, compared with full-dose vaccination, supporting adherence to recommended dosing to achieve consistent immunogenic responses in clinical practice. Leptospirosis is a bacterial disease that can cause serious illness in dogs. Sometimes a dog receives less than the intended vaccine dose because it moves during an injection or some of the vaccine leaks out. To explore whether this affects the antibody response, we gave 5 dogs a full dose and 5 dogs a half dose of a leptospirosis vaccine. Four weeks later, dogs given the full dose had more consistent antibody responses. Responses among dogs given the half dose varied more, and some had lower antibody levels against the bacteria included in the vaccine. This small study measured antibodies, not whether the dogs were protected from disease. Its findings support giving the full recommended dose and warrant further study in larger groups of dogs.

papers.title: K-number-based selection in Danish dachshunds: offspring outcomes and implications for genetic diversity.
papers.authors: Sullivan S, Kutzler MA
papers.abstract: In dachshunds, the number of calcified discs (K-number [KN]) is one heritable determinant of the risk of intervertebral disc disease and is used for breeding selection in some countries; however, there are no prior reports of offspring KN outcomes or the effect of KN selection on size of the effective breeding population (Ne). To determine whether progressively limiting breeding eligibility to dogs with lower KNs would: (1) improve offspring KN outcomes and (2) reduce the effective population size of the breeding population below a threshold that risks genetic bottleneck. Danish dachshunds (n = 2120) with KN recorded to a public database from 1993 to 2024. This retrospective study analyzed KN records from 2120 dogs screened between 1990 and 2024. Associations between parental KN and offspring KN phenotype were evaluated using parent-offspring regression and cumulative-link ordinal models. Worse offspring KN was predicted by both worse sire (P = 4.8 × 10-6; odds ratio [OR] 1.3; 95% CI, 1.16-1.45) and dam (P = 3.3 × 10-5; OR 1.3; 95% CI, 1.13-1.40) KN. Increasingly stringent parental KN selection was associated with improved offspring KN distributions, with predicted next-generation mean KN decreasing from 2.26 under K ≤ 4 selection to 1.54 under K0 selection. However, more stringent selection reduced effective breeding population size below thresholds associated with genetic bottleneck risk (eg, standard wirehaired: Ne = 179 under K ≤ 4 vs Ne = 52 under K0). Increasingly stringent limitation of parent KN was associated with lower-KN offspring groups but also decreased effective population size, highlighting the need to balance disease-risk reduction against preservation of genetic diversity. Intervertebral disc disease (IVDD) is a common health problem in dachshunds. We evaluated a Danish breeding program designed to reduce IVDD prevalence in dachshunds by selecting breeding dogs based on their K-number (KN), which is the number of calcified discs visible on radiographs. K-number is inherited and associated with a dog’s risk of IVDD. Compared with FGF4L2 (CDDY)-based selection, KN-based selection might be preferable because it better reflects overall inherited IVDD risk in a disease influenced by multiple genes. We found that parent KN was a predictor of offspring KN. The heritability of KN supports its use in selective breeding, and dogs produced through the program had improved KN scores corresponding to an estimated 19% reduction in IVDD prevalence. Stricter breeding restrictions resulted in better offspring KNs but also reduced the size of the eligible breeding population. For most dachshund varieties, stringent restrictions reduced breeding populations to levels that risk loss of genetic diversity. Although KN-based selection is currently limited by the number of scored breeding dogs, mandatory KN screening of all dachshunds used for breeding in Denmark as of 2026 might increase the effective breeding population sizes.

papers.title: Primary hyperparathyroidism in a cat with synchronous bilateral parathyroid carcinomas: a case report.
papers.authors: Choi U, Kwon G, Lim JH, Oh SI, Ock S
papers.abstract: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPTH) is a rare endocrine disorder in cats, and bilateral parathyroid carcinoma is exceptionally uncommon. A 14-year-old neutered male Russian Blue cat presented with decreased appetite, reduced activity, vomiting, and persistent hypercalcemia. Hypercalcemia was documented by increased ionized calcium (iCa; 1.90 mmol/L) and total calcium (14.3 mg/dL), and an increased intact parathyroid hormone concentration (18.6 pg/mL) supported a diagnosis of PHPTH. Cervical ultrasonography, computed tomography, and fine-needle aspiration cytology identified bilateral parathyroid-associated lesions but could not determine malignancy or the functional contribution of each lesion. During preoperative stabilization with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride and furosemide, the iCa concentration decreased from 1.90 to 1.47 mmol/L. On the fourth day of hospitalization, complete right thyroid lobectomy with excision of the associated right parathyroid mass and left parathyroidectomy with partial left thyroidectomy were performed. Histopathologic examination supported the diagnosis of synchronous bilateral low-grade, well-differentiated parathyroid carcinomas, with infiltrative growth into adjacent non-neoplastic parathyroid tissue in the left lesion and focal capsular penetration in the right lesion. Postoperative hypocalcemia was managed with intravenous calcium gluconate and oral calcitriol during hospitalization, followed by oral vitamin D supplementation after discharge. Serum iCa normalized by postoperative day 28 and remained within the reference interval thereafter. On postoperative day 161, serum iCa and iPTH concentrations were within their respective reference intervals, and follow-up CT showed no evidence of local recurrence or detectable metastasis. This case highlights that bilateral parathyroid carcinomas may exhibit subtle histopathologic evidence of malignancy that is not predicted by preoperative imaging or cytology, while lesion-specific functional status and anatomical relationships to the thyroid gland may independently influence surgical planning.

papers.title: Limitations of transmucosal ketamine administration for chronic pain in dogs with osteoarthritis.
papers.authors: Seabolt RA, Elam LH, Griffenhagen GM, Duerr FM
papers.abstract: This prospective, open-label clinical trial aimed to evaluate the efficacy of low-dose keta-mine (0.5 mg/kg) administered by oral transmucosal route every 8 h in client-owned dogs with refractory, chronic osteoarthritis pain. Objective gait analysis was the primary outcome measure for orthopedic function relating to pain. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry was used to quantify plasma ketamine and norketamine concentrations 30 and 60 min after administration of an oral transmucosal ketamine (TMK) gelatin lozenge. Enrollment was discontinued early due to difficulty of administering TMK in the formulation provided (administration success = 54%; 181/334 doses in n  = 9 participants). The result-ing sample size was too small for the intended statistical analysis of objective outcome da-ta to determine treatment efficacy. Mean plasma concentrations of ketamine and norketa-mine ( n  = 8 patients) were 4.5 ng/mL (+/- 3.0) and 47 ng/mL (+/- 38.3) at 30 min, and 1.7 ng/mL (+/- 1.2) and 65.7 ng/mL (+/- 46.7) at 60 min post administration. These values suggest that TMK is absorbed and subsequently metabolized into norketa-mine. However, the low success rate of administration demonstrated that an oral transmu-cosal gelatin lozenge is an impractical delivery method for low-dose ketamine in a clinical setting. Evaluation of alternative TMK formulations and further research with an appropriate sample size is recommended to evaluate efficacy, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacody-namics before TMK can be used clinically.

papers.title: Randomized comparative field clinical trial of hydrocortisone aceponate/gentamicin/miconazole otic suspension vs. mometasone furoate/florfenicol/terbinafine otic solution for the treatment of canine otitis externa.
papers.authors: Griffin J, von Simson C, Poincelot L, Jasmin P
papers.abstract: This randomized, masked, multi-center field clinical trial compared two otic formulations: a gentamicin, miconazole, and hydrocortisone aceponate otic suspension (Easotic™, Virbac) administered once daily for five days, and a single-dose florfenicol, terbinafine, and mometasone furoate otic solution (Claro™, Elanco). Eighty-six client-owned dogs with acute otitis externa (OTIS3 score ≥ 5) were evaluated at 4 h post-application and on Days 2, 7, and 28. Based on the percentage of dogs achieving an OTIS3 score ≤ 3 at Day 28, both treatments (Easotic™ vs. Claro™) showed high efficacy (Intention-to-Treat (ITT): 85% vs. 79%, p = 0.400; Per Protocol (PP): 94% vs. 88%, p = 0.261). Easotic™ demonstrated a higher percentage of OTIS3 score reduction compared to Claro™ from Day 2. At Day 2, Easotic™ achieved greater improvements in ear discharge, odor, dirtiness, and stenosis compared to Claro™. Veterinarians' overall assessment of " Excellent " response was higher for Easotic™ at Day 7 (ITT: 50% vs. 26%, p = 0.009; PP: 49% vs. 29%, p = 0.010) and Day 28 (ITT: 62% vs. 36%, p = 0.017; PP: 76% vs. 44%, p = 0.002;). Similarly, 91% of the owners assessed the response to treatment as " Good " or " Excellent " with Easotic™, and 89% with Claro™. Notwithstanding the differences in dosing regimens, both products received comparable evaluations from owners regarding their physical and functional characteristics. The results of this study confirm the efficacy of Easotic™ in the management of otitis externa, notably to reduce ear discharge, stenosis, odor and dirtiness from Day 2.

papers.title: Pharmacokinetics of HDM7006, a high-potency balanced GLP-1/GIP dual agonist, in healthy domestic cats.
papers.authors: Zhang Z, Cui S, Jiang C, Teng L, Pan H, Dong Z, Peng L, Wang B, Liu D
papers.abstract: HDM7006 is a GLP-1R/GIPR dual agonist developed for body weight management in obese or overweight cats. To Investigate the pharmacokinetic (PK) characteristics of HDM7006 in cats. Forty-eight healthy adult cats were enrolled. In the single-dose PK study, 40 cats were divided into five groups receiving 0.1, 0.5, 1.0 or 2.0 mg/kg (SC) or 1.0 mg/kg (intravenous, IV) of HDM7006, respectively. In the multiple-dose PK study, 8 cats were received 0.5 mg/kg of HDM7006 once weekly for five consecutive doses. Plasma samples were collected before and after drug administration to determine PK parameters and evaluate immunogenicity. No gender differences were observed in system exposure of HDM7006 after IV or SC injection. HDM7006 exhibited a low clearance, a low apparent volume of distribution, and a half-life of 43.7 h in cats after IV injection. Following single SC injection, the median T max ranged from 18.0 to 24.0 h, the T 1/2 ranged from 39.8 to 47.1 h, and the bioavailability ranged from 42.23 to 78.38%. Linear PK characteristics were observed within the dose range of 0.1-2.0 mg/kg. Anti-drug antibodies (ADAs) were detected only in one male animal at 336 h post-dose in the 2.0 mg/kg dose group. After five consecutive doses of 0.5 mg/kg, steady state was clearly achieved, and no significant accumulation observed; all ADA test results were negative. HDM7006 exhibits predictable, dose-proportional PK and low immunogenicity, supporting a QW SC regimen in cats, and may offer a long-acting therapeutic option for feline weight management and metabolic regulation.

papers.title: Distribution and viral load of canine respiratory coronavirus in naturally infected dogs: evidence from clinical sampling sites and tissue detection.
papers.authors: Poonsin P, Zahro AN, Wiwatvisawakorn V, Punyathi P, Lacharoje S, Lean FZX, Piewbang C, Techangamsuwan S
papers.abstract: Canine respiratory coronavirus (CRCoV) is a respiratory pathogen associated with the canine infectious respiratory disease complex (CIRDC). Although CRCoV is primarily considered a respiratory virus, its distribution beyond the respiratory tract remains poorly understood. This study investigated the prevalence, anatomical distribution, viral loads, and tissue localization of CRCoV in naturally infected dogs using both antemortem and postmortem samples. A total of 267 dogs were sampled using nasal (NS), oropharyngeal (OS), and rectal swabs (RS). CRCoV RNA was detected in 10.49% of dogs tested by reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), and viral loads were quantified using reverse transcription digital PCR (RT-dPCR). CRCoV RNA was detected across all sampling routes, with significantly higher viral loads in NS than in OS (p < 0.001) and RS (p < 0.001), and higher viral loads in OS than in RS (p < 0.01). Longitudinal sampling demonstrated that viral RNA became undetectable within one week in most dogs; however, viral shedding persisted in one severely ill dog that subsequently died. In postmortem samples, CRCoV RNA was detected in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, and was successfully localized within the mesenteric lymph node by in situ hybridization, consistent with possible extra-respiratory detection. These findings provide new insight into the tissue distribution of CRCoV in naturally infected dogs, demonstrating a predominance in the respiratory tract while suggesting possible extra-respiratory detection. Further studies are needed to determine the biological significance of these findings and to confirm whether CRCoV undergoes systemic dissemination or active replication beyond the respiratory tract.

papers.title: A rare case of disseminated mucocutaneous candidiasis in a dog.
papers.authors: Soares FS, Pimentel PAB, Almeida IO, Cravo DLM, Horta RDS
papers.abstract: A 6-year-old, neutered, male, mongrel dog was referred to the oncology team with numerous ulcerated nodules distributed throughout the skin and mucocutaneous regions. With the initial suspicion of a recurrent canine transmissible venereal tumor, fine-needle aspiration cytology was performed on a 5 × 4 cm ulcerated nodule in the ventral abdomen; however, the findings were similar to reactive cutaneous histiocytosis. The dog was then referred for biopsy and histopathological examination, which confirmed chronic pyogranulomatous dermatitis with intralesional fungal structures. Culture enabled a conclusive diagnosis of a rare case of disseminated mucocutaneous candidiasis (DMC). Treatment with itraconazole was administered, with complete clinical remission achieved within two months, demonstrating the importance of appropriate diagnosis and therapy.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Biomechanical evaluation of feline sacroiliac joint stabilization using a single short cannulated compression headless screw: A cadaveric study.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Kornmayer M, Wachsmuth L, Zablotski Y, Thorwaechter C, Wieser J
papers.abstract: The aim of this study was to compare interfragmentary compression and rotational stability achieved with a single short cannulated compression headless screw (CCHS) with those obtained using longer CCHSs and cortical lag screws in a feline sacroiliac luxation (SIL) model. In this experimental study, 12 cadavers of adult domestic short-haired cats with a simulated unilateral SIL were stabilized using a single 2.5 mm CCHSs engaging 40 % of the sacral width and mounted in a mechanical testing machine. To assess compressive forces, pressure-mapping sensors were inserted into the joint space before fracture reduction. Total force (N), area of compression (mm2), and total pressure (N/mm2) were recorded. For rotational mechanical testing, the pelves were subsequently loaded through the acetabulum to replicate hindlimb ground reaction forces. A constant displacement rate of 0.5 mm/s was applied until maximal failure. Yield and ultimate load, stiffness, and failure modes were recorded. Results were compared with previously obtained data for CCHSs and cortical lag screws engaging 60 % of the sacral width. Group comparisons were conducted using Fischer's ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Post-hoc pairwise comparisons were conducted using Student's t-tests and the Dunn test. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. No statistically significant differences were identified among groups or in pairwise comparisons for total force (p=0.35), area of compression (p=0.76), total pressure (p=0.37), yield load (p = 0.55), ultimate load (p = 0.82), or stiffness (p = 0.57). All failures occurred due to screw loosening. A single CCHS engaging 40 % of the sacral width provides interfragmentary compression and rotational stability comparable to that of screws engaging 60 % of the sacral width lengths under the specific ex vivo testing conditions used in the feline SIL model.

papers.title: In vitro susceptibility of antimicrobial resistant strains of Escherichia coli isolated from the urine of dogs to pivmecillinam and fosfomycin.
papers.authors: Pohlmann M, LeCuyer TE, Woerde D, Palm C, Westropp JL
papers.abstract: Multidrug resistant (MDR) and extended spectrum beta-lactamase-producing (ESBL) uropathogenic Escherichia coli are a cause of urinary tract infection (UTI) in dogs. Limited antimicrobial options are available for these infections. Determine the in vitro susceptibility of MDR and ESBL urinary E. coli isolates to pivmecillinam and fosfomycin using isolates collected from dogs with either UTI or subclinical bacteriuria. The secondary aim was to compare 2 susceptibility test methods for pivmecillinam: agar dilution and gradient strip testing. Thirty-four banked frozen urine isolates stored at the University of California, Davis Microbiology Laboratory collected from 33 dogs. Gradient strip tests and agar dilution were used to evaluate E. coli susceptibility to mecillinam, the active form of pivmecillinam. Median paired mecillinam minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) differences by the 2 test methods were compared. For mecillinam resistant isolates, genomic sequencing was performed to determine resistance genes. Fosfomycin MICs were determined by gradient strip susceptibility testing. All isolates were susceptible to fosfomycin (34/34) and most isolates were susceptible using mecillinam agar dilution (31/34) and gradient strip (32/34), respectively. The paired log2-transformed mecillinam MIC results were significantly higher for agar dilution compared with gradient strip testing (V = 21.5, r = -0.91). Pivmecillinam and fosfomycin are potential antimicrobial treatment options for dogs with MDR or ESBL E. coli UTI. Agar dilution is the preferred testing method for mecillinam susceptibility.

papers.title: Correction to: Single Enema Fecal Microbiota Transplantation in Cats With Chronic Enteropathy.
Acute Levothyroxine Overdose Followed by Serial Monitoring of Total Thyroxine and Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone in a Hypothyroid Dog.
papers.authors: Park S, Seo J, Lee T, Ahn W, Song W, Nam A
papers.abstract: Reports of acute levothyroxine overdose in dogs are rare with limited monitoring data. An 8-year-old spayed female Pomeranian receiving long-term hypothyroidism treatment presented 9 h after ingesting a one-month supply of levothyroxine (3 mg; 1.13 mg/kg). Except for transient tachycardia, the physical examination revealed unremarkable findings. The total thyroxine (T4) level exceeded the upper limit of quantification. Levothyroxine was discontinued, and activated charcoal and intravenous fluid were administered. The dog showed normal vital signs and no further clinical abnormalities during the 5-day hospitalisation. The total T4 concentration decreased and normalised by 73 h after the overdose. The canine thyroid-stimulating hormone (cTSH) concentrations were initially normal but exceeded the upper reference limit at 98 h. The patient was discharged on Day 5. Two days later, levothyroxine was resumed because the dog exhibited signs of recurrent hypothyroidism with persistently elevated cTSH levels. Hypothyroidism was well-controlled for 6 months. To our knowledge, this is the first report to document a levothyroxine overdose in a hypothyroid dog using daily total T4 and cTSH monitoring. These findings suggest that acute overdose is less severe than chronic levothyroxine exposure.

papers.title: Case Report: Delayed epirubicin extravasation-induced ulceration in a dog managed without surgical intervention using adjunctive hyperbaric gaseous cryotherapy.
papers.authors: Kim CG, Park JH, Jeong SW
papers.abstract: Extravasation of anthracyclines can result in progressive tissue injury, ulceration, and necrosis, and may ultimately require surgical intervention. Management of delayed presentations remains challenging, as recommended treatments, including dexrazoxane, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and cold compresses, are most effective when initiated promptly after the extravasation event. A 9-year-old spayed female Poodle with suspected stage IV multicentric lymphoma developed a progressive ulcerative lesion 17 days after suspected epirubicin extravasation, by which time the recommended treatment window for standard interventions had elapsed. Given the progressive ulceration, severity of tissue injury, and delayed presentation, surgical debridement was considered. However, conservative management was pursued owing to the patient's limited prognosis and the owner's preference to prioritize quality of life. Treatment included hyperbaric gaseous cryotherapy (HGC) as the principal adjunctive modality, based on prior clinical experience in wound management and pain control. Dexrazoxane, topical DMSO, and ice-pack application were also incorporated despite the elapsed therapeutic window, as few alternative treatment options remained at that stage. Progressive wound healing was observed over the course of treatment, with complete re-epithelialization achieved by day 93 without surgical intervention. The wound remained fully healed until the patient died of progressive lymphoma on day 138. This case documents complete wound resolution without surgery in a dog with delayed epirubicin extravasation managed with multimodal conservative treatment incorporating adjunctive HGC.

papers.title: Body condition-linked alterations in dog owners' visual prosody.
papers.authors: Gergely A, Filep LA, Kukovič T, Kis A
papers.abstract: Visual prosody, the facial component accompanying speech, plays an important role in human social communication and is also a characteristic feature of dog-directed communication. Previous studies have shown that dog-directed visual prosody shares several features with infant-directed communication, although it also exhibits characteristics that differ between dogs and infants. Obesity has been associated with altered emotional processing and expression in humans, yet its potential effects on visual prosody have not been investigated. In the present study, we examined whether obesity is associated with variation in visual prosody during dog-directed communication. We analysed video recordings of 146 adult speakers interacting with their own dogs, infants, or adult human partners in semi-naturalistic settings, meaning that they were given instructions what to do, but these instructions were aimed to mimic real-life situations. Facial movements were quantified using automated facial coding software (Noldus FaceReader), and body shape was visually scored based on standard procedure. Linear mixed models were used to analyse Happy facial expression, facial Arousal, Valence, and activation of the cheek raiser muscle (AU6). Body condition-related differences depended on both the communication partner and the facial variable examined. Lower facial arousal was detected in speakers with higher body condition scores across all communication contexts. In contrast, differences in positive facial expressions were specific to dog-directed communication: speakers with higher body condition scores displayed less intense Happy facial expressions and lower facial Valence when interacting with dogs, whereas no such differences were observed in infant- or adult-directed communication. Unexpectedly, higher body condition scores were associated with stronger cheek raiser (AU6) intensity during infant- and adult-directed communication, but not during dog-directed communication, which might be a species-specific compensation mechanism. In addition, replicating previous findings, female speakers displayed more intense positive facial expressions and facial arousal than males, although these gender differences were reduced in dog-directed interactions. Our findings suggest that body condition is associated with variation in visual prosody, but these effects depend on the interlocutor and particularly pronounced during dog-directed communication. Different interpretations of these findings are presented in the discussion: altered mapping of muscle movement to FaceReader output, differences in FaceReader model quality, differences in habitual communicative style or expressivity, the amplifying or masking effect of communication differences, and a possible compensatory mechanism. The importance of these body condition-related alterations on the effectiveness of face-to-face communication, as well as social relationships need to be discussed.

papers.title: Beyond the ventricle: the atrial contribution to feline hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and implications for diagnosis, prognosis, and emerging therapy.
papers.authors: Kongchatree S, Rattanasrisomporn J
papers.abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the most common heart disease of cats and is conventionally characterised by its ventricular phenotype. The clinical events that determine quality and duration of life in affected cats, however, are atrial in their proximate pathophysiology. Congestive heart failure arises from elevated left atrial pressure transmitted to the pulmonary venous bed, arterial thromboembolism arises from blood stasis in a remodelled and dysfunctional left atrial appendage, and survival tracks left atrial size and function independently of left ventricular wall thickness. Recent longitudinal evidence indicates that lower left atrial fractional shortening can be detected before the diagnostic threshold for left ventricular hypertrophy is met, suggesting the atrium registers the disease before the ventricular wall-thickness criterion does. Despite this body of evidence, contemporary diagnostic frameworks, prognostic models, and the regulatory endpoint underpinning the recent conditional approval of delayed-release rapamycin remain anchored on the ventricle. This narrative review examines the atrial contribution to feline hypertrophic cardiomyopathy through five themes: atrial pathobiology, atrial imaging, atrial-driven outcomes, the implications for emerging disease-modifying therapy, and the practical implications for the cardiology consultation. We outline a framework for stage-anchored therapy decisions and a research agenda prioritising atrial trial endpoints and multicentre replication. In a disease affecting 14.7% of apparently healthy cats, with an 11.3% 10-year thromboembolic risk in preclinical cohorts, we propose that the atrium should now be at the centre of feline hypertrophic cardiomyopathy rather than at its periphery.

papers.authors: Carrasco-Martin M, Viñeta C, Martí-Carreras J, Roura X, Ferrer L, Busquets P, Vila A, Francino O

papers.title: Esophageal strictures associated with prolonged nasoesophageal tube placement in three cats.
papers.authors: Cho J, Kim M, Kim S, Lee J, Chae HK, Park C
papers.abstract: Nasoesophageal tube placement for a prolonged period of time has not previously been associated with esophageal stricture in cats. Three cats with suspected hepatic lipidosis required extended enteral nutritional support because voluntary food intake remained < 25% of the calculated resting energy requirement. The cumulative duration of nasoesophageal tube placement was 24-37 days. Regurgitation or retching developed within 1-3 days after tube removal, and esophagoscopy identified severe focal strictures in the cervical esophagus at the C4-C6 vertebral level in all 3 cats. One cat underwent 3 endoscopic balloon dilatation sessions at 1-week intervals, with enlargement of the esophageal lumen. The consistent anatomic location and temporal association with prolonged tube placement suggest that extended nasoesophageal intubation may be a risk factor for cervical esophageal stricture formation in cats. When prolonged nutritional support is anticipated, transition to a feeding tube intended for long-term use should be considered.

papers.title: Use of a novel low-fat hydrolyzed diet in the management of dogs with chronic enteropathy.
papers.authors: Hernández-Anllo C, Feo L, Hervera M, Puig J
papers.abstract: Dietary management plays a central role in the diagnosis and treatment of chronic enteropathy (CE) in dogs. Although hydrolyzed-protein diets are commonly used in patients with CE, and dietary fat restriction is recommended in selected gastrointestinal disorders, the combined effect of low fat and hydrolyzed protein has not been specifically evaluated. Assess clinical response and acceptability of a low-fat, hydrolyzed diet in dogs with CE. Thirty-one client-owned dogs. Prospective clinical study. Dogs were fed a commercial low-fat (2.01 g/100 kcal metabolizable energy) hydrolyzed salmon protein diet and stratified according to previous dietary history. Dogs were evaluated at baseline, 1 month, and 3 months. The primary outcome was clinical response, classified as complete response (CR), partial response (PR), or non-response (NR) based on gastrointestinal signs and the Canine Inflammatory Bowel Disease Activity Index (CIBDAI) score. Dogs with CR or PR were considered responders. Diet acceptability was assessed. At T1, 20 of 31 (64.5%) dogs were categorized as CR, 3 of 31 (9.7%) as PR, and 8 of 31 (25.8%) as NR. Twenty-three of 31 (74.2%) dogs had a positive clinical response. The CIBDAI scores decreased significantly from T0 to T1 (P < .001). At T2, 94.4% of initial responders maintained CR. Diet acceptability was excellent in 75.0% of cases. This low-fat, hydrolyzed diet had significant short- and mid-term effectiveness and was well tolerated in dogs with CE, reinforcing its potential as a treatment for food-responsive enteropathy.

papers.title: Ultrasound-measured renal length and corticomedullary thickness for the diagnosis and staging of chronic kidney disease in cats.
papers.authors: Brans M, Stock E, Duchateau L, Paepe D
papers.abstract: Ultrasonography is well established in veterinary practice, and renal dimensions may aid in diagnosing chronic kidney disease (CKD) in cats. Assess whether renal length, cortical and medullary thickness, and derived ratios identify CKD, reflect CKD severity, and are changed by hyperthyroidism. Evaluate effects of age, body weight, sex, laterality, and observer variability on renal dimensions. Two hundred fifty-nine client-owned cats: healthy (n = 179), CKD-affected (n = 38), and nonazotemic hyperthyroid (n = 42). Ultrasonographic renal dimensions were measured retrospectively. Group comparisons were performed using fixed effects and mixed models. Diagnostic accuracy was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Effects of age, body weight, sex, and laterality were evaluated using multiple linear regression. Intraobserver (novice) and interobserver (novice vs expert) variability were quantified using intraclass correlation coefficients from random effect models. Age, body weight, and sex accounted for biological variation in healthy cats, which also exhibited minor left-right kidney asymmetry. Cats with CKD were reliably distinguished from healthy and hyperthyroid cats by renal dimensions. Compared with age-comparable healthy cats, CKD-affected cats had shorter kidneys (-0.49 cm, -13.26%, P < .001), thinner cortices (dorsal: -0.10 cm, -16.23%, P < .001; transverse: -0.06 cm, -9.14%, P < .05), and thinner medullae (dorsal: -0.28 cm, -26.25%, P < .001; transverse: -0.24 cm, -19.7%, P < .001). Renal length and medullary thickness showed the highest diagnostic accuracy, but no renal dimension reliably reflected disease severity. Interobserver variability was considerable. Ultrasonographic renal dimensions may support CKD diagnosis in cats, but biological and observer variability must be considered.

papers.title: Comparative cytokine profiling in cerebrospinal fluid and serum of dogs with meningoencephalitis of unknown origin.
papers.authors: Gasser A, Démoulins T, Stein VM
papers.abstract: Meningoencephalitis of unknown origin (MUO) is a common inflammatory central nervous system (CNS) disease in dogs with unclear etiology, complicating diagnosis. Dogs with MUO exhibit distinct cytokine profiles in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) compared to other CNS diseases and controls. The study included 23 dogs diagnosed with MUO based on clinical signs, supportive CSF, and imaging findings. For comparison, 110 dogs were included, comprising dogs with CNS disorders, neurological diseases not involving the CNS (non-CNS), and orthopedic diseases. In this prospective cross-sectional observational study, 6 cytokines (interferon-γ [IFN-γ], TNF-α, IL-2, IL-6, IL-10, IL-15) were measured in paired CSF and serum samples using multiplex bead-based immunoassays. Primary outcome was the association between CSF cytokine concentrations and MUO, assessed by logistic regression. Meningoencephalitis of unknown origin showed significantly higher CSF concentrations compared to idiopathic epilepsy, intracranial neoplasia, intervertebral disc herniation, and non-CNS diseases in IFN-γ (MUO: median 108.4 pg/mL, IQR 25.8 vs comparison group: 10.5 pg/mL, IQR 0.0; β-coefficient 0.039, 95% CI, 0.021-0.057, P < .001) and interleukin (IL)-10 (MUO: 171.1 pg/mL, IQR 37.0 vs 8.5 pg/mL, IQR 0.0; β-coefficient 0.021, 95% CI, 0.011-0.030, P < .001). Moreover, TNF-α (β-coefficient 0.062, 95% CI, 0.023-0.102, P < .01), IL-15 (β-coefficient 0.080, 95% CI, 0.012-0.148, P < .05) and IL-2 (β-coefficient 0.055, 95% CI, 0.005-0.104, P < .05) concentrations were also elevated in MUO versus comparison group. Cerebrospinal fluid cytokine profiling identifies a characteristic intrathecal immune signature in MUO, advancing the understanding of its immunopathogenesis.

papers.title: Radiographic findings of the femora and tibiae in cats affected by patella fracture and dental anomaly syndrome.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Boulton S, Hernon T, Dancer S, Dirrig H, Major AC, Bourbos A, Piola V, Salgüero R, Guerin S, Langley-Hobbs SJ
papers.abstract: The objective of the study was to describe radiographic skeletal changes in cats affected by patella fracture and dental anomaly syndrome (PADS), with particular focus on the femora and tibiae, including bone density alterations, evidence of stress fractures and femoral morphology. Cats were retrospectively selected from a database of PADS-affected cats. Radiographs were independently evaluated by five veterinary radiologists and three orthopaedic surgeons for cortical thickening, medullary opacity changes, the presence of osteopetrosis, degenerative joint disease and additional fractures, and subjective assessment of the femoral shape. A total of 126 cats met the inclusion criteria. All had patellar fractures and 28 (22.2%) had additional fractures, most commonly involving the proximal tibia in 17 (13.5%) cases, proximal fibula in 15 (11.9%) cases and the pelvis. Four cats showed an incomplete radiolucent line in the cranioproximal tibia with surrounding sclerosis, consistent with developing stress fractures. Medullary opacity changes in the femora and/or tibiae were present in 11/126 (8.7%) cats, more often patchy than diffuse in appearance. In five (4.0%) cases, a generalised increase in bone opacity compatible with osteopetrosis was identified. Femoral shape was assessed in 74 cats, with 26 (35%) having a normal morphology, and seven (9.5%) and two (2.7%) having a stovepipe or champagne-fluted morphology, respectively. Consensus was not reached in 39 (52.7%) cases. Most PADS-affected femora and tibiae appeared radiographically normal; however, a subset of cats demonstrated radiographic features of osteopetrosis, altered femoral morphology and proximal tibial fissure lines suggestive of early stress fractures. These findings suggest that specific structural and morphological changes in the long bones may be present or may predispose cats to the insufficiency fractures characteristic of PADS, and emphasise the importance of clinicians recognising these subtle radiographic features to aid earlier diagnosis and appropriate case management. X-ray findings in the thigh and shin bones of cats with patella fracture and dental anomaly syndrome Patella fracture and dental anomaly syndrome (PADS) is a condition in cats associated with fractures of the kneecaps (patella) and dental abnormalities. Some affected cats also develop fractures elsewhere in the skeleton, suggesting that changes in bone structure may contribute to fracture risk. This study reviewed X-ray images of the thigh bones (femur) and shin bones (tibia) in 126 cats with PADS. The aim was to identify changes in bone density, bone shape and evidence of additional or early stress-related fractures. All cats had patella fractures and 22% also had other fractures, most commonly involving the tibia or bones of the pelvis. A small number of cats had subtle changes in the tibia that were considered suggestive of early stress fractures. Changes in bone density were identified in 9% of cats and were usually patchy. Five cats had a more widespread increase in bone density that was compatible with osteopetrosis, a condition in which bones become abnormally dense. The shape of the femur was assessed in 74 cats. Most had a normal appearance, while a smaller number had different femoral shapes, including stovepipe or champagne-fluted morphology. Overall, most cats had no obvious abnormalities of the tibia or femur on X-ray. However, some cats had changes in bone density, femoral shape or subtle signs of stress-related injury. These findings suggest that abnormalities in bone structure may contribute to the development of fractures in cats with PADS. Recognising these changes on X-rays may help veterinarians identify potentially important skeletal abnormalities in affected cats.

papers.title: Agreement between point-of-care and external reference laboratory RT-qPCR testing for feline coronavirus in cats with suspected feline infectious peritonitis.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Knies M, Hofman N, Jackson-Onis J, Broens EM, Teske E
papers.abstract: The aim of the present study was to evaluate the agreement of a commercially available point-of-care (POC) feline coronavirus (FCoV) quantitative RT-PCR (RT-qPCR) assay and external laboratories' RT-qPCR testing in cats with effusive and non-effusive feline infectious peritonitis (FIP), and in cats with other diseases presenting with similar clinical signs. Client-owned cats suspected of having FIP were enrolled with owner consent. Effusions and ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspirates (FNAs) from the liver, spleen or mesenteric lymph nodes were collected, split and analysed using both a POC RT-qPCR and an external laboratory RT-qPCR. FIP was diagnosed based on American Association of Feline Practitioners/EveryCat guidelines. Sensitivity and negative predictive values were calculated, agreement assessed with Cohen's kappa, paired differences tested with McNemar's test and correlation of crossing point (Cp) values analysed using Pearson's coefficient and paired t -tests. A total of 100 cats were included (effusions n = 62, FNAs n = 38). Overall agreement between assays was substantial (κ = 0.73), with near-perfect concordance for effusions (κ = 0.81) and lower agreement for FNAs (κ = 0.61). Relative sensitivity was highest in effusions (98.1% POC, 92.3% external) and lower in FNAs (63.3-64.5%), with negative predictive values showing similar trends. Cp values were moderately correlated between assays, with minor mean differences (~1 cycle). The POC FCoV RT-qPCR assay is a practical and reliable tool and shows very good agreement with external reference laboratory RT-qPCR testing. FNAs remain useful when effusions are unavailable but carry a higher risk of false negatives, likely due to low viral loads and heterogeneous distribution. POC care testing offers rapid turnaround, supporting timely clinical decision-making, but results must be interpreted alongside clinical presentation and other diagnostics. Agreement between point-of-care and external reference laboratory RT-qPCR testing for feline coronavirus in cats with suspected feline infectious peritonitis Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) is a serious disease caused by feline coronavirus. Diagnosing FIP can be difficult because there is no single test that can confirm the disease in every cat. One commonly used test is called RT-qPCR, which stands for quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction. This test first converts viral RNA into DNA (reverse transcription) and then amplifies it, allowing very small amounts of virus to be detected. The ‘q’ (quantitative) part means that the test also provides an estimate of how much viral material is present. In this study, we compared a point-of-care RT-qPCR test, which can be performed directly in the veterinary clinic, with RT-qPCR testing performed by external laboratories. We tested fluid samples from the chest or abdomen (effusions) and small needle samples from organs (fine-needle aspirates) from cats suspected of having FIP. We included 100 cats with clinical signs consistent with FIP. Samples were tested using both RT-qPCR methods when available. The final diagnosis of FIP was based on accepted international guidelines. We found that the two RT-qPCR tests showed similar performance overall, with good agreement between methods. Both tests performed very well on effusion samples, detecting viral RNA in most cats with FIP. In contrast, performance was lower for fine-needle aspirates, where both tests sometimes failed to detect the virus. This means that the point-of-care RT-qPCR test is a useful tool to support the diagnosis of FIP, especially when effusion is present. Its rapid turnaround time may help veterinarians make quicker clinical decisions. However, a negative result in a fine-needle aspirate does not exclude FIP, and results should always be interpreted together with clinical findings and other diagnostic tests.

papers.title: Comment on 'Fibroepithelial Polyps of the Ear Canal in Dogs: A Retrospective Analysis of 17 Cases'.
papers.authors: Lucas R, Tortoriello R

papers.title: Treatment of Canine Atopic Dermatitis: Updated Guidelines From the International Committee on Allergic Diseases of Animals (ICADA).
papers.authors: Mueller RS, Banovic F, Bensignor E, Santoro D, Nuttall T
papers.abstract: Canine atopic dermatitis (cAD) is a genetically, aetiologically, immunologically and clinically complex disease requiring both individualised immediate and long-term management. These updated guidelines from the International Committee on Allergic Diseases of Animals (ICADA) aim to substantially revise previous recommendations by organising treatment according to mechanism-of-action and by distinguishing two therapeutic phases: reactive therapy to resolve existing pruritus and skin lesions, followed by proactive therapy to maintain remission and reduce flares. The literature was reviewed and recommendations are based, where possible, on randomised controlled trials and systematic reviews, with evidence graded using the Strength of Recommendation Taxonomy. The guidelines review skin barrier care, antimicrobial and microbiome-modulating interventions, avoidance of nonallergenic and allergenic flare factors, allergen-specific immunotherapy, and anti-inflammatory, antipruritic and immunomodulatory treatments. Rapid-acting broad-spectrum drugs, particularly glucocorticoids, are recommended for reactive treatment. Janus Kinase (JAK) inhibitors and lokivetmab may be effective depending on lesion type, severity and inflammatory complexity. Secondary infections and flare factors must be addressed. Proactive management essential to prevent repeated cycles of inflammation may include skin barrier support, infection control, allergen avoidance, allergen immunotherapy, topical glucocorticoids, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, lokivetmab or JAK inhibitors, selected according to the patient's disease pattern and response. A number of interventions are suitable for the treatment of cAD. Interventions are neither universally required, interchangeable nor effective in all cases. Treatment selection should take into account efficacy, safety, practicality, cost, the quality-of-life of both dog and owner, and the legal regulations applicable in the country of use.

papers.title: Successful Treatment of Onchocerca lupi Auricular Infestation Causing Severe Otitis Externa in a Dog.
papers.authors: Martini F, Schnyder M, Schmid D, Fischer N
papers.abstract: We report the first successfully treated case of auricular Onchocerca lupi infection in a dog in Switzerland, causing severe unilateral otitis externa. Diagnosis was confirmed by molecular analysis after nematode extraction. Combined therapy led to complete remission within 6 weeks, highlighting O. lupi as a differential for chronic otitis with mass formation.

papers.title: Efficacy and Field Safety of the Second-Generation, Highly Selective JAK1 Inhibitor Atinvicitinib for the Treatment of Canine Atopic Dermatitis: A Multicentre, Blinded, Randomised, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Trial in Client-Owned Dogs.
papers.authors: Jirjis F, Kowalski TJ, Lynn RC, Overbey L, Cao Q, Stock M, Kuhlmann I
papers.abstract: Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors alleviate pruritus and clinical signs of canine atopic dermatitis (cAD). To confirm the optimal dosing regimen of atinvicitinib, a second-generation highly selective inhibitor of JAK1 in dogs. Sixty-one client-owned dogs, ≥ 12 months and ≥ 2 kg, with cAD. In a randomised, masked, placebo-controlled clinical trial, dogs received atinvicitinib, with food, at 0.8-1.2 mg/kg, once daily for 28 days (q.d. group, n = 21) or 0.4-0.6 mg/kg twice daily for 14 days followed by once daily dosing for 14 days (b.i.d.-q.d. group, n = 21); or placebo b.i.d.-q.d. (control group, n = 19). Owners assessed pruritus (Day [D]0-7, D14, D28) using a Visual Analog Scale (PVAS); veterinary surgeons assessed skin lesions (D0, D28) using the cAD Extent and Severity Index, 4th iteration (CADESI-04). On D0, D14 and D28, blood and urine samples were collected. Treatment success was defined as a ≥ 50% reduction from baseline PVAS or CADESI-04 on D28. Proportions of dogs with ≥ 2 PVAS reduction, and reduction in PVAS and/or CADESI-04 from baseline, also were assessed. Treatment success was 87.5% for the q.d. group (p = 0.011) and 73.3% for the b.i.d.-q.d. group (p = 0.033) (23.1% control group). There was ≥ 2 decrease in PVAS in 80.0% of q.d. dogs. (16.7% controls, p = 0.042). Compared to controls, atinvicitinib-treated dogs had a significantly greater reduction in PVAS (q.d., p = 0.003, b.i.d.-q.d., p = 0.001) and CADESI-04 (q.d. group, p = 0.046). Mean results of clinical pathological values remained within reference ranges. Treatment was well-tolerated. Once-daily atinvicitinib was safe, well-tolerated and effective at rapidly reducing pruritus and resolving cAD-associated skin lesions.

papers.title: Letter to the Editor: 'Fibroepithelial Polyps of the Ear Canal in Dogs: A Retrospective Analysis of 17 Cases'.
papers.authors: Mendes C, De Lucia M

papers.title: Radiation-Induced Alopecia in Dogs With Nasal Tumours: Coat Type Influences Development and Onset.
papers.authors: Nemoto Y, Aoki K, Yoshida A, Ueno H, Nakaichi M
papers.abstract: Radiation-induced alopecia (RIA) is a common adverse effect of radiation therapy, yet factors influencing its development in dogs remain unclear. To characterise acute RIA in dogs with nasal tumours and to evaluate associations with coat type and radiation dose. Thirty-eight client-owned dogs were treated with radiation therapy for nasal tumours. Medical records were reviewed retrospectively. Dogs were classified by coat type (straight versus curly or wire-haired). Time to onset of alopecia was assessed as the interval from the first irradiation to the first detection of alopecia, and cumulative skin dose was calculated up to alopecia onset. Dogs developing acute RIA during radiation therapy were compared with those without RIA. Dogs developing alopecia only after completion of radiation therapy were excluded. Seventeen of 34 dogs developed acute RIA during radiation therapy. Coat type was significantly associated with RIA development (p = 0.003), with all dogs with curly or wire-haired coats affected. These dogs developed RIA earlier than those with straight-haired coats (median 14 versus 20 days; p = 0.047). Within affected dogs, RIA developed first in regions receiving higher skin doses and subsequently progressed to regions receiving lower skin doses. Coat type influences the development of acute RIA in dogs, with curly or wire-haired breeds showing earlier onset and greater extent of alopecia. Alopecia progression reflects regional skin dose distribution. These findings may assist clinicians in predicting the risk of RIA and informing owners about the potential development and timing of radiation-induced alopecia.

papers.title: Systemic Inflammation in Dogs With Atopic Dermatitis Compared to Healthy Dogs and Dogs With Pemphigus Foliaceus: A Study Using a Limited Cytokine Panel.
papers.authors: Herrmann I, Mamo LB, Bizikova P
papers.abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common chronic, pruritic and inflammatory skin disease in both humans and dogs. In people, AD is increasingly recognised as a systemic inflammatory disease in which immune dysregulation drives chronic inflammation extending beyond the skin, particularly in moderate-to-severe disease. Whether a comparable systemic inflammation exists in canine AD, however, remains poorly characterised. We hypothesised that serum cytokine concentrations would differ between dogs with varying AD severity and healthy controls. This study aimed to identify systemic inflammatory markers correlating with AD severity, by comparing cytokine profiles in dogs with mild AD and moderate-to-severe AD against healthy dogs (negative control) and dogs with active pemphigus foliaceus (PF) lesions (positive control). Forty client-owned dogs were enrolled, with 10 dogs in each of four groups: healthy controls, mild AD, moderate-to-severe AD and PF. Serum concentrations of tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-α, TNF-β/lymphotoxin-α, interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, IL-12 and IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1RA) were measured using standardised immunoassays to evaluate systemic inflammation across groups. Marked interindividual variability was observed across all groups. No statistically significant differences in serum concentrations of any of the six cytokines were detected between the healthy, mild AD, moderate-to-severe AD and PF groups. In a limited cytokine panel, no evidence of differential systemic inflammation was detected across groups, including dogs with moderate-to-severe AD compared to healthy controls. These findings may reflect true lack of systemic inflammation in dogs or may be attributable to the small sample size, high interindividual variability or the limited scope of the cytokine panel evaluated.

papers.title: Comparison Between Colorimetric and Subjective Evaluation of Intradermally Injected Histamine-Induced Erythema in Healthy Dogs.
papers.authors: Petak A, Samuel E, Aleksandrova S, Sofou EI, Chatzis MK, Saridomichelakis MN
papers.abstract: Currently used methods for the interpretation of intradermal allergen test results either ignore the erythema of the wheals (objective method) or evaluate it subjectively (subjective method, and global wheal score [GWS]). To compare the efficacy of GWSs in differentiating between wheals induced by intradermal injection of a negative control and histamine at three different concentrations, using either the objective colorimetric measurement of erythema or the subjective evaluation of erythema as absent, weak, or strong. Seven clinically healthy dogs. Duplicate intradermal injections of a negative control, histamine 0.0001%, histamine 0.001%, and histamine 0.01% were administered on the lateral thorax of the dogs. A colorimeter was used to measure erythema before and 15 min after the injection and, at the same time, three blinded investigators scored erythema subjectively. The subtraction of the first colorimetric measurement of erythema obtained before intradermal injection from the first postinjection objective measurement (ΔEfirst) outperformed three other objective measurement methods and yielded GWSs capable of differentiation among the four solutions with efficiencies comparable to those of GWSs based on subjective erythema assessment. However, the stronger correlation between the later and wheal diameters may indicate bias in the subjective evaluation of erythema. A single colorimetric measurement of erythema before and after intradermal injection of a negative control and histamine at three different concentrations, followed by calculation of their difference, can replace the subjective evaluation of erythema for the calculation of GWSs and avoid possible bias.

papers.title: Diagnostic Performance of Immunoglobulin E Serology, Prick Test and Patch Test With Food Allergens in Dogs With Atopic Dermatitis and Adverse Food Reactions Using the Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Food Challenge as Gold Standard.
papers.authors: Sofou EI, Aleksandrova S, Samuel E, Chatzis M, Saridomichelakis MN
papers.abstract: In dogs with adverse food reactions (AFRs), immunoglobulin (Ig)E serology, prick test and patch test with food allergens have shown variable diagnostic performance for the identification of the offending foods, when the latter were identified using open food challenges. To evaluate the diagnostic performance of these tests in dogs with atopic dermatitis (AD) and AFRs, using the double-blind placebo-controlled food challenge (DBPCFC) as the gold standard. Twelve dogs with AD and AFRs underwent DBPCFCs with eight food items. IgE serology, prick test and patch test with the same eight food allergens were performed after the diagnosis of AD and before the diagnostic investigation for AFRs and the DBPCFCs. The sensitivity (3%-60.6%), specificity (54.8%-98.4%), positive predictive value (25%-66.7%) and negative predictive value (64.1%-72.3%) of the three tests and of their combination were unsatisfactory. Furthermore, their positive and negative likelihood ratio values were not in the clinically informative range, apart from the prick test having a weakly informative positive likelihood ratio value of 3.81. Under the conditions of this study, the diagnostic performance of IgE serology, prick test and/or patch test with food allergens was poor using the DBPCFC as gold standard.

papers.title: Time Required for Topical Difluprednate to Suppress the Intradermal Histamine-Induced Vascular Reaction in Dogs.
papers.authors: Takeo F, Murayama N, Orito K
papers.abstract: Topical glucocorticoid (GC) is used to manage inflammatory skin diseases in dogs. However, contact times associated with detectable topical GC effects have not been clarified in dogs. Uncertainty regarding contact time may lead to premature removal or overuse, compromising efficacy and safety. To determine contact times at which detectable GC effects are observed after topical difluprednate lotion application in dogs. Six male Beagle dogs. Suppression of the histamine-induced vascular reaction (HVR), based on the principles of the vasoconstrictor assay, was used as an indicator of detectable GC effects. Difluprednate lotion was applied to a circular area (2 cm in diameter) on the lateral trunk 5, 10 and 30 min before intradermal histamine injection. Fluorescein was administered intravenously 5 min before histamine injection to visualise HVR. HVR images were obtained 15 min after histamine injection under UV illumination, and the fluorescent area was measured using ImageJ. Statistical analysis was performed using Dunnett's multiple comparison test. When difluprednate application was performed 5, 10 and 30 min before histamine injection, HVR areas were smaller than untreated control sites (p < 0.01). No significant differences were detected among sites treated 5, 10 and 30 min before histamine injection. Difluprednate lotion suppressed the HVR when applied 5, 10 and 30 min before histamine injection, indicating detectable dermal GC activity at the evaluated time points. Information regarding contact times at which topical GC effects can be detected may help clinicians to provide contact-time instructions and improve treatment management.

papers.title: A Randomised Placebo-Controlled Study to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of a Two-Dose Topical Terbinafine and Betamethasone Gel for the Treatment of Yeast (Malassezia pachydermatis) Otitis Externa in Dogs.
papers.authors: Baks ZZ, Heinz HB, Grundke S, Thompson C, Garcia R
papers.abstract: Otitis externa (OE) with Malassezia pachydermatis overgrowth with limited bacterial involvement is common in dogs. Treatment with products containing antibiotics is unnecessary and not consistent with judicious use of antimicrobials. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of an otic gel containing 1% terbinafine and 0.1% betamethasone acetate for the treatment of yeast-predominant canine OE. 239 privately owned dogs were enrolled. Inclusion criteria were an otitis index score (OTIS3) of ≥ 6 and yeast-predominance on ear swab cytological evaluation. Dogs received either the study product containing terbinafine and betamethasone (TBG) or placebo (saline) on Day (D) 0 and D7. Follow-up visits were on D7, D14, D28 and D45. Clinical success was defined as an OTIS3 score ≤ 3 on D45. Overall clinical response (by the veterinary surgeon and owner) and yeast cytological count reduction also were assessed. Safety was evaluated based on clinical assessments, haematological and clinical chemical analysis, urinalysis and adverse events. The treatment success was significantly higher in the treated group compared to the placebo group (62.9% versus 20.0%, p < 0.0001). Dogs receiving TBG had a treatment response described as 'excellent' or 'good' by 61.9% and 71.1% of veterinary surgeons and owners, respectively. The safety evaluation demonstrated that the otic gel was safe. Efficacy and safety of an otic gel for the treatment of canine OE associated with Malassezia pachydermatis were demonstrated.

papers.title: Symmetrical Lupoid Onychodystrophy in Review: Lessons Learned From 31 Cases.
papers.authors: Calesso JR, Souza CP, Bruner SR, Bicalho APCV
papers.abstract: Symmetrical lupoid onychodystrophy (SLO) is a complex disease that exclusively affects the claws of dogs and represents a therapeutic challenge. Biopsy sampling of the third phalanx for histopathological evaluation has historically been the recommended diagnostic test, yet clinical diagnosis is currently encouraged. Numerous treatment protocols of varying success have been proposed for dogs with this condition. The goals of this study are to report clinical findings, treatment protocols and outcomes of dogs with SLO, to propose a rationale for the clinical diagnosis and to discuss therapies for SLO. Thirty-one dogs examined at a veterinary hospital from May 2004 to April 2024. Retrospective analysis of medical records from dogs diagnosed with SLO. The average age of dogs at disease onset and diagnosis was 7 years old. Nineteen breeds were represented. Thirty dogs were clinically diagnosed with SLO, mostly presenting with onychodystrophy and onychomadesis, and in one a biopsy sample was collected. Different therapeutic combinations including tetracyclines alone or with niacinamide, pentoxifylline, essential fatty acids (EFAs), vitamin E, biotin and ciclosporin were used for the initial and/or maintenance treatment of SLO.
