papers.authors: Bia T, Korba AA, Slimani KM, Villanueva-Saz S, Manseur H, Mekhloufi OA, Degui D, Khames M, Lafri I, Györke A, Benameur Q
papers.abstract: Leptospirosis is a globally important zoonotic disease caused by pathogenic Leptospira species and represents a public health concern, particularly for people in close contact with infected companion animals. As the seroprevalence of canine leptospirosis in Algeria remains unknown, this study aimed to estimate seroprevalence and identify potential risk factors in dogs from Tiaret Province. A total of 82 dogs of both sexes, aged 6 months to 10 years, were sampled between January and December 2022 and underwent a general clinical examination, general health status was recorded as good or poor, and the absence of clinical signs compatible with leptospirosis ( collapse, jaundice, difficulty breathing, heamaturia) was noted. Serum samples were tested using the Microscopic Agglutination Test, the international reference serological method. Overall seroprevalence was 29.3% (95% confidence interval (CI): 20.5-39.9). The most frequently detected reactions were to Patoc (8.5%; 95% CI:4.2-16.6; 7/82), Bratislava (8.5%; 95% CI:4.2-16.6; 7/82), Autumnalis and Copenhageni (7.3% each; 95% CI: 3.4-15.1; 6/82), Icterohaemorrhagiae (6.1%; 95% CI:2.6-13.5; 5/82), Canicola (4.9%; 95% CI:1.9-11.9; 4/82), and Pyrogenes (1.2%; 95% CI:0.2-6.6; 1/82). Among the 24 seropositive dogs, 66.7% (95% CI: 46.7-82.0) reacted to a single serovar, whereas 33.3% (95% CI: 18.0-53.3) reacted to two or three serovars, indicating exposure to diverse leptospiral antigens. Two dogs reacted simultaneously to Copenhageni and Icterohaemorrhagiae, both belonging to the Icterohaemorrhagiae serogroup. None of the investigated variables - sex, age, breed group, function (hunting vs. guard), geographical area, or health status - was significantly associated with leptospiral seropositivity (p > 0.05). These findings demonstrate a previous exposure to multiple Leptospira serovars among unvaccinated hunting and guard dogs in Tiaret and highlight a potential zoonotic risk to humans, particularly dog owners and other individuals in close contact with dogs.

papers.title: Clinical leptospirosis in a cat presenting with severe hypokalaemia and glucosuria.
papers.authors: Jagdhane R, Cattin R
papers.abstract: A 1.5-year-old, female spayed domestic mediumhair cat presented for lethargy, inappetence, weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia and severe generalised muscle weakness with cervical ventroflexion. She was noted to be severely hypokalaemic and to have severe glucosuria without significant hyperglycaemia. PCR and serological tests suggested a diagnosis of leptospirosis serovar Pomona. The cat was treated with doxycycline, potassium supplementation and spironolactone, after which the hypokalaemia improved and glucosuria resolved when assessed 2 weeks later. Cats are generally considered to be resistant to clinical infection with leptospirosis, and reports of clinical disease are rare. To the authors' knowledge, there have been no reports of hypokalaemia or severe glucosuria in clinically affected cats. In addition, this report highlights the importance of considering leptospirosis as a differential diagnosis in cats who are exposed to various risk factors reported for this disease.

papers.title: Primary Erythrocytosis (Polycythaemia) in a Neutered Male Dog Presenting With Right Hindlimb Lameness.
papers.authors: Belch R, Henry P, Ferreira M, Padros AA, Munoz ML, Lloyd-Bradley B, Isaac I, Llewellyn E, Nagendran A
papers.abstract: A 2-year-old male entire Cocker Spaniel was referred for investigation of progressive right hindlimb lameness and polyuria and polydipsia. Investigations conducted by the primary care veterinary surgeon revealed erythrocytosis (haematocrit of 78%, reference interval: 37%-55%) and urine concentration consistent with polyuria and polydipsia (specific gravity 1.014). Upon referral, physical examination revealed a dark red oral mucosa and right hindlimb lameness, characterised by intermittent non-weight bearing of the limb when standing. Neurological examination only revealed a mild short-strided gait, and orthopaedic examination was unremarkable. Secondary causes of erythrocytosis were excluded by normal arterial blood gas, low erythropoietin levels and normal thoracic and abdominal imaging, resulting in a diagnosis of primary erythrocytosis (PE). Focal ultrasonography identified a right external iliac venous thrombus, suspected to be the cause of the right hindlimb lameness and presumed to be associated with the PE. Initial management involved repeated phlebotomies, followed by long-term treatment with hydroxyurea (31 mg/kg twice weekly) and rivaroxaban (2 mg/kg once daily). At the 5-month recheck, the dog was asymptomatic, with resolution of the iliac thrombus and a normal haematocrit. This case highlights an unusual presentation of PE in a dog, not previously described in the veterinary literature, and re-examines the discussion on the optimal management of this rare condition, with a focus on the necessity of antithrombotic therapy.

papers.title: Surgical Site Infection and Antimicrobial Resistance After Mastectomy in Dogs and Cats: A 615-Case Multicentre Cohort and Infection-Control Audit.
papers.authors: Hedayatinia M, Gorjian F, Pato M, Maadi MA, Ahmadi R, Abdous A
papers.abstract: Surgical site infection (SSI) is an important complication after mastectomy and antimicrobial resistance may complicate treatment. To estimate 30-day SSI incidence after mastectomy in dogs (Canis lupus familiaris Linnaeus, 1758) and cats (Felis catus Linnaeus, 1758), evaluate patient- and procedure-related factors, describe perioperative antimicrobial use and microbiology and assess clinic infection-control practices. This multicentre retrospective cohort included 615 mastectomy procedures from 12 veterinary clinics in Tehran Province, Iran, between 2020 and 2025. SSI-positive records were independently re-reviewed by two investigators using contemporary veterinary SSI terminology. Clinic-stratified conditional logistic regression evaluated seven clinically selected predictors. SSI occurred after 54/615 procedures (8.8%; 95% CI, 6.8%-11.3%); 50 infections were superficial and four deep. Surgical duration per 30 min (aOR, 2.37; 95% CI, 1.61-3.49), intraoperative hypothermia (aOR, 3.66; 95% CI, 1.39-9.62), body condition score per point (aOR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.05-2.42) and previous major surgery (aOR, 3.57; 95% CI, 1.49-8.55) were associated with SSI. An MDR isolate was identified in 16/33 cultured SSI cases and antimicrobial-isolate discordance was present in 15/30 assessable comparisons. Mean clinic infection-control audit score was 4.6 ± 1.7/10. Longer surgery, intraoperative hypothermia, higher body condition score and previous major surgery were associated with SSI in this predominantly canine cohort of intact animals undergoing mastectomy without concurrent ovariohysterectomy. These associations were not independently demonstrated in cats. The findings support standardised surveillance, perioperative risk reduction, culture-guided treatment and antimicrobial stewardship. Not applicable. This was a retrospective observational study and clinic-level audit and was not a clinical trial.

papers.title: Toxoplasma gondii in Ethiopia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Infection Prevalence and Associated Risk Factors in Humans and Animals.
papers.authors: Wubaye AM, Shitu BF, Delie AM, Haimanot AB, Ayicheh YW, Mulugeta AM, Enawgaw AS, Ambaw YG, Bitewa MD, Wondie SG, Kassie TD, Mengie ZA, Kallu SA, Tafere BA, Mekonnen TS, Molla MG, Eshetu DM, Yewodiaw TK
papers.abstract: Toxoplasma gondii is a protozoan parasite with significant animal and public health implications. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to estimate the pooled prevalence of toxoplasmosis in ruminants and humans in Ethiopia and to determine the major risk factors associated with the disease. Five databases were used to search for all articles published between 2012 and 2025. The pooled prevalence of toxoplasmosis was calculated using a random-effects model. I 2 statistics were used to assess heterogeneity among the included studies. Publication bias was assessed through a meta-analysis Egger regression asymmetry test. The overall pooled prevalence of T. gondii was 42.0% (95% CI: 35.0%-49.0%) in ruminants and 61.0% (95% CI: 49.0%-74.0%) in humans. Female animals have higher odds of acquiring T. gondii (OR = 1.76; 95% CI: 1.56-2.00) than males. Similarly, adult animals were more likely to be exposed to the disease (OR = 2.39; 95% CI: 2.10-2.74) than young age groups. In humans, rural residence (OR = 1.23; 95% CI: 1.07-1.42) and cat ownership (OR = 2.04; 95% CI: 1.79-2.32) were significantly associated with T. gondii seropositivity. These results highlight the necessity of targeted monitoring and preventative measures to reduce T. gondii exposure in both animal and human populations in Ethiopia.

papers.title: Clinically relevant hypomagnesemia during recovery from severe leptospirosis-associated acute kidney injury in a dog treated with continuous renal replacement therapy: a case report.
papers.authors: Cho J, Kang S, Kim S, Kim M, Park C
papers.abstract: Leptospirosis is an important cause of acute kidney injury (AKI) in dogs and commonly induces renal tubular dysfunction. Although electrolyte abnormalities are frequently recognized during the course of leptospirosis, clinically relevant hypomagnesemia associated with neurological manifestations has rarely been reported in dogs. This report describes a dog that developed severe symptomatic hypomagnesemia during recovery from severe leptospirosis-associated AKI treated with continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). A 9 year old, 12 kg spayed female mixed-breed dog was referred for severe leptospirosis-associated AKI complicated by anuria, hyperbilirubinemia, thrombocytopenia, and pulmonary involvement. Blood and urine polymerase chain reaction assays confirmed Leptospira spp. Because of persistent anuria and progressive azotemia despite intensive medical management, the dog underwent two continuous renal replacement therapy sessions approximately 15 and 18 h, respectively. Urine production subsequently recovered, and the dog entered a polyuric recovery phase with progressive improvement in azotemia. On day 13 after admission, generalized tremors, hypersalivation, and altered mentation developed concurrently with severe hypomagnesemia (ionized magnesium, 0.24 mmol/L; total magnesium, 1.4 mg/dL). Fractional excretion of magnesium (FEMG) was markedly increased (38.8%), suggesting inappropriate renal magnesium loss despite improving renal function. Intravenous magnesium sulfate administered as a bolus followed by continuous rate infusion resulted in rapid resolution of the neurological signs. At follow-up evaluations performed 11 and 23 days after the hypomagnesemic episode, fractional excretion of magnesium remained increased at 30.2% and 28.4%, respectively, despite improvement in serum creatinine concentration, supporting persistent impairment of renal tubular magnesium handling during recovery. This case demonstrates that clinically significant hypomagnesemia may develop during the polyuric recovery phase of severe leptospirosis-associated AKI in dogs, even after apparent improvement in renal function. Serial measurements of fractional excretion of magnesium supported continued renal magnesium loss during recovery and emphasized the importance of monitoring magnesium concentrations in dogs with leptospirosis, particularly when neurological abnormalities develop.

papers.title: Dose-response effects of dietary luteolin-loaded chitosan nanoparticles on growth and physiological responses of post-weaning rabbits reared under summer heat stress.
papers.authors: Thagfan FA, Al-Hoshani N, Mohamed RAEH, Ahmed KAE, Abdelnour SA, Abd-Elkarim MM
papers.abstract: Applying nanotechnology to promote sustainable livestock production and mitigate the adverse impacts of rising global temperatures on animal health has received critical attention. In the existing research, we synthesized luteolin-loaded chitosan nanoparticles (NLU) and evaluated their efficacy in mitigating heat stress (HS) in growing rabbits by investigating growth performance, immune response, oxidative stress, tissues integrity, antioxidant defenses, inflammatory markers, and apoptotic cascades. A total of 120 weaned growing rabbits (New Zealand white breed) were randomly assigned to four experimental groups (30 rabbits per group, with 30 replicates per group) and raised under summer condition during a 9 weeks trial. Treatments consisted of a basal control diet (HS group) or the basal diet fortified with 25 (NLU25), 50 (NLU50), or 100 (NLU100) mg/kg of NLU. The temperature-humidity index (THI) was 30.65, calculated from ambient temperature and relative humidity, confirming that the rabbits experienced severe HS. The prepared NLU nanoparticles exhibited a mean hydrodynamic diameter of 138.5 nm, a polydispersity index of 0.380, and a positive zeta potential of + 54.5 mV. Dietary NLU supplementation exhibited a significant quadratic dose-response effect on growth performance (P < 0.05), with the NLU50 and NLU100 treatments eliciting the most pronounced protective effects relative to the HS group. Dietary NLU supplementation significantly decreased serum lipid profiles, liver enzymes, and renal function markers (P < 0.05). Specifically, NLU quadratically increased glutathione peroxidase (GPx), catalase (CAT) levels, and total antioxidant capacity (TAC, linear effect), alongside immunoglobulin concentrations (IgM and IgG) (P < 0.05). Conversely, oxidative stress indicators (myeloperoxidase and MDA) and cell death biomarkers (caspase-3 and CK-18) were markedly reduced (P < 0.001) in quadratic manner. Furthermore, NLU supplementation quadratically attenuated the inflammatory response by decreasing the serum inflammatory makers including nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-4 (IL-4), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin-8 (IL-8) alongside significant increase of nitric oxide levels (P < 0.001). Consequently, dietary NLU effectively preserved the histoarchitectural integrity of both hepatic and intestinal tissues under heat-stress conditions. Overall, dietary inclusion of 50 or 100 mg/kg NLU effectively showed beneficial effects on growth indices in rabbits exposed to heat stress by preserving tissue histoarchitecture, remodeling metabolic and redox homeostasis, boosting immune competence, and suppressing inflammatory and apoptotic signaling cascades.

papers.title: Prevalence and clinical relevance of hypocobalaminaemia and hypercobalaminaemia in cats.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Casas C, Dye C
papers.abstract: The aim of the present study was to investigate the prevalence of hypo- and hypercobalaminaemia in a cohort of cats with diverse disease pathologies and to assess associations with signalment and disease characteristics. Residual blood from cats presented to a large veterinary referral hospital during a 24-month period was used for serum B12 quantification. All cats requiring blood collection as part of diagnostic investigations were eligible for inclusion regardless of clinical presentation. Serum B12 concentration was assessed according to signalment, body weight, body condition score, primary affected body system and type of disease pathology as derived from the clinical notes. A total of 229 cats were enrolled: 128 male (119 neutered, 9 entire) and 101 female (88 neutered, 13 entire). Of these, 176 were domestic shorthair or longhair, and 53 were purebred. The median age was 9.9 years and median body weight 4.1 kg. Of the 229 cats, 80 (34.9%) had high serum B12, 86 (37.6%) had normal, 18 (7.9%) had borderline and 45 (19.7%) had low serum B12. Median serum B12 concentration was higher in cats aged <8.0 years than ⩾8.0 years, and there was a weak but significant negative correlation between age and serum B12. Median serum B12 concentration was lower in cats weighing <3.0 kg than in those ⩾3.0 kg, and a weak but significant positive correlation was found between body weight and serum B12 concentration. No associations were found between serum B12 and sex, breed, body condition score, affected body system or pathology type. Vitamin B12 aberrations were common in this cohort of cats, with approximately one-third and one-fifth having abnormally high and low serum concentrations, respectively. Serum vitamin B12 concentration declined with advancing age, and hypocobalaminaemia was more prevalent in cats with body weights <3.0 kg. Hypo- and hypercobalaminaemia were documented in cats with a wide variety of clinical presentations, and no specific disease associations were elucidated.

papers.title: A case of pseudo-obstruction in a cat associated with amebiasis.
papers.authors: de Sousa Filho RP, Lopes Neto BE, Ferreira CB, Sampaio KO
papers.abstract: This report describes a 9-year-old, spayed female domestic shorthair cat presenting with a 7-day history of anorexia and previous chronic constipation. Clinical examination revealed abdominal distension and discomfort. Radiographic and ultrasonographic imaging showed severe, generalized gaseous distension of the entire gastrointestinal tract without evidence of mechanical obstruction. An exploratory celiotomy confirmed severe, non-obstructive dilation of the stomach and intestines, with aperistalsis of the ileum and large intestine. Histopathological analysis of intestinal biopsies revealed neuritis and necrosis of the myenteric plexus, along with the presence of protozoan trophozoites consistent with Entamoeba histolytica . These findings led to a diagnosis of intestinal pseudo-obstruction secondary to amebiasis-associated ganglionitis. Treatment was initiated with pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, and metronidazole. The cat responded favorably, with resolution of clinical signs and normalization of defecation. This case documents a rare instance of intestinal pseudo-obstruction in a cat, uniquely associating it with amebiasis and demonstrating a successful therapeutic outcome with pyridostigmine. To our knowledge, this is the first report of intestinal pseudo-obstruction associated with amebiasis in a feline patient. Furthermore, it adds to the limited literature on the successful use of pyridostigmine for treating severe gastrointestinal dysmotility in cats, offering a potential therapeutic option for this challenging condition.

papers.title: Bendamustine induces peripheral lymphodepletion in dogs with relapsed lymphoma.
papers.authors: Lenz JA, Upton L, Ma J, Talone MM, Peng B, Jiang L, Ghanian A, Didehvar D, Yang E, Fraietta JA, Atherton MJ
papers.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has improved outcomes for many human patients with B-cell lymphoma and provides a rational template for analogous canine patients. To date, the expansion, persistence, and activity of CAR T cells in dogs have been limited. Lymphodepletion supports CAR T-cell engraftment and antitumor activity. In human medical oncology, bendamustine has emerged as a well-tolerated lymphodepleting agent. However, prospective use of bendamustine for dogs with lymphoma has not been characterized. To determine the lymphodepleting activity and tolerability of bendamustine in dogs with relapsed lymphoma. Secondary objectives included monitoring serum cytokines and short-term changes in peripheral tumor burden. Eleven client-owned dogs with relapsed lymphoma. Luminescent assays were used to assess the direct cytotoxic activity of bendamustine against canine lymphoid cell lines. A prospective rapid dose-escalation pilot trial was undertaken in 11 dogs with relapsed lymphoma to evaluate tolerability while tracking peripheral lymphocyte counts, serum cytokine concentrations, and lymph node measurements. Bendamustine induced concentration-dependent cytotoxicity in all cell lines tested. Two-dose bendamustine regimens up to 90 mg/m2 were generally well tolerated, with no dose-limiting toxicities observed, and resulted in peripheral lymphodepletion (pretreatment median, 880 cells/μL; posttreatment median, 310 cells/μL), an exploratory decrease in circulating interleukin-6 (pretreatment median, 5.32 pg/mL; posttreatment median, 1.33 pg/mL), and a short-term decrease in peripheral nodal burden in 8 of 11 dogs. Bendamustine was generally well tolerated and induced lymphodepletion in our cohort. These findings support further evaluation of bendamustine as a preconditioning agent before autologous canine CAR T-cell infusion.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Elbow luxation treatment in cats using external fixation.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Yener K, Hurma MS, Karadağ MS, Dikmen Ilginoğlu K, Hünerli H, Bayir ÖY, Yavuz Ü, Hayat A
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo describe outcomes and complications of open reduction, collateral ligament repair and temporary epoxy resin Type Ia transarticular external skeletal fixation (TaESF) in cats with traumatic lateral elbow luxation after failed closed treatment.MethodsTen cats were referred 3-4 days after injury. Closed reduction failed in four cats and reluxation occurred in six after reduction and Robert Jones bandaging. All underwent open reduction, apposition of identifiable collateral ligament ends and four-pin epoxy resin Type Ia TaESF. Clinical and orthogonal radiographic examinations were performed weekly until frame removal at 3 weeks and at 6 weeks. Lameness was graded 0-3, and Campbell's test was performed after frame removal and at 6 weeks. At 6 months, three cats underwent orthopaedic examination and seven were assessed by structured owner telephone interview. Complications were classified according to Cook et al.ResultsReduction was maintained in all cats through 6 weeks. Grade 0/1 lameness was recorded in seven/three cats at 3 weeks and eight/two cats at 6 weeks (Cases 3 and 9). Functional outcome was full in eight cats (80%) and acceptable in two (20%). A contralateral proximal ulnar fracture contributed to residual lameness in Case 3. Case 1 required unplanned intervention for proximal humeral pin migration and seroma. The pin was repositioned under sedation without replacement or additional epoxy resin. Radiolucency and periosteal reaction surrounded the distal ulnar pin. The seroma resolved without recurrence, and the frame was removed as scheduled. No comparable pin-site radiographic abnormalities were identified in the other cats. At 6 months, all cats had normal owner-reported walking, running and jumping without observable lameness.Conclusions and relevanceIn this small retrospective series, open reduction and collateral ligament repair protected by epoxy resin Type Ia TaESF maintained reduction and yielded satisfactory short-term outcomes after failed closed treatment. One cat required unplanned intervention for a pin-related complication. Comparative studies with objective long-term clinical and radiographic follow-up are warranted.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Feline granulocytic anaplasmosis in Europe: anamnesis, clinicopathological abnormalities, bacterial DNA load, treatment, and outcome.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Meyer L, Moritz A, Baneth G, Strube C, Jindal K, Müller E, Schäfer I
papers.abstract: Feline granulocytic anaplasmosis (FGA) is caused by Anaplasma ( A. ) phagocytophilum . Fever and thrombocytopenia are the most common clinicopathological abnormalities.ObjectivesThe aim was to investigate regionality, seasonality, clinicopathological parameters, treatment, and outcomes in cats with FGA.MethodsThe database of a commercial laboratory was retrospectively screened for A. phagocytophilum -polymerase chain (PCR)-results on EDTA-blood submitted by European veterinarians from 01/2022 to 12/2025. Hematological data and bacterial DNA loads quantified by digital droplet-PCR were analyzed. Questionnaires were sent to the veterinarians asking for underlying diseases, anamnesis, clinicopathological abnormalities, treatment, and outcome in cats with FGA.Results43/702 cats (6.1%) tested positive by A. phagocytophilum -PCR in Europe. Questionnaires were available for 29/43 cats (67.4%), all of which had outdoor access. Lethargy (23/29; 79.3%), anorexia (22/29, 75.9%), and fever (>39.5°C, 18/29, 62.0%) were the most reported findings. Thrombocytopenia was detected in 14/18 cats (77.8%) without concurrent diseases, anemia and leukopenia in 2/20 cats each (10.0%), eosinopenia in 10/17 (58.8%), and lymphopenia in 8/17 cats (47.1%). The bacterial DNA load was available for 27/43 cats (25 x 10 2 -87 x 10 6 , median 124 x 10 5 /ml EDTA-blood), revealing no significant correlation with hematological parameters. 20/21 cats (95.2%) were treated with doxycycline and one (4.8%) with enrofloxacin. Uncomplicated course of disease was reported in 19/21 cats (90.5%). In one cat treated with doxycycline for 10 days, another positive PCR was recorded one month later. Clinical signs recurred immediately in another cat treated with doxycycline for five days only.Conclusions and relevanceFGA should be considered in cats with outdoor access, lethargy, inappetence, and most often mild thrombocytopenia and/or anemia, regardless of fever. Infected cats usually responded well to doxycycline with individual relapses if treated for 10 days or shorter. Treatment for 14 days to clear the infection, and PCR monitoring after finishing treatment are recommended.

papers.title: Intraoperative Indocyanine Green Fluorescence for Assessment of Suspected Venous Invasion in a Dog With Thyroid Carcinoma.
papers.authors: Kim M, Kim Y, Lee S
papers.abstract: Accurate intraoperative assessment of vascular involvement in canine thyroid carcinoma remains challenging when preoperative imaging findings are equivocal. This case describes the use of intraoperative indocyanine green fluorescence imaging to assist real-time assessment of suspected venous involvement during canine thyroidectomy. A 5-year-old spayed female Maltese dog was presented with a cervical mass and clinicopathological findings consistent with hypothyroidism. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography identified a left thyroid mass with suspected external jugular vein compression but no definitive evidence of vascular invasion. During left thyroidectomy, dilation and distal tapering of the thyroid veins raised concern for venous involvement. Indocyanine green (0.5 mg/dog) was administered intravenously for intraoperative near-infrared fluorescence imaging. Diffuse fluorescence of the thyroid mass and segmental intraluminal fluorescence within the dilated thyroid vein were observed, with signal loss at the tapering point. Based on these findings, en bloc resection including a short segment of the involved vein was performed. Histopathology confirmed thyroid carcinoma without evidence of regional lymph node metastasis. This case illustrates that intraoperative indocyanine green fluorescence imaging may provide adjunctive real-time information for assessing suspected venous involvement during canine thyroid carcinoma surgery and may complement preoperative imaging when vascular invasion is uncertain.

papers.title: Sarcocystis sp. infection associated to encephalomyelitis and myositis in a Brazilian dog.
papers.authors: do Nascimento Iara ÍH, Martins AFG, de Sousa Ribeiro L, Boabaid FM, de Oliveira LGS, da Silva EMS, Driemeier D, Torres BBJ
papers.abstract: Sarcocystis sp.-induced disease is known especially in horses, in which S. neurona is the primary causative agent of Equine Protozoal Myeloencephalitis in the Americas. While horses are aberrant hosts, the range of susceptible species includes marine mammals, raccoons, and cats. Reports of clinical disease in dogs are rare, remaining unreported in South America. This study describes the clinical, pathological, and immunohistochemical findings of a naturally occurring, fatal case of meningoencephalomyelitis and myositis caused by Sarcocystis sp. in a dog in Brazil. A 5-year-old mixed-breed bitch presented with acute non-ambulatory tetraparesis, generalized muscle atrophy, and blindness. Despite supportive therapy, the patient deteriorated and was euthanized. Gross findings included enlarged lymph nodes, moderate splenomegaly and hepatomegaly, with multifocal mild fibrin deposition on the liver capsule, accompanied by multifocal mild hemorrhages in the pancreas. Histopathology demonstrated severe, multifocal necrotizing meningoencephalomyelitis, myositis, splenitis, lymphadenitis and interstitial pneumonia, associated with intralesional protozoal schizonts. Immunohistochemistry supported immunolabelling consistent with Sarcocystis sp. while excluding Toxoplasma gondii and Neospora caninum. To the authors' knowledge, this represents the first report of clinical canine sarcocystosis with this severity in South America supported by histopathological and immunohistochemical findings. These findings support that Sarcocystis sp. should be considered a differential diagnosis for canine progressive neurological disease, highlighting the potential role of wildlife reservoirs in the disease's epidemiology.

papers.title: Novel liquid biopsy based on comprehensive small RNA profiling for screening of cancer in dogs utilizing machine learning.
papers.authors: Harako S, Yuki M, Noguchi S, Ohno T, Nozaki N, Nishida R, Hojo H, Horikawa R, Kawata D, Noda Y, Miura N, Mizuno T, Momoi Y
papers.abstract: Recent investigations have demonstrated the relevance in cancer of a variety of small RNAs, beyond microRNAs (miRNAs). However, the comprehensive application of these RNAs to cancer detection in dogs remains unexplored. We investigated whether combining miRNAs and other small RNAs using a custom database improves the accuracy of machine learning cancer screening in dogs compared with models using only miRNAs. A total of 389 dogs were enrolled: 85 with cancer, 77 with nonmalignant diseases, and 227 healthy controls. Small RNAs in blood samples were sequenced, and miRNAs (via miRBase) and other small RNAs (via a custom database) were profiled. Based on these profiles, 2 datasets were prepared: one with only miRNAs and another combining miRNAs with other small RNAs. For each dataset, 12 classification models were constructed using identical methods to enable paired comparisons of performance, with 5-fold cross-validation and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) as the primary metrics. The model that integrated both miRNAs and other small RNAs yielded a significantly higher AUC compared with the miRNA-only model (median AUC: 0.926 [95% CI, 0.911-0.944] vs 0.881 [0.860-0.897]; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P < .001), indicating enhanced capability in discriminating malignant tumors in dogs. We investigated the comprehensive integration of diverse small RNA species, beyond miRNAs, using a machine learning approach for cancer screening in dogs. Although further prospective validation in independent cohorts is needed, our results indicate that this strategy improves the performance of cancer classification models in dogs.

papers.title: A newly derived formula outperforms published formulae for estimating urine osmolality in healthy dogs receiving intravenous fluids.
papers.authors: Jeong Y, Qu Y, Kim MS, Her J
papers.abstract: To derive a formula to estimate urine osmolality (Uosm) in dogs with urine sodium, potassium, glucose, and urea nitrogen and to compare the performance of the derived formula with published formulae. A prospective observational study was conducted using purpose-bred Beagles housed at a university research facility. Healthy dogs, confirmed by physical examination and laboratory testing, received isotonic or hypotonic IV fluids in a randomized sequence for 48 hours, with a 10-day washout period between treatments. Urine samples were collected through indwelling urinary catheters at baseline and every 12 hours. Urine osmolality and urinary osmolytes were measured. Linear mixed models were used to derive formulae, and agreement was assessed using the concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), Bland-Altman analysis, and Passing-Bablok regression. Performance was compared with published formulae. 9 dogs provided 89 urine measurements. The proposed formula was Uosm = 2 X sodium + 1.8 X potassium + urea nitrogen2.5 (mg/dL) + glucose3.9 (mg/dL). The CCC was 0.96 (95% CI, 0.94 to 0.97), and the fixed bias was +7.99 mOsm/kg. Passing-Bablok regression revealed no proportional or constant bias. Compared with the published formulae, the proposed formula had the highest CCC and lowest fixed bias. The proposed formula provided a simple and reliable method to estimate Uosm in healthy dogs receiving isotonic and hypotonic IV fluids and outperformed the published formulae. Further validation in pathologic states is warranted. This formula improves the assessment of renal water handling, fluid balance, and kidney concentration ability when measuring Uosm is unavailable.

papers.title: Clinical presentation, computed tomographic findings, treatment, and outcome of traumatic jaw fractures in domestic rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus): 21 cases (2014-2025).
papers.authors: Charrasse M, Hahn H, Phillips K, Boutoille F, Sanchez-Migallon Guzman D, Huynh M
papers.abstract: To present clinical features, CT findings, treatment, and outcome for traumatic jaw fractures diagnosed via CT. Medical records from 2014 through 2026 were reviewed, and 21 rabbits with traumatic jaw fractures diagnosed by CT were selected. Among the 21 rabbits that fit the inclusion criteria, trauma sources included involuntary owner-inflicted trauma (n = 10), sofa-related falls or entrapment (3), dog bites (2), post-dental trimming issues (1), trauma with a table (1), fall of cardboard onto the head (1), fall of a folding table onto the head (1), and unknown (2). Fractures of the mandibular ramus were identified in 85.7% cases (unilateral, n = 14; bilateral, 4). Concurrent fractures were common (intermandibular suture (n = 5), body of the mandible (4), zygomatic arch (5), frontal bone (1), presphenoid bone (1), tympanic bulla (1)). A recurrent mandibular fracture pattern was seen in 47.6% of cases (n = 10). Complications in 13 rabbits that had a follow-up included dental malocclusion of incisors (n = 8) and cheek teeth (6), chronic dacryocystitis (2), hyperthermia (2), mandibular abscess (1), and persistence of vestibular syndrome (1). Notably, 11 rabbits were still alive 581 days after the trauma. Traumatic jaw injuries in rabbits frequently involve multiple concurrent fracture sites and associated craniofacial lesions. Computed tomography allowed detailed anatomical characterization of fracture configurations and associated injuries, supporting its value for comprehensive lesion assessment. Mandibular ramus fractures were the most common injuries and were generally associated with favorable survival, although long-term dental complications were frequent.

papers.title: Fixation of proximal humeral Salter-Harris type 1 fractures in a 3-dimensionally printed skeletally immature canine bone model: a biomechanical assessment of fully threaded headless cannulated screws.
papers.authors: Hwang TW, Kang E, Kim JM, Kim HY
papers.abstract: To compare the biomechanical stability of 4 fixation techniques for proximal humeral physeal fractures in skeletally immature canines using 3-D-printed models. This experimental in vitro study was conducted from September 25, 2025, through April 22, 2026. To strictly control biological variability, identical 3-D-printed models of juvenile canine proximal humeral Salter-Harris type 1 fractures (CT-derived from a 6-month-old 26-kg Labrador Retriever) were evaluated across 4 groups: pin and tension band wire (group A), partially threaded cannulated screw (group B), fully threaded headless cannulated screw (FTHCS) alone (group C), and FTHCS with a 1.6-mm Kirschner (K)-wire (group D). Tensile loading was applied at 10 mm/min at 105° to simulate supraspinatus traction. Outcomes included loads at 1- and 2-mm displacements, maximum failure load, and failure modes. Twenty-four models were tested (n = 6/group). Group D exhibited significantly higher resistance at 1-mm (663.95 N) and 2-mm (1,080.33 N) displacements than other groups. At 1-mm displacement, group D outperformed groups C, A, and B (mean differences [MD]: 206.2 N, 380.6 N, and 405.7 N, respectively; P < .0083). Maximum failure load did not differ significantly. Group B failed via localized proximal crushing and subsidence, whereas FTHCS groups (C, D) preserved proximal integrity, failing distally. In this 3-D-printed model, FTHCS combined with a K-wire provided superior resistance to tensile displacement compared with other tested constructs. FTHCS augmented with a K-wire may offer a biomechanically robust alternative mitigating subhead bone collapse, providing sufficient standalone stability for early rehabilitation in immature canines.

papers.title: Most dogs transported to a veterinary teaching hospital are unrestrained during vehicular travel.
papers.authors: Steinolfson C, Odunayo A, Ng Z, Stone A, Domaracki C, Mandese W, Wuerz J, Griffin F, Schaub J, Rooks J, Okafor C
papers.abstract: To evaluate the frequency and type of vehicular restraint use in dogs transported to a veterinary teaching hospital and to identify factors associated with restraint use. This prospective, survey-based study was conducted at a veterinary teaching hospital from May 28 to August 2, 2024. Dog owners presenting their dog for emergency, sick, or wellness visits completed a questionnaire regarding transportation practices, including restraint use, type of restraint, travel duration, anxiety level, and administration of previsit pharmaceuticals. Logistic regression analysis was performed to assess associations between patient and transport variables and restraint use. A total of 195 of 533 (36.6%) dogs were transported using a restraint system, whereas 338 of 533 (63.4%) were unrestrained. The most common restraint type was a seat belt-based device. Each 1-kg increase in body weight was associated with a 3.3% decrease in the odds of restraint use (OR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.95 to 0.98). Administration of previsit pharmaceuticals (OR, 1.8; 95% CI, 1.02 to 3.01) and having pet insurance (OR, 1.5; 95% CI, 1.01 to 2.34) were associated with restraint use. Age, reason for visit, travel duration, anxiety level, and mode of transportation were not associated with restraint use. Most dogs in this population traveled unrestrained during vehicular transport. Restraint use was not associated with visit type, travel duration, anxiety level, or transportation mode. Increased veterinary client education may improve safe transport practices and reduce the risk of injury during vehicular travel.

papers.title: Targeted quantitative polymerase chain reaction-based bacterial and fecal metabolite markers show early stability in healthy puppies after 8 weeks of age.
papers.authors: Birk D, Weidinger AK, Schmidt T, Bachmann S, Spring I, Felten S, Meunier SM, Blake AB, Suchodolski JS, Unterer S
papers.abstract: To assess longitudinal stability of targeted quantitative PCR (qPCR)-based fecal microbial and metabolomic markers in healthy puppies from 8 weeks to 1 year of age. This prospective longitudinal cohort study was conducted at the Clinic for Small Animal Internal Medicine, Vetsuisse Faculty, University of Zurich, Switzerland, from August 2023 to January 2025. Clinically healthy client-owned puppies were sampled at 8 to 12 weeks, 16 weeks, 6 months, and 1 year. Eligible dogs had no gastrointestinal signs, no previous systemic antibiotics, and negative parasitology. Primary outcomes were the qPCR-based dysbiosis index, selected qPCR-targeted bacterial taxa, fecal bile acids, long-chain fatty acids, and sterols, quantified by mass spectrometry. Mixed-effects models assessed time point associations. 23 dogs contributed 62 fecal samples. Dysbiosis index values and most targeted bacterial taxa remained within reference intervals, with no significant longitudinal changes. Bacteroides spp abundance was lower at 8 to12 weeks than at 6 months (difference, -0.73 logDNA copies/g feces; 95% CI, -1.40 to -0.06; Tukey-adjusted P = .028). Secondary unconjugated bile acids dominated at all ages. The concentration of 12-oxo-lithocholic acid was lower at 16 weeks than at 1 year (ratio, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.14 to 0.79; Tukey-adjusted P = .007) but not after multiple-testing adjustment. Long-chain fatty acid and sterol profiles showed no age-related changes. The qPCR-based dysbiosis index and targeted microbial and metabolomic markers were largely stable from 8 weeks to 1 year, supporting early functional maturation of measured markers. These findings establish age-specific baseline information for fecal bacterial and metabolite markers, supporting interpretation in young dogs with gastrointestinal disease.

papers.title: Intramuscular tranexamic acid results in lower peak plasma concentrations but comparable systemic absorption to intravenous administration in healthy dogs.
papers.authors: Kwak EJ, Zersen K, Tucker C, Lavender C, Talbot C, Gustafson D, Hendry-Hofer T, Hall K
papers.abstract: To determine the pharmacokinetics of IM and IV tranexamic acid (TXA) in healthy dogs. There were 6 healthy client-owned dogs that received TXA (20 mg/kg) in a randomized crossover study design with a 6-week washout period between IM and IV administration. Venous blood samples were collected from baseline to 8 hours after injection. Plasma TXA concentrations were measured using LC-MS-MS. For IM administration, mean ± SD maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) was 46.8 ± 26.6 μg/mL, total area under the curve was 173.8 ± 25.0 μg/mL·h, time to Cmax was 1.6 ± 1.4 hours, half-life (t1/2) was 2.8 ± 2.1 hours, and bioavailability was 120.9 ± 10.0%. For IV administration, Cmax was 119.8 ± 17.6 μg/mL, total area under the curve was 143.3 ± 10.5 μg/mL·h, and t1/2 was 2.1 ± 1.8 hours. IM Cmax reached approximately 39% of IV Cmax and exhibited a 33% longer t1/2, consistent with slower absorption. Despite the lower Cmax, bioavailability was 120.9%, suggesting that IM TXA maintained a higher plasma concentration for a longer duration. Although the prolonged time to Cmax associated with IM administration may limit its use in patients requiring rapid intervention, it offers practical advantages when IV access is delayed, allowing prehospital treatment prior to definitive veterinary care. Further investigation into IM dosing protocols is needed before it can be recommended in clinical patients.

papers.title: A randomized controlled trial of intravenous magnesium sulfate shows no analgesic or anti-inflammatory benefit in dogs undergoing thoracolumbar disk herniation surgery.
papers.authors: Mallet G, Gaitero L, Sanchez A, James FMK, Wood G, Monteith G, Samarani F
papers.abstract: To investigate the analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects of intraoperative IV magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) continuous rate infusion in dogs undergoing thoracolumbar hemilaminectomy for intervertebral disk extrusion (IVDE). 30 client-owned dogs presented at the Ontario Veterinary College Health Sciences Centre were enrolled from October 2022 through October 2023. Prospective, randomized, double-blind, controlled clinical trial dogs received either MgSO4 (magnesium group) or an equal volume of saline (control group) intraoperatively. All dogs followed standardized anesthesia and analgesia protocols. The primary outcome measures were postoperative pain assessed using the Glasgow Composite Measure Pain Scale-Short Form at recovery and 4, 8, 12, and 24 hours after surgery and serum IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α concentrations measured preoperatively and 1 hour postoperatively to assess anti-inflammatory effects. Serum magnesium concentrations were measured as a secondary outcome to monitor for potential toxicity. There were no significant differences in the pain scores and the IL-6 levels between the 2 groups. Tumor necrosis factor-α levels were undetectable in most dogs and were not analyzed statistically. The placebo group did not significantly require additional pain medication. Magnesium sulfate administration provided smoother anesthesia recoveries. Serum magnesium concentrations were significantly higher in the magnesium group immediately and 1 hour postoperatively but not at 24 hours. Intraoperative IV MgSO4 did not significantly improve postoperative analgesia or decrease inflammation compared to placebo in dogs undergoing surgery for IVDE. There was no significant evidence to use intraoperative IV MgSO4 to improve postoperative analgesia or decrease inflammation in dogs undergoing surgery for IVDE. However, no adverse effects were reported.

papers.title: Treatment of Refractory Vomiting With Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine in Two Dogs and a Cat: A Cases Series.
papers.authors: Wang X, Yang L, Ma W
papers.abstract: Refractory vomiting in dogs and cats is a common clinical condition in small animal practice, typically characterized by recurrent vomiting, belching and related symptoms, which is a great challenge to veterinarians. According to Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine (TCVM), this condition is primarily attributed to dysfunction of the spleen and stomach in transformation and transportation, leading to the upward rebellion of stomach Qi. Derived from the Shang Han Lun (Treatise on Cold Damage), Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction functions to direct rebellious Qi downward, resolve phlegm, tonify Qi and harmonize the stomach. It is mainly indicated for conditions resulting from stomach Qi counter flow. In this report, three cases of refractory vomiting in two dogs and a cat diagnosed as stomach Qi rebellion according to TCVM were treated with modified Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction based on syndrome differentiation. The results showed that all three cases achieved favourable therapeutic outcomes. These findings suggest that, for refractory vomiting caused by stomach Qi rebellion in dogs and cats, individualized treatment with modified Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction based on specific clinical presentations can achieve stable and reliable efficacy.

papers.title: Neglected but Not Harmless: Characterising Nonantibiotic Antimicrobial Use in Small Animal Practices in Colombia.
papers.authors: Correa-Valencia NM, Arango-Arcila S, Mendoza NK, Sierra-Zapata DA, Guzmán-Mejía VA, Carmona Ramírez A, Restrepo Salazar JG
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing global threat, yet stewardship efforts have largely overlooked nonantibiotic antimicrobials (NAAs), despite their widespread use and potential role in resistance selection and environmental persistence. Evidence on NAA use in small animal practice, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, remains scarce. To characterise patterns of NAA use and assess prescription quality in dogs, cats, and other small animal species treated at a university veterinary hospital in Colombia. A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted using veterinary prescription records from January to December 2022. A systematic sampling approach (first four prescriptions per day) yielded 1460 prescriptions, of which 731 involved NAAs. Data on animal characteristics, consultation type, and prescription details were extracted, and NAAs were classified by pharmacological group, pharmaceutical form, and route of administration. Bivariate analyses were performed to identify stewardship-relevant patterns. NAAs accounted for a substantial proportion of prescriptions, predominantly in dogs (91.5%). Topical antiseptics (49.9%), external antiparasitics (21.3%), and internal antiparasitics (17.1%) were the most frequently used classes. Cutaneous (58.7%) and oral (41.3%) routes predominated, with chlorhexidine as the most common active ingredient (22%). Dermatology consultations were more likely to involve topical antiseptics (55.0% vs. 45.5%; OR = 1.47; 95% CI 1.06-2.02), whereas general consultations showed substantially higher odds of internal antiparasitic use (OR = 5.58; 95% CI 2.93-10.62). While 67.6% of treatments adhered to standard duration, only 38% matched recommended dosing, and key prescription elements were frequently missing, including International Nonproprietary Names (7%), concentration (12.2%), and complete administration instructions (5.5%). NAAs are widely used in small animal practice but are frequently prescribed with incomplete documentation and suboptimal dosing practices. These findings highlight a critical and underrecognised gap in antimicrobial stewardship and support the need to formally integrate NAAs into surveillance, regulatory frameworks, and stewardship interventions under a One Health approach.

papers.title: Efficacy of Oral Lotilaner in Controlling Clinical Signs in Cats Naturally Infested With Lynxacarus radovskyi.
papers.authors: da Mota de Magalhães Y, Marques DM, Christ LX, Campos DR, Fernandes JI
papers.abstract: Lynxacarus radovskyi is a pilicolous mite that may cause pruritus and coat or skin lesions in cats. Evidence regarding the efficacy of oral lotilaner for the treatment of feline lynxacariasis remains limited. To evaluate the parasitological and clinical efficacy of oral lotilaner in cats naturally infested with L. radovskyi. Twenty client-owned cats naturally infested with L. radovskyi. A prospective, longitudinal, parallel-group study was conducted with 20 cats allocated to a treated group (n = 10) or an untreated control group (n = 10). Treated cats received oral lotilaner on Day (D)0 and D30. Parasitological assessment was performed every 7 days from D0 to D63 using trichograms obtained from three anatomical sites and scored using a semi-quantitative scale. Pruritus and clinical lesion scores also were recorded. Treatment with lotilaner resulted in a significant reduction in parasitological scores from D7 onwards (p = 0.0033), while untreated cats remained persistently infested. Mite-count reduction increased progressively, reaching 98.0% at D35 and 100% from D42 onwards after the second administration. Pruritus and clinical lesion scores also decreased significantly compared with baseline (p = 0.0117). Oral lotilaner administered twice (D0 and D30) was effective for the treatment of feline lynxacariasis under natural infestation conditions, resulting in rapid parasite reduction and significant clinical improvement.

papers.title: A species comparison of videofloroscopic metrics of swallowing in healthy dogs and cats.
papers.authors: Grobman M, Luciani E, Reinero C
papers.abstract: Videofluoroscopic swallow studies (VFSS) are the criterion standard for diagnosing dysphagia in veterinary species. However, a lack of normative swallowing variables in cats hinders assessment of cats with potential aerodigestive disease. Species variation in swallowing could lead to over- and under-interpretation of findings on VFSS, resulting in misdiagnosis. Compare differences in objective swallowing metrics between cats and dogs using VFSS. We hypothesize that cats will show differences in objective swallowing metrics on VFSS compared with dogs. Healthy adult cats (n = 13) and dogs (n = 12) without clinical signs (CS) of respiratory or alimentary disease. Prospective, cross-sectional study. Cats and dogs underwent standardized VFSS. All were evaluated according to 16 objective metrics and compared between species. Between group comparisons were made using Mann-Whitney-U, T-test, or Fischer's exact test with a P < .05 significance level for all comparisons. Cats had significantly longer inter-swallow intervals, shorter pharyngeal transit times, and more pharyngeal swallows to generate primary peristalsis compared with dogs (P < .05). Cats were also more likely to have esophageal volume accumulation and slowing of distal esophageal transit time compared with dogs (P < .05). Physiologic reflux was identified in 2 (15.4%) cats vs 6 (50%) dogs. Pathologic penetration-aspiration (P-A score: 7; aspiration without attempt to cough) was found in 1 cat despite a lack of respiratory or alimentary CS. Species variation should be considered when interpreting VFSS. In 1 cat, occult tracheal aspiration of contrast (P-A score 7) was detected without accompanying cough.

papers.title: Rapid test performance for the diagnosis of canine visceral leishmaniasis using blood, serum, and saliva.
papers.authors: Lamattina D, Sánchez-Fernández C, Depasquino AF, Laiño MA, Siccardi FM, Salomón OD
papers.abstract: A key aspect of controlling canine visceral leishmaniasis (CVL) is the availability of accurate diagnostic tools capable of reaching most of the population. In endemic areas with socially vulnerable populations, facilitating rapid CVL diagnosis by reducing sampling difficulties and diagnostic costs could provide substantial benefits. This study evaluated the performance of the Kalazar Detect™ Canine Rapid Test for CVL diagnosis using blood, serum, and saliva samples, and compared the results among sample types and with PCR detection in lymph nodes. Samples were collected from 100 dogs. Prevalence detected by the rapid diagnostic tests (RDT) was 21% using blood and serum and 17% using saliva, whereas PCR detected a prevalence of 46%. Agreement between serum and blood-based RDTs was 100%, while comparison between serum/blood and saliva showed a kappa index of 0.87, indicating almost perfect agreement. Using PCR as the reference standard, RDTs on serum and blood showed a sensitivity of 0.39 and specificity of 0.94, whereas saliva-based RDT showed a sensitivity of 0.33 and specificity of 0.96. The low sensitivity of the RDTs currently used by the National Leishmaniasis Program indicate that an additional diagnostic method should be incorporated into CVL surveillance in endemic areas. Nevertheless, our results suggest that saliva may be a suitable sample for the Kalazar Detect Canine Rapid Test, as it is easy to collect, less expensive, and less invasive. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate the performance of this RDT for CVL diagnosis using saliva samples.

papers.title: Medial Tympanic Membrane Displacement in Five Dogs Resembling Tympanic Membrane Retraction in Humans.
papers.authors: Botelho CB, Ferreira TS, Gmyterco VC, Alves C, Nuttall T, de Farias MR, Fernandes JI
papers.abstract: Five dogs with head tilt, ataxia, incoordination or deafness without a history of otitis externa (OE) were diagnosed with otitis media by computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Otoendoscopy showed possible tympanic membrane retraction with opaque, fibrotic membranes and advanced imaging showed middle ear involvement. The clinical significance requires further investigation.

papers.title: Pyelonephritis in cats and dogs - a scoping review.
papers.authors: Pelander L, Ekstrand C, Scahill K
papers.abstract: There is a lack of consensus regarding the diagnosis and treatment of bacterial pyelonephritis (PN) in dogs and cats. The aim of this scoping review was to increase knowledge by describing published scientific literature on the subject, specifically to collate definitions and diagnostic criteria, antimicrobial regimens, reported outcomes, and to identify knowledge gaps. A structured search was performed of the bibliographic databases Biosis, CAB Abstracts, Medline, Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus. We included 176 original studies written in English or German that reported on any aspect of spontaneous PN (risk factors, signalment, history, clinical findings, diagnostic criteria, treatment, prognosis, and outcome) in cats or dogs. Three types of PN were identified in the literature: histologically diagnosed PN, clinically diagnosed PN, and pyonephrosis. Multiple information gaps regarding clinical aspects of PN in dogs and cats were detected. There were no universally accepted clinical criteria for clinical diagnosis of PN and no clinical trials evaluating antimicrobial or other treatment options. Information about short-term outcomes for dogs and cats with PN was scarce, and there were no data regarding long-term outcomes. More information regarding all aspects of clinical PN in dogs and cats is needed.The study protocol was registered prospectively in 2023 ( https://syreaf.org/protocols/ ).

papers.title: Chondroprotective Effect of PCSO-524 (Green-Lipped Mussel Extraction) Application Evaluated by Ultrasonography in Pomeranian and Chihuahua With Medial Patellar Luxation Grade II.
papers.authors: Soontornvipart K, Sathienbumrungkit R
papers.abstract: This research evaluated the chondroprotective efficacy of PCSO-524 in dogs with osteoarthritis (OA) secondary to medial patellar luxation (MPL) using ultrasonography - a non-invasive technique recommended for early OA detection. Animals: 25 dogs total (21 with MPL grade II, 50 stifle joints evaluated) divided into three groups, including control group: 10 dogs receiving placebo, treatment group: 11 dogs receiving PCSO-524 (50 mg daily) and normal group: 4 healthy dogs (reference) Duration: 16 weeks Evaluations: Lameness scores, blood profiles, ultrasonographic findings, radiographic assessments and owner questionnaires at baseline, weeks 2, 4, 8, 12 and 16. The treatment group showed significant improvement in lameness scores within 8 weeks. The cartilage lesions improved within 4 weeks of PCSO-524 administration. Synovial fluid scores decreased significantly by week 4 in the treatment group. Radiographic OA scores improved mildly at 12 weeks in the treatment group versus progression in the control group. Owners observed better gait and quality of life by week 2. No adverse effects on blood chemistry or organ function. PCSO-524 demonstrates effective cartilage protection in dogs with OA secondary to MPL, with improvements in clinical signs, ultrasonographic findings and radiographic outcomes. For dogs that cannot undergo surgical correction, PCSO-524 supplementation combined with quadriceps muscle training and environmental management is recommended for improved quality of life.

papers.title: Occurrence and antimicrobial resistance of Acinetobacter baumannii in cats, veterinary hospital environments and medical wastes in Bangladesh.
papers.authors: Hasan M, Lira SA, Islam A, Miti AA, Rahman A, Suchy SA, Jahan I, Ali SB, Parvin MS, Islam MT
papers.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii presence in veterinary hospitals and companion animals is still poorly investigated despite its significance. The present study aimed to investigate the prevalence, antimicrobial resistance patterns, and resistance genes of A. baumannii in cats, veterinary hospital environments, and veterinary medical wastes in Bangladesh. Samples were collected from oral, rectal, and wound swabs of cats (n = 100) attending ten veterinary hospitals, as well as from environmental surfaces (n = 111) and wastes (n = 61) generated within these facilities. Isolates were identified by PCR targeting 16S rRNA (genus) and bla OXA-51-like (species) genes; antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed by disk diffusion and broth microdilution following CLSI standards, and resistance genes (bla OXA-23-like , bla NDM-1 ) were screened by PCR. A high prevalence of A. baumannii was observed in cats (37%), while 26.1% in environmental samples and 21.3% in waste samples. Apparently sick cats had significantly higher prevalence (p = 0.049) than apparently healthy cats. All isolates were imipenem resistant, consistent with carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB). High resistance was also observed against cefotaxime and ceftriaxone. Multidrug resistance (MDR) was detected in 26.7%, 37.9%, and 30.8% of isolates from cats, environmental, and waste sources, respectively. The bla OXA-23-like gene was detected in only two cat isolates, whereas bla NDM was identified in one cat isolate and one environmental isolate. In conclusion, these findings identify cats, which live in close proximity to humans, as a possible CRAB reservoir, and veterinary hospital environments and waste as potential sources of persistence and dissemination, raising concern for zoonotic spread and underscoring occupational and public health risk.

papers.title: EXPRESS:Management of Distal Hindlimb Injuries in Cats Using an Exvet External Skeletal Fixation System: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Uygur S, Dogan A, Yardımcı C, Ulusan S, Beale BS, Immler M, Vidoni B, Schnabl-Feichter E
papers.abstract: To evaluate the clinical use of an Exvet external skeletal fixation (ESF) system applied using minimally invasive techniques for the management of distal hindlimb injuries in cats. Cats with distal hindlimb injuries treated using the Exvet Tarsal Fixator (ETF) at four institutions between September 2022 and January 2026 were included. Data collected included fracture type, surgical approach, postoperative complications and additional treatments, time to first limb use, time to fixator removal, radiographic findings, and clinical outcome. Of 73 cats evaluated, 35 cats with 36 distal hindlimb injuries met the inclusion criteria. Twenty-four cats (68.6%) were managed with a closed reduction, while 11 cats (31.4%) were managed with a limited open surgical fashion. Thirty-two of 35 cats (91.4%) started weight bearing immediately after surgery. Complications were recorded in 7 of 35 cases (20.0%), of which 5 cases (14.3%) were classified as minor and 2 cases (5.7%) as major complications. At a mean ESF removal time of 34 days (median: 28 days; range: 21-56 days), a full functional outcome was achieved in 25 of 35 cases (71.4%), while 10 cases (28.6%) showed an acceptable functional outcome. The ETF is an anatomically designed ESF implant specifically developed for feline distal hindlimb injuries. The findings of this multicenter retrospective study support its safe and effective use for the management of feline distal hindlimb injuries.

papers.title: EXPRESS: BENEFITS OF CONTRAST-ENHANCED COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY OVER PLAIN COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY FOR HEAD TRAUMA IN 41 CATS.
papers.journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
papers.authors: Mariaud V, Arinal P, Masson A, Mortier J
papers.abstract: The aim of this study is to evaluate whether contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) provides clinically useful information beyond Plain computed tomography (PCT) in cats with head trauma, and whether this benefit is influenced by the radiologist's level of experience. Forty-one cats that underwent head CT with both pre- and post-contrast sequences were included. Images were independently reviewed by three radiologists with different experience levels, assessing extracranial soft tissue injuries, bone fractures, and intracranial abnormalities. Intra- and interobserver agreements were analyzed using Cohen's kappa statistics. Substantial to almost perfect agreement was obtained for extracranial soft tissue injuries and bone fractures. The most commonly fractured sites were the temporomandibular joints, hard palate, mandibular bones, and pterygoid bones. For intracranial lesions such as hemorrhage and cerebral edema, intra- and interobserver agreements were low and variable, regardless of contrast use or reviewer experience. There was no significant difference found between PCT and CECT for any of the three categories. These results suggest that contrast medium injection is not useful for assessment of bone fractures and extracranial soft tissue and that computed tomography of the head is poorly reliable for intracranial lesions in cats presented for trauma.

papers.title: Feline-Derived Lactiplantibacillus plantarum -Aloe Vera Polysaccharide Hydrogel as a Topical Control Strategy for Staphylococcus pseudintermedius -Infected Wounds.
papers.authors: Chen Q, Dong H, Wang W, Wang H, Yao J, Ma M, Zhu S, Zhu L, Du Z, Xia Z, Xiong W
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus pseudintermedius (SP) is an important opportunistic pathogen in companion animals, and the increasing prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant strains highlights the need for alternative approaches to local infection control. This study evaluated a topical hydrogel containing feline-derived Lactiplantibacillus plantarum ZYpet-014 and Aloe vera polysaccharides (AVEs) for the treatment of SP-infected wounds. AVEs promoted LP growth and organic-acid production and improved short-term LP viability within the carbomer hydrogel. The LP+AVE-hydrogel inhibited planktonic SP growth and biofilm formation in vitro and caused pronounced morphological disruption of SP cells. Therapeutic efficacy was further evaluated using a full-thickness murine wound model challenged with SP. LP+AVE treatment accelerated wound closure, reaching 95.75% by day 14, while qualitative histological observations suggested improved tissue organization and differences in collagen-associated staining patterns. Treatment was also associated with reduced TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 levels and increased IL-4, IL-10, TGF-β1, and serum VEGF concentrations. In wound tissues, LP+AVE treatment decreased CD80 and increased CD206 immunoreactivity, consistent with a shift in macrophage-associated responses toward a reparative profile. Moreover, 16S rRNA gene sequencing showed reduced relative abundance of Staphylococcus and increased relative abundance of Lactobacillus in treated wounds. Together, these findings demonstrate antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against SP in vitro, accompanied by improved wound healing, modulation of inflammatory responses, and changes in wound microbial composition in vivo, although direct reduction in SP burden in wound tissue remains to be established.

papers.title: Exploratory Evaluation of Refractometric, Biochemical, and Body Weight Change Parameters for Diagnosing Failure of Passive Transfer in Puppies.
papers.authors: Kara H, Şenel Y, Kaya U, Güven M, Şenol A
papers.abstract: Failure of passive transfer (FPT) is an important determinant of survival in neonatal puppies. Practical indirect indicators that could serve as alternatives to measuring serum immunoglobulin G (IgG) have not yet been adequately characterized. In this exploratory study, 76 Turkish Kangal puppies aged 48 ± 4 h, born to 12 dams (mean age 40.2 months) were evaluated. Serum IgG measured by ELISA was the reference method, with values below 2.3 g/L classified as FPT. Whole-blood, fresh-serum, and frozen-thawed serum Brix values were evaluated together with serum total protein, albumin, globulin, gamma-glutamyl transferase, canine parvovirus antibody levels, and percentage change in body weight from birth to sampling, using receiver operating characteristic analysis. FPT was identified in six puppies (7.9%). The area under the curve (AUC) values for total protein, globulin, and percentage change in body weight were 0.986, 0.981, and 0.948, respectively, with the associated cutoffs considered exploratory; each detected all six cases with 82.9-94.3% specificity. Fresh-serum Brix showed moderate discrimination (AUC: 0.771), whereas whole-blood Brix was inconclusive (AUC: 0.432). Total protein, globulin, and early body weight change are promising screening indicators for detecting FPT. However, because of the limited number of cases, their cutoffs should be validated in larger populations, including other breeds, before clinical use.

papers.title: Cardiac Vagal Decoupling in Canine Anesthesia: A Physiological Concept for Graded Vasopressor Titration.
papers.authors: Nagahama S
papers.abstract: During general anesthesia in dogs, vasopressor-induced increases in mean arterial pressure (MAP) may be partly opposed by reflex sinus slowing. Subsequent administration of atropine or another antimuscarinic may cause an abrupt increase in sinus rate; when vascular tone is already elevated, this increase may in turn contribute to an abrupt or excessive MAP rise. This article examines cardiac vagal decoupling, defined as reduced vagally mediated muscarinic restraint at the sinoatrial node, as a physiological concept for graded vasopressor titration. The hypothesis is that reducing this restraint before substantial vasopressor escalation, followed by MAP-guided dose adjustments, may permit more graded pressure control: reaching and maintaining a specified MAP range with fewer abrupt or excessive pressure increases. Canine studies support muscarinic control of sinus rate, baroreflex responses during anesthesia, and modification of vasopressor responses by prior antimuscarinic administration. These findings support components of the proposed concept, but whether it improves graded MAP titration has not been directly tested. The article contrasts the two hemodynamic patterns, evaluates the supporting evidence, and considers the limits of the hypothesis. Effects of such titration on cardiac output, tissue perfusion, and clinical outcomes require separate evaluation.

papers.title: CT-Clinical Dissociation and Focal Obstruction in Feline Chronic Rhinosinusitis: A Pilot Study.
papers.authors: Lee G, Chang J, Lee J, Song KH
papers.abstract: Feline chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is common and difficult to manage, and the relationship between computed tomography (CT) findings and clinical severity remains unclear. This exploratory retrospective pilot study included 10 cats with chronic upper respiratory signs for at least 4 weeks that underwent CT of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses at a single referral hospital. Newly developed, unvalidated semiquantitative scores graded CT severity (0-12) and clinical severity (0-12), and cats were grouped into four provisional clinicoradiologic patterns using integrated CT, clinical, and cytologic findings and, where available, microbiologic findings. CT scores ranged from 2 to 10 (median 8.0) and clinical scores from 4 to 11 (median 6.5), without a consistent monotonic association (Spearman r s = 0.250, 95% bootstrap confidence interval (CI) -0.558 to 0.885, p = 0.486). The provisional patterns were active/exudative ( n = 2), structural/remodeling ( n = 4), obstructive ( n = 3), and immune/mucosal ( n = 1). Focal obstruction defined both the obstructive pattern and the conceptual surgical candidacy categories, so their overlap is by design; of interest is that cats with the highest CT scores did not necessarily have focal obstruction. No cat underwent surgery. These hypothesis-generating findings require validation in larger prospective studies with validated scores.

papers.title: Regulatory Science for Veterinary Therapeutic Innovation: A Comparative Analysis of Drug Development Incentives Within the One Health Framework.
papers.authors: Hong S, Lee SM
papers.abstract: Rapid advances in antiviral therapeutics, targeted biologics, RNA medicines, and precision veterinary medicine are generating unprecedented scientific opportunities for veterinary healthcare, yet translation of these innovations into approved veterinary products remains disproportionately slow. This review employs a comparative regulatory science framework to identify the regulatory and economic determinants of this innovation gap across four jurisdictions-FDA-CVM (US), EMA-CVMP (EU), PMDA/MAFF (Japan), and APVMA (Australia)-and to compare existing incentive instruments and identify the regulatory gaps between them. Two illustrative case studies, GS-441524 for feline infectious peritonitis and canine osteosarcoma therapeutics, illustrate how the absence of breakthrough pathways, limitations in the practical translation of Minor Use/Minor Species (MUMS) eligibility, and unresolved intellectual property barriers can suppress development investment. The multi-jurisdictional analysis indicates that this innovation gap is evident across the jurisdictions examined and is consistent with differences in the availability and strength of regulatory incentives, though scientific and market factors likely also contribute. Policy reforms are proposed, including a Veterinary Breakthrough Drug Designation, a One Health Innovation Designation with enhanced exclusivity, adaptive regulatory pathways, and strengthened VICH harmonization. Additionally, the regulatory preparedness for advanced veterinary therapeutics-including gene therapies, mRNA-based vaccines, and cell-based products-is examined as a critical frontier. The analysis highlights the role of regulatory science in translating emerging veterinary therapeutics into clinical practice within the One Health framework.

papers.title: Dietary Pieris japonica Leaf Powder Enhances Hepatic Antioxidant Capacity, Modulates Cecal Microbiota, and Improves Eggshell Thickness in Laying Hens.
papers.authors: Wu Y, Chen J, Chen F, Liu Y, Lian J, Tang Y, He B, Lin Q
papers.abstract: Oxidative stress and intestinal health are critical factors that are closely linked to the production performance and physiological status of laying hens. This work assessed how dietary incorporation of Pieris japonica leaf powder (PJP) shapes egg quality attributes, hepatic antioxidant defence, gut tissue morphology, and cecal microbial community profiles in layers. A total of 360 healthy 56-week-old Hy-Line Brown layers were randomly assigned to four treatments, each containing six replicate pens housing 15 birds apiece. Animals received basal feeds containing 0.00% (control), 0.05%, 0.10%, or 0.20% PJP throughout the 10-week experimental run that including a 2-week adaptation period. Relative to the control group, diets with 0.05% PJP significantly increased eggshell thickness ( p < 0.05). Hepatic total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC), catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px) were significantly elevated in PJP-supplemented groups ( p < 0.05). The 0.10% PJP addition improved duodenal villus-height-to-crypt-depth ratio (V/C). Regarding cecal microbiota, 0.10% PJP reduced the Simpson index while elevating Collinsella relative abundance ( p < 0.05). Noticeably, the 0.20% supplementation exerted adverse effects on egg-related indices. Correlation analysis indicated that cecal microbiota was closely associated with hepatic antioxidant indices and eggshell-related indicators. In summary, dietary PJP inclusion may improve the eggshell thickness of eggs from laying hens by enhancing host antioxidant defense, reshaping the composition of cecal microbial communities. It was reported that 0.10% PJP supplementation yielded the most favorable comprehensive responses under the conditions adopted within this trial.

papers.title: Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia with Secondary Pseudomonas aeruginosa Infection in a Dog: Endoscopic and Diagnostic Findings.
papers.authors: Maggi G, Pirgher F, De Lorenzi D, Aresu L, Marchesi MC
papers.abstract: A 7-month-old, 3.6-kg, intact male Dachshund was presented with a lifelong history of chronic respiratory signs. Multiple courses of antimicrobial therapy resulted in partial or complete clinical improvement, followed by recurrence after treatment discontinuation. To investigate the underlying cause of the persistent respiratory disease, rhino-tracheobronchoscopy was performed. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid and respiratory mucosal biopsy specimens were collected for cytological, histopathological, and ultrastructural evaluation. Cytological examination of BAL fluid revealed septic neutrophilic inflammation, and bacterial culture yielded P. aeruginosa. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) identified ultrastructural abnormalities of the ciliary axoneme in 50% of the examined respiratory cilia. Based on these findings, primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) was diagnosed. PCD is a rare congenital disorder characterized by structural and functional abnormalities of motile cilia, resulting in impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent respiratory infections. This case highlights the diagnostic value of a detailed clinical history, endoscopic examination, and TEM in dogs with suspected PCD.

papers.title: Pulmonary Neoplasms with Pleuropulmonary Blastoma-like Features in Two Young Labrador Retrievers: Clinicopathological, Molecular and Comparative Characterisation.
papers.authors: van der Weyden L, Francis BA, Olson DR, Schultz KAP, Di Palma S, Ryan T, Kamieniarz K, Miguel-Garces M, Thompson L, Jones R, Nix C, Haugland S, Ortiz AL
papers.abstract: Pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB) is a rare, paediatric, mesenchymal, pulmonary neoplasm that can be highly aggressive. To date, there are only two reports of PPB in animals. We describe the finding of pulmonary neoplasms with PPB-like features in two unrelated Labrador Retrievers. Both dogs presented with acute dyspnoea, pneumothorax and pulmonary lesions. Treatment consisted of emergency thoracostomy tube placement followed by lung lobectomy. At follow-up, one dog experienced no recurrence 20 months post-surgery, whereas recurrence developed in the second dog 2 years postoperatively. Histopathological examination revealed spindle-shaped neoplastic cells with blastematous-to-sarcomatous appearance, associated with cystic spaces lined by non-neoplastic respiratory epithelium. Immunohistochemistry showed that the neoplastic cells were positive for mesenchymal markers but negative for epithelial and neuroendocrine markers, with some tumour cells showing desmin positivity, supportive of myogenic differentiation, possibly compatible with rhabdomyoblastic differentiation. Genome profiling revealed a heterogeneous somatic landscape. No pathogenic somatic or germline DICER1 variants were found. We compared these findings with those reported in human PPB. This is the first comprehensive analysis of pulmonary neoplasms with PPB-like features in animals, and reveals parallels with PPB in humans, further supporting the 'One Medicine' approach.

papers.title: Prostaglandin-Endoperoxide Synthase 2 (PTGS2) Expression Is Increased in Chronic Asymptomatic Orchitis in the Dog.
papers.authors: Packeiser EM, Körber H, Morawietz J, Goericke-Pesch S
papers.abstract: Chronic asymptomatic orchitis (CAO) in dogs lacks effective treatment options. To elucidate the involvement of prostaglandin endoperoxide synthase 2 (PTGS2), associated with inflammation and physiological steroidogenesis, testicular PTGS2 and StAR gene (via RT-qPCR) and protein expression (via immunohistochemistry) were analyzed in 11 canine CAO samples and compared to five normospermic control group (CG) samples. The percentage of immunopositive area (PIA) and mean gray scale (MGS) intensity were evaluated in the interstitial and tubular compartments. In CAO, PTGS2 and StAR gene expression levels were significantly increased compared to CG ( p < 0.001 and p = 0.0034). Leydig cells and some peritubular cells stained immunopositive for PTGS2 and StAR and Sertoli cells positive for PTGS2. PIA and MGS for PTGS2 differed significantly between groups in the interstitial (PIA: p < 0.0001; MGS: p = 0.0051) and tubular (PIA: p = 0.0006; MGS: p = 0.0413) compartments. For StAR, PIA, but not MGS, was significantly higher in CAO ( p = 0.0010). Except for PTGS2 gene expression, higher degrees of spermatogenetic impairment correlated with more prominent expression changes. This study demonstrates an association between increased PTGS2 expression and CAO. Further research is needed to investigate potential clinical benefits of selective PTGS2 inhibitors.

papers.title: Perioperative Glycemic Changes Following Partial Pancreatectomy for a Pancreatic Islet Cell Neoplasm in a Dog: A Case Report.
papers.authors: Choi CH, Kim JW, Park MS, Cho JS, You DH, Kim JH, Eom KD, Kim HY, Kim JM
